News.title: Cops probing murder of celebrity plastic surgeon in Marbella identify woman suspected of ordering hit
News.content:
DOCTOR HIT Cops probing murder of celebrity plastic surgeon in Marbella identify woman suspected of ordering hit







Next

COPS investigating the murder of a celebrity plastic surgeon have identified a woman they suspect of ordering his execution.

Dr Alexander Aslani, 57, whose clients included Towie’s Chloe Sims, was gunned down at his Marbella clinic on Wednesday.

Detectives believe a furious patient may have hired a hitman after a row over cosmetic surgery.

An 18-year-old Swede arrested on Thursday has admitted shooting the surgeon, according to Spanish sources.



Police are now trying to find out who hired him and how much he was paid.

A woman is said to have sent Aslani angry messages demanding a refund and threatening him just hours before he was killed.

Her partner had also allegedly threatened staff at the clinic days earlier.

Aslani’s clinic claimed to have carried out more than 14,000 operations, but the surgeon also faced complaints from former patients, including one who accused him of botching three procedures.

Cops have ruled out an earlier theory that Aslani was killed in revenge for a patient dying during surgery, after finding no evidence of any such death.

The Swedish teenager was arrested at a holiday apartment in Benalmádena as he prepared to flee Spain.

Aslani, known for his Brazilian butt lift operations, was shot several times by a masked gunman who walked into his office.

News.title: My pal Ranulph Fiennes ‘shouldn’t be in a care home’ Jeremy Clarkson blasts, saying the idea ‘fills me with despair’
News.content:
TOP GEAR PAL My pal Ranulph Fiennes ‘shouldn’t be in a care home’ Jeremy Clarkson blasts, saying the idea ‘fills me with despair’







Next

JEREMY Clarkson has said his life-long pal Sir Ranulph Fiennes shouldn’t be in a care home and the idea fills him with “despair”.

The 82-year-old world famous explorer has not been seen in public for two years and reportedly even his actor cousin Joseph Fiennes had to sneak secretly in to see him.



The former presenter of Top Gear, 66, said “Ran” was “by far the most memorable“ guest on the motoring show.

Normally on the show, guests were given a slot lasting eight to 10 minutes, Sir Ranulph’s interview ran for 17.



Even the audience were asked what they wanted to see, a road test of the Renault Clio or the interview. Sir Ranulph won the day.

Along with extraordinary tales of how he’d sawn off his own fingers and how he lost his toes, he also told about his days in the SAS.



He had stolen some explosives so that he could blow up a dam that had been built by Twentieth Century Fox in order to make Doctor Dolittle.

Jeremy added that Sir Ranulph had become a family friend when his mum had made a soft toy incarnation of his dog Bothie.



The presenter of Clarkson’s Farm wrote in The Times: “That’s why I’ve been sad over the last few weeks to learn of his current problems.

“But there’s more to it than that. A man like that should not be in a bloody care home.

“The idea of him sitting there doing beetle drives and eating fish fingers fills me with despair.”

Sir Ranulph is being illegally kept in care homes under fake names by his wife, it is claimed.

Earlier this year a care watchdog found Sir Ranulph – who was diagnosed with Parkinson’s – was being deprived of his liberty unlawfully.



Several friends and family members are now contemplating a legal challenge to Ms Millington-Cotes’ guardianship, the Telegraph reports.

Concerns over his whereabouts emerged after the former explorer failed to attend a Royal Geographical Society gala evening celebrating his life on October 23, 2024.

He instead appeared in a brief pre-recorded video – and has not been seen in public since.

It’s alleged Sir Ranulph spent time at a care home in London last year where his wife allegedly asked visitors to sign non-disclosure agreements before they could see him.

He was later moved to care facilities in Wales and Cheshire.

News.title: Two Ole Miss students found dead on same day ‘bought Kratom pills days before’
News.content:
DEADLY DRUG Two Ole Miss students found dead on same day ‘bought Kratom pills days before’







Next

TWO students found dead in separate incidents at the University of Mississippi had bought Kratom pills days before, investigators believe.

It comes as their cause of death was revealed in court on Friday during a court hearing involving two men accused of selling drugs at a smoke shop near the college’s campus.



The college’s student newspaper identified the undergraduate students as Aidan Hamilton, 18, and Robert Strang, 20.

Both were found dead in separate incidents at the University of Mississippi on September 21.



A defence lawyer for one of the two men accused of selling narcotics told the court one of the students died from a combination of substances, including cough syrup, Action5 News reported.

The other student died from inhalation asphyxiation, meaning breathing in toxic gases, the attorney said.



Aidan was a freshman from Englewood, Colorado, and Robert a junior from Atlanta, Georgia.

Investigators say both students had three kratom-related substances in their systems.

They included mitragynine, MGM-15 and MGPI.

Kratom is a supplement sold at gas stations that’s advertised as an energy booster and mood lifter but has no legitimate medical use.



Investigators think Aidan bought pills from Puffs Vape, Tobacco and Beer Store in Oxford in the days before his death, according to court records.

Robert reportedly bought similar pills from another shop around 20 miles away.

An undercover informant visited the first store, cops said.

A worker there confirmed the store sold the pills and warned them to be careful because people were dying from them, according to an arrest affidavit.

Cops later raided the store and seized around 500 units of kratom and kratom-like products.



They also seized suspected THC products.

A narcotics agent told the court that one of the students had been found dead in a dorm with white foam around his mouth.

They said the second student, found off campus just an hour later, had the same white foam.

Two drug store workers have been hit with federal drug charges linked to the investigation.

The Lafayette County Metro Narcotics team previously stressed they were conducting two separate death investigations, adding “we have no confirmed evidence indicating that the two deaths are connected.”



Authorities said they did “not have confirmed information indicating that kratom or any other substance was a contributing factor in either death.”

Local coroner Glenn Coleman told the Clarion Ledger that autopsies and toxicology tests have been ordered for Hamilton and Strang, and results are expected in two to three weeks.

Kratom, an addictive herbal extract that comes from the leaves of an evergreen tree called Mitragyna speciosa, is legal in parts of Mississippi, but is restricted in Lafayette County.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

There have been several reported cases of deaths involving kratom, as it is possible to overdose on it, but typically an overdose happens when it is mixed with other drugs or substances.

Healthcare providers have raised concerns over the use of kratom in recent years as the supplement is not standardized, and therefore the potency can vary between brands and batches.

News.title: Green Party may have been captured by ‘extremists and racists’, warns top party MP after Polanski skips crucial vote
News.content:
Next

THE GREENS may have been captured by “extremists and racists”, a senior party MP has warned.

Zack Polanski’s party has been plunged into civil war after they passed a motion saying “Zionism is racism” – effectively demanding the end of the Israeli state.



Mr Polanski is facing questions over his leadership after he skipped the crucial vote – and then failed to win the Kings Cross St Pancras by-election.

Green MP Ellie Chowns slammed Mr Polanski’s “lack of leadership” in an interview with the BBC.



Asked repeatedly if the party had been taken over by racists , she said: “I don’t know if there are extremists and racists in my party, but I want to make sure that my party isn’t vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists.

“I want to make sure that my party’s policies represent the views of the majority of members of the Green Party who absolutely are not that sort of person at all.”

Mr Polanski has repeatedly refused to say he would have voted against the motion and said it is up to members if he stays as leader.

“What I’m experiencing, though, is an immense amount of people who are saying actually they’ve never been prouder to be a Green Party member.”

Meanwhile, Lib Dem leader Ed Davey is also facing a plot to oust him after frontbencher Charlie Maynard quit as Treasury spokesman in a bid to launch a leadership challenge.

A Lib Dem insider said: “Ed may see this challenge off but it is probably the beginning of the end.



“He is on a clock now. If someone better challenged him they would win in a second.

But an ally of Sir Ed insisted he is going nowhere saying: “Ed is fired up and focused on the next General Election.”

The party civil wars mean both the Greens and Lib Dems could face leadership contests before the next election.

News.title: Three joyriders who killed two police officers in crash racked up £20k in taxpayer-funded legal aid since they were kids
News.content:
Next

WRONG-WAY joyriders who died ploughing into a police car killing two officers racked up £20,000 in tax-funded legal aid since they were kids, The Sun on Sunday can reveal.

Three of the five who died with PCs Tom Clough, 38, and Matthew Blades, 37, near Middlesbrough in August had cash help since aged 12.



Makai Saddington, 18, and 17-year-olds Theo Rae and Cole Worthy drew legal aid from 2021.

Saddington had £1,460 in 2025 and 2026 including £284 over “offences against the person”.



Rae racked up £5,545 including £170 relating to taking a car at 12 — and hundreds more from 2022 to 2024 for offences including theft and drugs.

Worthy had £13,774, our Freedom of Information request shows.

The total legal aid bills for the three comes in at £20,780.46.

Police have previously confirmed all five of the youths had links to organised crime with four of those killed having clocked up extensive criminal records with 37 convictions among them including for drug offences, assault, and robbery.

Last week it was revealed Cole Worthy’s father, Gye Worthy, was facing jail for attacking the celebrant at his son’s funeral.

The 40-year-old flew into a rage when Paul Maull failed to mention him in the eulogy to son Cole Worthy but did reference the teen’s stepdad.



He hurled insults and then attacked him as shocked mourners looked on.

The Legal Aid Agency was unable to locate any legal aid payments for Michael Robert Cahill, 23, or Jacob Matusiak, 23, the two other men killed in the crash.

The Ministry of Justice said: “Legal aid is not paid directly to individuals.”

News.title: ‘Significant concerns’ were raised about sick nursery worker 3 years before he was arrested for abusing sleeping kids
News.content:
Next

“SIGNIFICANT concerns” were raised about a sick paedophile nursery worker three years before he was arrested, according to reports.

Vincent Chan was jailed in February having pleaded guilty to 56 offences on three-year-old girls in his care at Bright Horizons nursery in north-west London.



Following his conviction, prosecutors describe Chan as a “prolific sexual predator”.

It has now been revealed Chan was the subject of a previous safeguarding investigation, carried out by Bright Horizons, with the oversight of Camden council, The Guardian reports.



It came after “significant concerns” were raised with the nursery in 2021 about Chan’s conduct and behaviours by the parent of a young girl, including concerns about what her daughter was saying to her about Chan.

The nursery referred the matter to Camden council, which advised it to investigate.



While the investigation was carried out, Chan was put on duties that involved no contact with children.

He was cleared to return to his role caring for young children at the nursery.



Just a year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself sexually abusing three-year-old girls at the Bright Horizons nursery.

In June 2024, he was arrested, initially on suspicion of child cruelty, after videos were discovered by nursery staff that Chan had filmed of distressed children in his care.

Cops then searched his devices and discovered he was a prolific sexual offender with tens of thousands of child abuse images on his computer.

It was also revealed he had committed sexual offences in his previous job as a teaching assistant at St Mary’s Church of England primary school in Dollis Park, North London, including upskirting female pupils.

He was sentenced to 18 years in prison in February this year.



The case raises serious concerns about whether existing safeguarding measures for nurseries are adequate.

Before Chan was arrested, other parents claim they raised concerns with Bright Horizons about Chan’s conduct at work.

They say concerns were raised with the nursery that their children were telling them that Chan shouted at them, was “angry” and a “bad man”.

The parents say their concerns were dismissed.

The Bright Horizons nursery on the Finchley Road closed in June 2025.



When there are concerns that a nursery work has been accused of harming or posing a risk of harm to children, may be guilty of criminal conduct or has exhibited behaviour that makes them unsuitable to work with children, nurseries have a responsibility to refer to local authority designated officers (LADOs)

The ultimate responsibility for managing allegations raised that relate to adults who work with children lies with the local authority.

If the concerns meet a criminal threshold, LADOs can recommend the matter is referred to the cops.

It is understood the Met Police didn’t receive a referral in 2021 regarding Chan and were only later told of the concerns.

Once Chan’s sexual offending came to light, Camden council carried out a rapid review of the decision to clear him to return to work, following the Bright Horizons investigation.



That review ended in November 2025 and Camden council then commissioned a local child safeguarding practice review to look at how Chan was able to abuse children at the nursery as well as offences committed in his previous job.

The review, which has been repeatedly pushed back, is now likely to be published in early 2027, according to Camden council.

It is expected to be critical of the safeguarding culture within Bright Horizons.

However, Camden council has said it cannot investigate Bright Horizons under health and safety laws because it is conflicted due to its participation in the safeguarding review.

Local authorities have the power to prosecute businesses that do not comply with health and safety legislation.



A letter sent to the parent of a child at the nursery, Camden council said the purpose of the safeguarding review was “not conducted to hold individuals, organisations, or agencies to account,” The Guadian says.

The parents of Chan’s victims are unlikely to be satisfied by the review as it is unlikely to apportion blame to executives at Bright Horizons.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The review was first due in the summer this year.

There has been no explanation as to why it was delayed.

News.title: Migrant patrols in the Med set to be helped with £82k hovercraft Home Office chiefs plan to buy – funded by you
News.content:
Next

TAXPAYERS are to fund a hovercraft to help migrant patrols — in the Med.

Home Office chiefs plan to spend £82,000 on the vessel to scour the coast of Tunisia, which is a main staging post for Africans trying to reach Europe and the UK.



It is part of a long-standing deal with the North African country to reduce illegal migration.

The hovercraft is set to be based in Tunisia and manned by Border Force crews.



The Home Office has issued a procurement tender.

It reads: “The buyer wishes to appoint a supplier to provide a search-and-rescue hovercraft, trailer, training, spares, warranty and after-sales support for deployment in Tunisia.”

In January last year, The Sun travelled with then Foreign Secretary David Lammy to Tunisia, where he signed a £5million deal with the country to help smash people-smuggling gangs.

Some of the cash is being spent on training Africans so they will be less tempted to make dangerous crossings.

The Home Office said: “We’re working with partners across Europe and beyond to stop illegal migration before it reaches our shores.

“Small boat crossings are down significantly and this summer recorded the lowest number of arrivals since 2020.



“But there is more to do.

“That’s why we’re removing the pull factors that draw migrants across the world and increasing removals of people here illegally.”

News.title: Further tax hikes will be ‘final nail’ for Britain’s high streets, top retail bosses warn Healey ahead of Budget
News.content:
Next

TOP retailers have warned further tax hikes will be the “final nail” for Britain’s high streets.

Big firms fear being stung in Chancellor John Healey’s Budget later this month.



John Lewis boss Jason Tarry said targeting the biggest names in “a crude ‘large versus small’ equation doesn’t add up”.

He told the Daily Telegraph: “Penalising anchor retailers through higher business rates risks harming the smaller businesses operating in their orbit.”



Meanwhile, Marks & Spencer boss Stuart Machin hit out at former Chancellor Rachel Reeves over her tax raises.

He urged Mr Healey to reverse “the mistakes of the last two Budgets”.

It comes as figures show UK employers pay almost £2,000 more in tax on an employee earning £30,000 compared to bosses of firms in Florida.

The British Chambers of Commerce said more taxes in the Budget would be fatal for the country’s economic outlook.

Kate Shoesmith, its director of policy, said the Chancellor must cut business costs to enable firms to grow. She added: “Any further tax rises on firms in the budget would be the final nail in the coffin for the country’s economic ambitions.”

Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said: “Thanks to Labour’s Jobs Tax and employment red tape, unemployment is up, leaving hundreds of thousands out of work and living off welfare.”



A Treasury spokesman said: “We are backing firms through business rates cuts, a cap on corporation tax and a £4.3billion package to help businesses manage costs and keep investing.”

Treasury sources said there are no plans for a warehouse tax.

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle to hold first joint UK appearance in days
News.content:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle to hold first joint UK appearance in days

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle are set to make their first joint public appearance in the UK since returning from the US, with the Duke and Duchess of Sussex expected to visit Nottingham this week

View Image (Image: Eric Charbonneau, Archewell Foundation via Getty Images)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's first joint public engagement since their return to the UK has been confirmed. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are set to appear together in Nottingham this week .

‌



‌



This comes as the pair continue to position themselves under new titles as "public figures" rather than "private citizens," according to the Times.

‌



The Sussexes are expected to visit CRS Nottingham to take part in an acting workshop, before joining the women of the Grenfell Hubb Community Kitchen at a local food bank. They are also anticipated to meet with Epic Partners, an organisation that supports young people through sport.

‌



Since Harry and Meghan touched down in the UK a month ago, following six years living in the US, the couple have been embroiled in a very public row with Buckingham Palace over their royal status. Their children have also changed schools after concerns were raised by their security team regarding the school run.

It appears that they will avoid any awkward missed invites to Sandringham this Christmas, as a friend of the couple has told the Daily Mail that the Duke and Duchess of Sussex intend to spend the festive period at their multi-million-dollar home in Montecito, California.

‌



The source claimed Harry and Meghan are trying to "keep their heads down between now and Christmas, when they will go back to California for the holidays".

The Sussexes unexpectedly relocated to the UK from California in late August. They stepped away from royal duties six years ago and remain non-working royals.

Harry spoke to Canadian network CTV, saying things are going "great" since the family's return to Britain on August 26. Speaking of Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, he said: "The kids are happy in school and it gives me a chance to really focus on Invictus in Birmingham."

Article continues below

"The games are in July next year."

Reflecting on his homecoming, Harry added: "It's been great. It's been great to be back on British soil. "It's great to be back on terra firma, actually!

News.title: How hero Yorkshire Wildlife Park zookeepers ended tiger's fatal attack on man who 'jumped into enclosure'
News.content:
How hero Yorkshire Wildlife Park zookeepers ended tiger's fatal attack on man who 'jumped into enclosure'

Disturbing footage posted online appeared to show the victim standing inside the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster while pointing at a tiger

View 9 Images The scene at Yorkshire Wildlife Park which was evacuated and closed after the incident (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

Horrified families screamed in terror as a man was mauled to death in a zoo's tiger enclosure today.

‌



‌



Disturbing footage posted online appeared to show the victim standing inside the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park in Doncaster while pointing at a tiger. He was seen being bitten and shoved around by the big cat while crying out “no, no” and "back", as visitors desperately shouted from a viewing gantry in a bid to distract the animal.

‌



One male onlooker was heard exclaiming “Jesus Christ”, while a woman was heard saying: “I tried to stop him”. She was also heard telling a fellow witness: “Don't look,” as the horror continued.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 9 Images Altai, one of Yorkshire Wildlife Park's Amur Tigers, pictured there last year (Image: Yorkshire Wildlife Park / SWNS)

Hurricane Isaias tears through US with horror 120mph winds and three confirmed dead READ MORE :

Hero keepers later managed to scare the animal away by firing several gunshots into the air, causing it to flee to a nearby hide. It was left uninjured.

‌



Visitor Tia Hanson said: "It looks as if someone has jumped into the enclosure. There were loads of police and ambulance people and a stretcher in the enclosure as well. It wasn’t nice - there were lots of people who looked really upset. They put up all sort of black tarpaulin so you couldn’t really see."

View 9 Images Police at the scene this afternoon (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

Police and ambulance workers rushed to the scene before a “black screen” was later erected around the enclosure. An insider said: "Shots were fired into the air to make a noise and distract the tiger. The animal wasn't shot and is absolutely fine and not injured.

‌



"The barriers are huge. You would have to really want to get inside the enclosure to be able to do it. From start to end the incident was over within minutes. The keepers did everything they could. It's horrific."

View 9 Images The scene at Yorkshire Wildlife Park (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, was on a family day out when staff told them the park was being evacuated. She said: "We were in a lemur enclosure and somebody asked us to start leaving. Then, all of a sudden, we were being ushered further and further into the park."

‌



She said she had then heard several gunshots before a helicopter began circling. She said: "That's when we started thinking, 'Oh, something's happened'."

A woman who was visiting the park with her husband and two children, aged six and three, described seeing blood where the tiger had dragged the man as visitors shouted in a bid to distract the animal.

View 9 Images The park was evacuated earlier today (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

‌



"You could see the blood where the tiger had dragged the man. Someone who saw it said it had him by the neck," midwife Amy Wright, 36, told The Sun. "There was a lot of blood. People were shouting to try and distract it."

Doncaster Mayor Ros Jones said in a statement she was "deeply saddened to hear of the tragic incident that has taken place today at Yorkshire Wildlife Park". She added: "My thoughts and prayers are with all those involved at this immensely difficult time."

Yorkshire Wildlife Park was opened in April 2009. In 2011, its Land of the Tigers’ attraction opened allowing visitors to view the cats from a 300 meter-long raised walkway above the enclosure. The park has two Amur tigers, a 17-stone female called Tschuna and a male called Altai, who only arrived in March last year.

‌



View 9 Images Police rushed to the park before closing off the entrance to the park on Saturday afternoon (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

A statement on the park's website said: “We can confirm a serious incident has occurred at the tiger enclosure. Our emergency response procedures were immediately activated.

“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened. The safety and wellbeing of our visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority The park is now closed and will remain closed tomorrow..”

‌



A South Yorkshire Police spokesman said: “At 1.35pm today (Saturday 10 October) we received reports of a man entering a tiger enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park.

View 9 Images Police at the park's entrance (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

"The tiger subsequently attacked the man, resulting in serious injury. Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene.

‌



"The man's family is aware and is being supported by specialist officers. Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time. Regarding rumours surrounding the condition of the tiger, the animal was uninjured and remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public.

View 9 Images Witnesses said a “black screen” was erected around the tiger enclosure after the horror (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

"Following the incident, Yorkshire Wildlife Park was evacuated and officers remain on scene carrying out enquiries."

‌



A Yorkshire Air Ambulance spokesperson said: “We can confirm that Yorkshire Air Ambulance was dispatched to an incident at Yorkshire Wildlife Park today, alongside other ambulance resources."

View 9 Images A black screen was erected around the tiger enclosure (Image: Charley Atkins / SWNS)

The horror comes after a three-year-old boy was seriously injured after being thrown into a crocodile enclosure back in July. The boy was visiting Johnsons of Old Hurst, near Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire, on 18 June when he ended up in the crocodile enclosure before being attacked.

Article continues below

A 30-year-old man from Norfolk, understood to have learning difficulties, was later arrested on suspicion of attempted murder following the incident and was later bailed as police said he was “assessed as not being fit for interview”.

News.title: Donald Trump takes control of horror decision to live stream execution by firing squad
News.content:
Donald Trump takes control of horror decision to live stream execution by firing squad

US president Donald Trump said he will 'make a decision' after the Pentagon announced shock plans to livestream the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan

View 3 Images Donald Trump said he would 'make a decision' on the plan to livestream an execution (Image: Ron Sachs/UPI/Shutterstock)

Donald Trump has vowed to 'make a decision' around the controversial bid to livestream the execution of a former soldier.

‌



‌



Plans were unveiled by the Pentagon earlier this week to broadcast the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, an ex-army major who carried out the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting, killing 13 unarmed soldiers and wounding 32 others.

‌



On Friday, Trump said he had "absolutely" approved the livestream announcement - but after a wave of backlash, including from fellow Republicans, the US president suggested today that he was yet to make a decision on whether this would go ahead.

‌



View 3 Images Nidal Hasan killed 13 unarmed soldiers and wounded 32 others (Image: BELL COUNTY SHERIFFS DEPARTMENT/AFP via Getty Images)

He told reporters in the White House: "There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it. Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but I’ll make a decision,” the president told reporters at the White House.

Trump said of Hasan: "He’s a vicious killer - killed 13 people in cold blood, wounded over 20. Some of those people will never have their lives back in a true sense."

‌



It comes after Vice President JD Vance said he wasn't sure if the livestream was "actually going to happen" - and said he would not be watching if it did.

"Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said.

"Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it".

‌



View 3 Images JD Vance said he would not watch the livestream if it went ahead (Image: Getty Images)

Trump turns on Zelensky again

Donald Trump also called for Ukraine to get rid of President Volodymyr Zelensky after Kyiv labelled his oil deal a "gift" to Vladimir Putin.

The US president announced the £3.3bn deal to purchase Russian diesel on Friday after Ukraine refused demands stop targeting Putin's oil sites at a joint summit in Florida.

Article continues below

"I said to him: ‘do what you want, don’t hit refineries", Trump said today in the White House.

"You’ve lost 30% of your country and you’ve had over a million people killed. … I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president"

News.title: Hurricane Isaias tears through US with horror 120mph winds and three confirmed dead
News.content:
Three people have died and hundreds of thousands left without power as Hurricane Isaias made landfall in the US.

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis urged residents to remain indoors and avoid unnecessary travel amid a "hazardous situation" in the state, where high winds, isolated tornadoes and flooding are expected to continue today.

"The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads", he said, as photographs showed homes and businesses battered by the storm and falling debris.

Authorities in the state confirmed that a woman had died after a tree fell on her house amid peak winds of 120mph, with two more casualties confirmed in Alabama on Saturday.

‌



Christa Pike discharged from hospital 10 days after botched execution in major update READ MORE :

View 5 Images Trees crashed into homes in the worst-hit areas across the southeastern US (Image: DAN ANDERSON/EPA/Shutterstock)

Kay Ivey, governor of Alabama, said: "This storm brought in heavy winds throughout Alabama, taking down trees, knocking out power and doing some damage. Unfortunately, we have also learned that two Alabamians have lost their lives. I am praying for their loved ones this morning."

Around 840,000 people remained without power across the southeastern US on Saturday after winds hit substations and downed power lines overnight.

View 5 Images Over 800,000 people have been left without power (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



The Gulf Coast Electric Cooperative utility company said they had been temporarily forced to halt efforts to restore power, as conditions had become too dangerous for work to be carried out.

A statement read: "Unfortunately, weather conditions have deteriorated to the point that, for the safety of our crews, we must temporarily suspend outage restoration efforts until conditions improve and it is safe to resume work. We understand how frustrating it is to be without power, and we sincerely appreciate patience and understanding".

View 5 Images The storm will bring more flooding as it heads inland, authorities warned (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Emergency alerts had been sent to phones across Florida, Alabama, Georgia and Mississippi ahead of the hurricane warning residents to "take cover now".

‌



The National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned that the remnants of Isaias would continue to produce torrential tropical downpours and strong winds as the storm moves north through Alabama and Georgia.

View 5 Images Huge waves were also witnessed in California as Tropical Storm Rachel approached (Image: Jake Lee Green/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

It marks the beginning of the North American hurricane season, which has begun later than usual due to the effects of the El Nino weather phenomenon.

Large waves began lashing beaches in southern California on Saturday ahead of the impending Tropical Storm Rachel, while Hurricane Simon - expected to become a severe Category 4 storm - will make landfall on the eastern coast of Mexico on Sunday.

News.title: Trump blasts Zelensky and demands Ukraine 'gets leader who can make a deal'
News.content:
Trump blasts Zelensky and demands Ukraine 'gets leader who can make a deal'

Trump was accused of betraying Ukraine after cutting a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel to America, in a bid to drive down prices ahead of next month's Midterm elections

View Image Trump and Zelensky earlier this month at the United Nations General Assembly (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Donald Trump has demanded Volodymyr Zelensky be replaced, claiming Ukraine's president failed to "settle" the war.

‌



‌



It comes after the US President was accused of betraying Ukraine yesterday after cutting a deal with Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel to America, in a bid to drive down prices ahead of next month's Midterm elections

‌



Trump made the shocking remarks as he left the White House to travel to Texas for a political rally.

‌



He said "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,″ adding that "for some reason [Zelensky] never does."

Andy Burnham spoke on the with President Zelensky today, and reiterated the UK's support for Ukraine.

A Downing Street spokesperson said: “The Prime Minister began by recognising the last 24 hours had been difficult for Ukraine and reiterated his complete solidarity.

‌



“The two leaders next discussed the importance of maintaining pressure on Russia: the Prime Minister made it clear that the UK would continue to strengthen its sanctions on Russia and to take further action to constrain the Russian war machine, building on new UK designations against Russian targets announced this week.

“They underlined that Russia should agree to an immediate energy ceasefire, ending its brutal strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure and its attacks on shipping in the Black Sea. This would immediately release more energy and food supplies into the global market.

“The two leaders agreed to meet in person in the coming days to continue their discussion.”

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Asked if he was concerned his deal with Russia would prolong the war, Trump said: "I see it a little differently. Zelensky could have settled this war many times...and he chooses not to."

Zelensky "settling" the war, as Trump puts it, would involve ceding territory illegally invaded by Russia.

‌



He added: "We said 'you can do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries, because that's a world problem that's caused."

In an apparent bid to link Ukraine defending itself against Russia to the midterm elections, in which his Republican Party is expected to suffer heavy losses, Trump went on: "He wants to make problems for the world.

"He wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel. Because Russia supplies the diesel fuel throughout the world. And we told him 'do whatever you want, but don't hit the diesel fuel...and what does he do? He goes and hits refineries.

Article continues below

"He'd better damn well stop."

Asked about the daily suffering of the Ukrainian people from Russian rocket attacks, Trump said: "I agree with you. Do you know what I suggest? I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal."

He added: "You've lost 30% of your country and you've had over a million people killed. Between the two of them over 2m people killed. That's a war that should have never started, and I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new President."

News.title: 'Spineless MPs have failed to tackle Royal Family's gravy train as your bills go up'
News.content:
'Spineless MPs have failed to tackle Royal Family's gravy train as your bills go up'

Writing for The Mirror, author and former Lib Dem MP Norman Baker has criticised the government for approving a £100million-a-year Sovereign Grant for the Royal Family

View 2 Images The Sovereign Grant settlement handed to the Royal Family will be £99.7million next year (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

Times are tight. Your bills for heating, for food and for fuel may be soaring, but that won’t worry the royals who have just been given yet another bumper pay rise by the government and will – kerching - now get a handout of £100 million a year.

‌



‌



And that’s after we have spent £359 million on a no-expense-spared upgrade of Buckingham Palace, only for Charles to say he has decided not to live there.

‌



The last year of the Civil List, the predecessor to the current Sovereign Grant, was held in check by Gordon Brown and gave the royals £7.9 million in 2011. Overall our bloated royals are now costing us about HALF A BILLION a year.

‌



Majority of voters want funding for royals slashed after £50m hike in three years READ MORE :

View 2 Images Former Lib Dem MP Norman Baker has criticised the government (Image: In Pictures via Getty Images)

Successive governments have tried to stop MPs debating royal matters. And MPs are restricted by the rules of parliamentary procedure from criticising the royals.

Just to make sure, each MP when elected has to swear an oath of true allegiance to the monarch, and their heirs and successors, before they can take their seat. These heirs and successors, by the way, include in the top ten the disgraced Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, and the opted-out Prince Harry.

‌



But earlier this month, for the first time in 15 years, MPs were given a chance to scrutinise royal finances. By law the government had to introduce an amendment to push through this big increase, but did their best to smother it as much as possible.

They scheduled the debate at short notice for the first day back after the recess, and as late towards midnight as possible. They needn’t have worried. Very few MPs showed up and almost no questions were asked. With the chancellor scrabbling round to find any spare cash to help deliver the promised “breathing space” for people, you might think MPs would have tried to put a brake on this royal gravy train, even if the chancellor was prepared to wave it on.

You might have thought the Tories, who are so keen to cut benefits for the poorest amongst us, would have had something to say about the huge benefit bill for the royals, but no. Sadly, our MPs have backbones like chocolate eclairs when it comes to the monarchy.

‌



Maybe the culture of institutional deference intimidates them. Or perhaps the lure of rubbing shoulders with our unelected royals at garden parties is just too much of a pull.

And so we look to the Lords, who tend to show rather more independence and who will have their chance to have a say on the matter next week. But wait. The government has decided that the amendment to the law is a “money Bill,” meaning the Lords are unable to vote to reduce the massive increase.

They can only express their views, which the government will then ignore. Meanwhile don’t be surprised if the royals are quietly raising a glass or two of expensive wine to toast out craven MPs.

News.title: Chief of Met Police volunteer force sacked over intimate images after Palantir probe
News.content:
Chief of Met Police volunteer force sacked over intimate images after Palantir probe

Special Chief Officer James Deller, who led the Met Police's volunteer officers, was removed by the force after a probe using tech from controversial company Palantir

View 2 Images Special Chief Officer James Deller was removed from his position by the Met Police (Image: Met Police)

The head of the Metropolitan Police's volunteer officers was sacked by the force after an investigation using Palantir technology found he used his work phone to copy intimate images of a woman.

Special Chief Officer James Deller, who led the Met's Special Constabulary, was kicked out of his role after an accelerated misconduct hearing on Friday. A probe found that in July and August 2025, SCO Deller had used his police-issued phone to photograph intimate images of a woman sent to his personal phone.

Investigators used lawful business monitoring and Palantir's Foundry system, which uses artificial intelligence, to uncover his conduct.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 2 Images The probe used technology from the US firm Palantir (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

I visited Ukraine where brave families face Putin's terrifying daylight air raids READ MORE :

The original images were sent using WhatsApp's "view once" feature, designed to make images disappear after they have been opened. Deller then sent copies of these images back to his personal device before deleting them from his work phone.

SCO Deller will be added to the College of Policing's barred list, making him ineligible for future police service. This came to light during a week-long operation using advanced technology targeting professional misconduct and corruption within the Met.

Software company Palantir, founded by controversial tech billionaire Peter Thiel, holds contracts with other UK public sector bodies, including the NHS and the Ministry of Defence. Palantir was previously blocked from a £50m contract with the Met over objections by City Hall and concerns over the company's "values and ethics".

The tech company in July announced it was suing the Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime at the High Court. Palantir's lawyers called the move to block the deal, in May, an "unlawful veto".

Commander Pete Stevens said: "The vast majority of Met officers and staff serve London with dedication and integrity, and they rightly expect robust action against the small minority who abuse their position and undermine public trust.

"That is particularly true of those who serve in the Special Constabulary. They are volunteers who selflessly give up their time to keep London safe. They deserve to be led by people who demonstrate the highest standards in all parts of their lives.

"SCO Deller failed to meet that bar. He let himself down but more importantly, he let the Special Constabulary down. His actions were an abuse of the trust put in him and it is right that he is no longer able to serve in policing."

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is under significant pressure from Labour MPs and unions to end Government contracts with Palantir. Former Labour deputy leader Lord Tom Watson, who recently joined Palantir, warned against "mob rule" in Government procurement practices.

Lord Watson of Wyre Forest told BBC's Political Thinking With Nick Robinson: "One of the things I'd say to my former colleagues is 'Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want to let mob rule to lead procurement practices?' Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one."

In May, Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner Matt Jukes told the London Assembly Police and Crime Committee that officers were not under any "additional surveillance in the workplace" after the force used AI in a bid to root out bad behaviour.

Article continues below

He said the force had weighed the reputational risk of using the "divisive" technology, which he said identified "unacceptable, dishonest, corrosive behaviours" from officers.

News.title: Ed Miliband hits out at Zack Polanski as Green Party rocked by Zionism row
News.content:
Ed Miliband hits out at Zack Polanski as Green Party rocked by Zionism row

EXCLUSIVE: The Foreign Secretary weighed in the controversy engulfing the Greens over a motion that effectively called for Israel to be abolished and replaced with a single Palestinian state

View 2 Images Green leader Zack Polanski is under fire over an anti-Zionism motion backed by members (Image: Jordan Pettitt/PA Wire)

Ed Miliband has hit out at the Green Party over a controversial motion equating Zionism with racism - and said Zack Polanski should have called it out.

‌



‌



The Foreign Secretary weighed in on the row that has rocked the Greens, after members voted to back the position that effectively called for Israel to be abolished and replaced with a single Palestinian state.

‌



Vivien Lichtenstein, the chair of the Jewish Greens, called for Mr Polanski to resign on Friday, accusing him of a dereliction of duty for failing to intervene on the vote.

‌



Asked about the motion, Mr Miliband, who is Jewish, said: "I profoundly disagree with them. I think it’s a very retrograde step for them to have taken this position.

Zack Polanski rocked by resignation and Jewish Greens chief says she may quit over Zionism motion READ MORE :

View 2 Images Ed Miliband said he profoundly disagreed with the Greens over the anti-Zionism motion (Image: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing via Getty Images)

"Because they are exactly falling into the trap that you should avoid which is to somehow confuse and label those who are strong supporters of the state of Israel as being racist. Why?

‌



"It’s wrong. I think Polanski to be honest should have called it out. I think he’d have been in a much better place if he’d have called it out. It’s not what we need in our politics."

Mr Polanski's leadership was already under intense pressure over the vote, which he missed to campaign in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election where he was standing as a candidate. His woes deepened on Friday when he was defeated by Labour's Sagal Abdi-Wali, who won with a majority of 3,364.

The Green Party leader said on Friday that he would not have voted for the motion as it stood, and said it was for the Israelis and the Palestinians to decide on the future of the region.

‌



Asked if he supported the motion, he said: “I would have supported the motion as amended. It wasn’t amended, so no.”

But he added: “Ultimately, I agree with the substance of the motion. Where I disagree is the idea the Green Party should be deciding what the future of the region looks like.”

On BBC Radio 4’s Today programme Mr Polanski, who is Jewish, refused to say whether Israel had a right to exist. “I believe Israelis and Palestinians should have equal rights in a democracy,” he said.

‌



Asked to give a yes/no response, he said: “At the moment Palestinians don’t have equal rights, so I think I’m answering your question really clearly.”

Ms Lichtenstein told Times Radio she was considering leaving the party as she said it was "absolutely" a dereliction of duty by Mr Polanski for failing to intervene.

She said: “It was a big mistake for Zack not to find a place, a quiet place, where he could have gone online for the motions debate, where he could have spoken to the two amendments that he supported.

‌



Asked if he should remain as leader, she said: “No, I think he should resign.”

It comes as a Green Party MP has said she wants to make sure her party is not “vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists”.

Ellie Chowns, said there had been a “lack of leadership” from Mr Polanski, but that he now had an “opportunity” to bring the party together in its wake.

Article continues below

Elsewhere, former Greens leader Caroline Lucas warned Mr Polanski must “urgently address the crisis that has overtaken the party”.

Writing in this newspaper, she claimed the country needed a “strong Green party”, but that the Zionism is Racism motion had caused hurt.

She said: “Those of us who spoke against the motion were clear: the policies and approach of this Israeli government are racist, its horrific actions in Gaza constitute genocide, and a campaign of boycott, divestment and sanctions is necessary and legitimate. But supporting a motion which effectively denies Israel the right to exist crosses a very significant red line.”

News.title: Man dies after tiger attack at wildlife park
News.content:
A man has died after being attacked by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, police have confirmed.

South Yorkshire Police said it had been called at 13:35 BST to reports of a man entering the tiger enclosure at the attraction near Doncaster. The tiger then attacked the man and he died at the scene, the force said.

His family had been informed and were being supported by officers, it added.

Yorkshire Wildlife Park will remain closed on Sunday following the incident and said in a statement: "Our thoughts and heartfelt sympathies are with the family and loved ones of the person who has lost their life."

Police said the tiger was uninjured, remained in the enclosure following the incident and there had been no wider risk to the public.

The force added: "We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this footage."

Earlier, in a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened".

News.title: US justice department investigates TV networks over Trump pool coverage
News.content:
The US justice department (DoJ) says it is investigating several television networks over whether they broke federal competition laws when they recently suspended pool coverage of President Donald Trump.

The agency has asked ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News to hand over communications related to the White House TV pool, a system where networks switch off covering the president and providing the footage to other publications.

The networks temporarily suspended this system last month for several days after the president blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House.

Members of the pool share their material - pictures and descriptions of the president's movements - with the wider media.

"Group boycotts among commercial competitors âcan violate the Sherman Act," a DoJ spokesperson said, referring to the federal law that bars companies from engaging in monopolistic business practices.

"The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these ânews organisations have violated the antitrust laws."

Trump blocked CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House last month after accusing the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his team.

The White House later reinstated their access after a ruling from a judge. The three outlets had sued the Trump administration, arguing the restricted access violated their First Amendment rights.

The First Amendment forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.

The Trump administration has taken a number of legal actions against news publications in the US, including lawsuits over coverage of the president.

In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association.

The same month, the Trump administration moved to bar Associated Press (AP) reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing.

News.title: UK launch flood taskforce to prepare for extreme winter weather
News.content:
The government has launched a new taskforce to respond to extreme weather, including the risk of flooding this winter.

After a summer of record breaking temperatures, the group will meet this week to assess how prepared the UK is for what the Met Office has described as the "heightened potential" for wet, windy, stormy weather in the coming months.

"We're facing extreme weather, with flood and drought intertwined but the government is taking decisive action," Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) Minister Emma Hardy said in a statement ahead of the meeting.

The Environment Agency has warned approximately 6.3 million homes and businesses in England remain at risk of flooding.

Defra will host the first meeting on Wednesday, bringing together the Met Office, Environment Agency and mayoral authorities as well as the farming, water and insurance industries.

Hardy said: "This will put communities and businesses at the heart of our work and will make sure the UK is ready for whatever the weather brings next."

The government has committed at least Â£10.5 billion up to 2036 to protect homes, businesses and critical infrastructure from the growing threat of flooding.

The Met Office has said the current seasonal outlook suggests an increased likelihood of wetter than average conditions during autumn, in part due to the El NiÃ±o weather event.

It has warned that this year's iteration of the climate phenomenon is likely to be the strongest in living memory, with the peak not expected until the end of the year.

The Environment Agency has said that while flooding is not guaranteed, the odds of repeated storms, prolonged rain and saturated catchments are higher than average this winter.

It has urged households to check their flood risk, sign up to alerts and make a flood plan to prepare for any emergencies.

The warnings follow 12 months of extreme weather across the UK, with the summer of 2026 the country's hottest on record.

Last winter brought four named storms to the UK - Bram, Goretti, Ingrid and Chandra - and several significant flooding events, with the Met Office reporting that England received 42% more rainfall than its winter average.

News.title: Bid to overturn ruling which stops police being sued for failings
News.content:
Backbench MPs are seeking to roll back a court ruling they say will have "devastating consequences" for victims of crime by preventing them taking legal action against the police, even when there have been grave investigative failings.

The 2025 Court of Appeal judgment, which applies to England and Wales, held that police officers are immune from civil litigation both in their role as witnesses, and for conduct or statements they make when carrying out criminal investigations.

Conservative Andrew Mitchell and Labour's Jess Phillips have submitted an amendment to a bill being debated in Parliament next week seeking to counteract the ruling.

Separately, the judgment could also be overturned at a Supreme Court appeal this month.

The MPs are seeking to stop immunity applying, including in cases where police have fabricated evidence, been dishonest or negligent, and where there has been a reckless disclosure of confidential information relating to victims.

The ruling came in a case brought by a victim of serious domestic violence who fled her abuser for a secret refuge, but Sussex Police included her new address in a file sent to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) without sufficiently flagging its confidentiality.

A CPS lawyer subsequently disclosed her address in court during a bail hearing, thereby revealing it to her abuser. As a result, she had to flee again.

The woman said the disclosure of her address had meant the place she was supposed to be safe "no longer felt safe at all" and she was still living with the impact of what happened and that loss of security.

She brought claims against both the police and CPS, arguing their failure placed her in fear for her life, compelled her to leave her home, caused her to suffer loss of earnings, and resulted in her developing a psychiatric injury. Her claims were initially rejected, reinstated on appeal, then struck out again.

The key issue was who could be held legally responsible for what happened, and who would benefit from legal immunity. Witnesses and lawyers have what is known as "core immunity" for things they say in court, so that they can speak freely there.

The Court of Appeal ruling further expanded such immunity, holding that it extends to an extremely broad range of police activity, including conduct or statements which are part of an investigation leading to a potential prosecution

Most types of legal claim are thus blocked by this immunity, including cases about serious human rights abuses and data breaches, and there are no exemptions for unjustifiable conduct.

Officers can still be prosecuted in the criminal courts and held accountable by police misconduct processes.

News.title: Northern Lights stun UK down to England's south coast
News.content:
Residents across the UK were left stunned as the sky was illuminated by the spectacular colours of the Northern Lights on Friday and Saturday evenings.

The natural phenomenon, known as the Aurora Borealis, is the result of increased solar activity.

Such occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland, but particularly strong activity levels meant they could be seen as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent on Saturday night.

The Met Office has said sightings could continue to be possible during clear skies until Tuesday.

News.title: Three friends on their student debt: one paid off, one chipping away and one creeping up
News.content:
When Lizzy, Libby and Charlotte met as freshers in 2012, their main responsibility was making it to lectures on time after early morning sports practice.

Their student debt, growing with interest from the day they took out their loans, was the last thing on their minds.

"The conversation was just so much less relevant at that time," says Charlotte. "As our careers have gone on and our paths have diverged more and more... those conversations start to come more to the forefront."

The friends, now in their early 30s, went to the University of Newcastle in the same year tuition fees tripled to Â£9,000 a year in England and Wales, and new loans called Plan 2 were introduced. Each borrowed about Â£37,500 to cover three years of tuition and living costs.

This year marks a decade since the first students in their year started repaying.

They may have started out in the same position, but over that time their career trajectories, life choices and earnings have shaped how much they've repaid, how much interest they've racked up, and how much they owe - with very different outcomes.

Student loans have come under scrutiny this year and there's been a particular backlash over Plan 2 loans. The government has said it wants to make the whole system fairer and campaigners are waiting to see what, if anything, changes in this month's Budget.

News.title: Inside the room: What it was like to be with Blackpink's Lisa as race scandal erupted
News.content:
What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?

That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal â one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.

The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.

The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.

The scandal blew up while Lisa was rehearsing for a pivotal performance at the Coachella Festival in 2025.

Offended and upset, some fans demanded an apology - but the band's record label, forbade the members from issuing a statement.

With Lisa's team in crisis mode, documentarian Sue Kim followed Lisa into her dressing room.

"I said, 'Look, I know this is new. I know you guys are wildly confused and hurt, but this is your time to say whatever you want to say - even if you're just processing your thoughts and telling us what you're feeling," Kim tells the BBC.

The film-maker "honestly expected her to say no".

Instead, Lisa lay down on a sofa and spoke from the heart.

"It's bad," the singer says in the documentary, with a mixture of shame and nerves.

Lisa explains she was "15 or 16" when the videos were shot and "didn't know that [word] was sensitive because I'm from Thailand and my first language is not English".

Having only heard the term in rap music, she was unaware of its offensive history.

"Now I would never ever do that because, now, I've got education," she says. "Now I know better.

"But I did wrong."

It is a vulnerable and human response - and nothing like the scripted PR apology you might expect. (Lisa has since apologised publicly, external in an interview with Variety, although some people remained unconvinced, external).

Kim says Lisaâs in-the-moment reaction is "one of the most important scenes" in her documentary, Always Lalisa, which hits cinemas on Monday, 12 October.

"There was no premeditation on Lisa's part, there was no media training," she adds.

"I asked her one question and she just talked for an hour, and everything came out, and it's all stream of consciousness.

"And what you see with Lisa in that moment is so genuine, it's impossible not to feel compassion for her."

News.title: AI is creating a 'human premium' for art made by people. But will it hold?
News.content:
The music platform Deezer says 44% of tracks uploaded to it are AI-generated. Its research also found that 97% of listeners couldn't tell what was AI-generated and what wasn't. But here's a third statistic: more than half of those surveyed said they did care if it was made by AI. They want humans to be involved.

Daniel Susskind, an economics professor at King's College London, says many of us place huge value on the human role in making art. It's what makes the creative process different from more functional, practical tasks, he thinks.

"I was once in a room of accountants, and one of them stood up and said, 'My clients come to me for the personal touch, the human process'," he remembers. "And I said, 'That isn't why they come to you, they come because they want their taxes done properly'."

But it's different with art, he says. "If I walk into the Sistine Chapel and look at the ceiling, I think not only is that extraordinarily beautiful, but isn't it amazing that a human hand, flesh and blood like my own, came up with that. A mind like mine dreamt that up," he says.

As Susskind describes it, what we value isn't just the destination, it's the knowledge that a human - one of us - got us there. We can wonder at that achievement.

News.title: King warns malicious online actors are evolving tactics
News.content:
King Charles III has warned of the challenges disinformation and other "hostile online activity" pose to trust and security in the digital age.

The comments, made in a letter to the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) to mark its 10th anniversary, spoke of "malicious actors" continuing to "evolve their tactics by using automated technologies".

"From threats to our international order, to the need to balance the risks and opportunities of powerful new technologies, strong cyber security is fundamental to making the online environment safer and more resilient," he wrote.

Last month, the King warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

In the letter published on Saturday by NCSC, the King praised the government agency. He said its achievements over the past decade have included defending the country against cyber attacks, safeguarding democratic institutions and protecting "the critical infrastructure upon which daily life depends".

"You have built resilience across our public services, businesses and communities, equipping us all to prosper in our ever-evolving digital world," the monarch added.

The King said he was "acutely aware" that much of the work done by the NCSC cannot be praised publicly and that he was filled with "profound gratitude".

The NCSC was established in 2016 as part of the Government Communications Headquarters to protect the UK against cyber threats.

Earlier this week, the NCSC offered assistance to online shopping store Asos after customers received a notification from its app sent by hackers, the BBC understands.

The high profile hack made global headlines on Tuesday when cyber criminals used Asos's own app system to send a pop up notification to potentially millions of people.

Asos said it was investigating "unauthorised activity" involving third-party platforms. The company told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the company's users - including names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

The letter from the King to NCSC came after he spoke to AI executives at Dumfries House in Ayrshire last month on how the tech can be used to benefit security.

News.title: Head of Met's volunteer force fired after AI tool found deleted intimate images on work phone
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has fired the head of its Special Constabulary after Palantir's AI monitoring uncovered that he had used his work phone to copy intimate images of a woman.

Special chief officer James Deller, who led the force's volunteer officers, was dismissed following a misconduct hearing on Friday.

The Met said investigators used lawful business monitoring and Palantir's Foundry system, which uses artificial intelligence (AI), to find the misconduct by Deller.

Cdr Pete Stevens said: "SCO Deller failed to meet that bar. His actions were an abuse of the trust put in him and it is right that he is no longer able to serve in policing."

Investigators found that in July and August 2025, Deller used his police-issued phone to take photos of two intimate images that had been sent to his personal phone.

The pictures had been sent using WhatsApp's "view once" feature, which makes them disappear after they are opened.

He then sent the copied images back to his personal device before deleting them from his work phone.

The misconduct was discovered during a week-long operation called Project Galatasaray, which used the AI technology in a bid to identify corruption and professional misconduct within the Met.

Deller will be added to the College of Policing's barred list, meaning he will not be able to serve in policing again.

Stevens added: "The vast majority of Met officers and staff serve London with dedication and integrity, and they rightly expect robust action against the small minority who abuse their position and undermine public trust.

"That is particularly true of those who serve in the Special Constabulary. They are volunteers who selflessly give up their time to keep London safe.

"They deserve to be led by people who demonstrate the highest standards in all parts of their lives."

News.title: Green Party MP wants to make sure it is 'not vulnerable to extremists'
News.content:
A Green Party MP has said her party needs to make sure it is not "vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists" after members voted for a motion that claimed Zionism was racism.

The motion put forward by activists, which became formal policy after it was approved at the Green's conference earlier this month, has divided senior party figures and been criticised by Jewish groups.

Westminster leader Ellie Chowns told the BBC it was a "significant and damaging policy" and she would work to reform the Green Party.

It comes after ex-leader Caroline Lucas said it was not being protected from entryism - where people sign up to a party to try to change it.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Saturday, Chowns said: "I don't know if there are extremists and racists in my party. But I want to make sure that my party isn't vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists."

The MP described Zionism as a "contested concept" and said the motion did not represent the views of the large majority of Green Party members, "nor of people in the country".

Chowns said the motion would be a "distraction from the very important work" the party has been doing campaigning for Palestinian rights.

She added: "I think it is clear that if we have policy, such significant and damaging policy, made by a vote of just 0.4% of our members, that something isn't working in our structures and our policy-making process."

Members of the Green Party of England and Wales endorsed the policy motion by 1,022 votes to 813.

There are 230,000 members of the Green party overall and not everyone attended the conference.

The policy also backs a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

It defines Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council, which criticised the motion, said: "Zionism is anti-racism, creating a refuge for Jews in their ancient homeland after millennia of persecution outside it."

News.title: Drumcree parade ban was in 'best interests of peace', says Bryant
News.content:
The Northern Ireland secretary of state has said his decision to ban the contentious Orange Order Drumcree parade "was in the best interests of peace".

The decision on Friday came after agreement couldn't be reached between the Portadown District Lodge and the Garvaghy Road residents over whether the march would be allowed down the predominantly nationalist road.

Sir Chris Bryant said he received advice from the PSNI chief constable that allowing the procession to go ahead could lead to serious injury, disorder and wider unrest.

On Saturday, a legal challenge by Orangemen against the decision to ban the parade was adjourned until Monday after the judge said it was not an "emergency" case.

The stalemate has reopened what was once the most bitter parading dispute in Northern Ireland, with stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.

The Parades Commission was established in 1998 to regulate contentious processions.

Its decisions restricting the Drumcree march have been challenged by the Orange Order for decades.

Earlier this year, a court overturned the commission's original decision to stop the parade, ruling it could go ahead, with restrictions on 27 September.

But Garvaghy Road residents blocked the road that morning, preventing the Orangemen from marching, and a stand-off has continued for almost two weeks.

The Court of Appeal has reserved judgment on a legal challenge brought by Garvaghy Road residents against the decision to allow the march.

Sir Chris said he had spent almost two weeks trying to broker a deal and believed the two sides had come close to an agreement.

He said two outcomes were discussed. One would have allowed the Orangemen to complete one final march along the Garvaghy Road, on the condition it would not apply to march the route again.

The other would have seen the group accept that it had won the right to march, but agree not to exercise that right, but neither proposal secured agreement from both sides.

News.title: Sara Sharif's grandfather granted guardianship of her siblings in Pakistan
News.content:
Sara Sharif's paternal grandfather has been granted guardianship of her siblings by a court in Pakistan.

The decision comes after years of legal limbo following the murder of 10-year-old Sara by her father and stepmother in 2023.

All five children, who are now aged between 16 and four, have been living in Pakistan since 2023. They were asked to speak to the judge in court, where the eldest said they were comfortable and the siblings were settled.

Sara's grandfather, Muhammed Sharif, told the BBC he was relieved to be granted guardianship after three years of legal battles, saying his hope is that the children "stay healthy" and receive "a good education".

"It is my responsibility to ensure they get the best possible education and care," he said.

When told by the judge that the grandfather would become their guardian, the eldest child responded saying "that's all good".

The five children have been in Pakistan since August 2023, when they were brought to the country by Sara's father, stepmother and uncle after Sara was killed.

The family was in hiding for weeks before the children were discovered by police at the grandfather's house. They were initially put into state childcare.

The adults flew back to the UK and were arrested at the airport. Sara's father Urfan Sharif and stepmother Beinash Batool were found guilty of Sara's murder. Sharif was sentenced to a minimum of 40 years in prison and Batool received a minimum of 33 years.

Her uncle, Faisal Malik, was found guilty of causing or allowing her death and given a 16-year sentence.

Sara had been hooded, burned and beaten during a "campaign of torture" that lasted two years before her body was found at the family home in Woking, Surrey.

News.title: Ceremony marks return home of kiwi feather cloak
News.content:
A ceremony has been held to mark the return of a MÄori kiwi feather cloak to New Zealand by a British museum.

The kahu kiwi was one of the farewell gifts presented by MÄori leaders in 1900 to Dr George Cleghorn, a medical doctor who had been working in New Zealand.

It was loaned to the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford by Cleghorn's widow in 1913.

The return was organised by the charity the Homebound Project which specialises in reuniting indigenous artefacts with their country of origin.

Dr Lorraine Eade, chair of NgÄti RÄrua o Te Wairau Society, which now owns the item, said the cloak was "crying to come home".

News.title: Eight men arrested by Greater Manchester Police days after early release from jail
News.content:
Eight men have been arrested by Greater Manchester Police days after leaving prison under the government's early release scheme.

About 700 prisoners from across the country were released early on 1 October in a bid to tackle overcrowding, with about 50 of them being from Greater Manchester.

GMP confirmed that five men had been arrested for breaches of criminal orders, including a domestic abuse prevention order, and others were held on suspicion of robbery, drug offences and domestic violence.

In response, the Ministry of justice (MOJ) said: "We inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse. If we had failed to act, the police would have been forced to halt arrests."

News.title: Rail disruption after overhead line fault
News.content:
Rail passengers are being urged to check before they travel due to overhead line problems on the West Coast Main Line in Staffordshire.

Work was ongoing to fix a fault with the 25,000-volt wires which power trains near Penkridge, causing disruption between Stafford and Wolverhampton.

At 12:00 BST, National Rail confirmed that lines have reopened between Stafford and Birmingham New Street, but residual disruption can still be expected until 16:00 BST on Saturday.

Adam Checkley from Network Rail, said: "Our teams have now cleared the issue allowing the route to reopen, but with trains and their crew out of position, delays and cancellations will continue throughout the day."

Rail replacement buses are in place at Birmingham, Stafford and Wolverhampton.

Checkley added: "We're sorry to passengers impacted by the overhead line problems at Four Ashes near Penkridge.

"With disruption to train services likely throughout the day, I'd urge people to check National Rail Enquiries before they set off on their journey."

Ticket acceptance is in place on alternative routes including the East Coast Main Line, and Midland Main Line via Sheffield.

News.title: Texas, Florida fall in upsets as Georgia-Alabama showdown takes center stage
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The top-ranked Texas Longhorns’ first loss of the season came at the hands of an unranked Oklahoma Sooners team, as kicker Tate Sandell drilled a 47-yard field goal to seal the 27-24 upset in the Red River Rivalry on Saturday night.

Two of Oklahoma's three scores stemmed from special teams or defense, as Danny Okoye blocked the Longhorns' punt, which Dakoda Fields scooped up and returned for a touchdown, and Peyton Bowen notched a 42-yard pick-six off Arch Manning.

It was a much-needed morale boost for the Sooners and coach Brent Venables after dropping to 2-2 after a 41-13 beatdown from Georgia in Week 4.

And across the conference, South Carolina coach Shane Beamer similarly silenced critics with a road upset over No. 16 Florida.

The Gamecocks held running back Jadan Baugh to under 60 rushing yards, outscored Florida 21-9 in the second half and forced three turnovers in the 38-19 win.

Quarterback LaNorris Sellers accounted for five touchdowns — four passing and one on foot.

The Gamecocks improved to 3-3 on the season, potentially quieting questions about Beamer’s job security for another week.

UCLA dumps Oregon

No. 21 UCLA kept its undefeated record alive with a 17-15 win over No. 13 Oregon in a messy, turnover-filled outing.

The Ducks threw two interceptions and lost five fumbles in the upset loss. The fifth fumble came during Oregon's final drive with less than a minute left and aspirations of a game-winning field goal on the line.

UCLA quarterback Nico Iamaleava had 162 yards and two interceptions before sitting out the second half with a lower leg injury. Ty Dieffenbach took over under center and threw for 43 yards and a touchdown.

Oregon backup quarterback Dylan Raiola's heroic performance against USC felt like a distant memory as he completed just 6-of-18 passes for 43 yards and two interceptions before being replaced by Brock Thomas.

Indiana improves to 6-0 — barely
