Sports.title: Carrick ‘massively disappointed’ after United drop points against 10-man Spurs
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick was left “massively disappointed” by Manchester United’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham at Old Trafford and admitted they need more points after managing six from their opening six league games.

This is United’s poorest start to the season since 1986, Saturday’s draw coming when conceding Dominic Solanke’s added-time equaliser for 10-man Spurs, following Rodrigo Bentancur’s 78th-minute red card. The midfielder was sent off five minutes after Bryan Mbeumo’s opener had left United heading for only a second league victory.

Carrick said: “I am massively disappointed with the result, for sure. A mixed performance. I’m not happy with the amount of points that we’ve had so far. There’s no hiding from that. I think it could have been different for a couple of little things here or there, but the reality is the reality, we’ve got to accept it, you know. We need to put things in a direction, in a positive direction quite quickly, that’s pretty plain.”

United were disjointed throughout. The manager was asked if he felt let down by the players. “I don’t feel let down, because you can make mistakes. You can make mistakes, things go against you,” said Carrick. “I’ve made mistakes in games, and it’s not so much letting everyone down. We’ve all got standards, we’ve all got levels, the players have got levels and standards, and they hold their hands up at times when something goes against them.”

United’s fans jeered at times during the game. “When things aren’t quite going to plan, I understand the reaction at times,” said the manager. “Obviously, it hurts a lot. It’s not nice to go through, but sometimes you have to go through it, that’s how it is.

“I care as much as anybody about this place, so sometimes you could say too much because then it overspills. But it’s coming from a good place, really, and so I understand it.”

View image in fullscreen Luke Shaw (right) clashes with Rodrigo Bentancur (centre) and other Tottenham players. Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty Images

Bentancur might have caused a serious injury had a scissors-challenge on Shaw connected. Roberto De Zerbi backed his midfielder, who was sent off for a head-butt in the resulting melee.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“I kiss Rodrigo and say thanks,” said the Spurs manager. “It is clear it is a mistake from Rodrigo, it is not the right reaction in football but in that moment maybe with 10 players we played with more courage, more energy and for a long time Tottenham played without this blood this character. I am the coach and I want to see this character every game.”

While Spurs have only three points and remain winless, they are now off the bottom though remain in the relegation zone. “Today has been the game where for the first time this season we showed we are a team, we played for the teammates, we played together,” said De Zerbi.

Sports.title: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Football, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. The Premier League is the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game.

What the Manchester City case has exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it’s perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales.

Football clubs in England and Wales still represent their communities, a relationship that may be strained in certain cases by the pressures of a globalised entertainment economy, but remains broadly true. Arsenal can feel like the club of choice for the nouveau fan from across the world, but the scenes of celebration when they ended their 22-year wait for the league title last season were an undeniable expression of local pride.

The idea that there was ever an idyll when clubs were run by benevolent potentates for the good of those communities is romantic nonsense. But just because there was no golden age is not to say that the situation has always been as bleak as this.

How did we get into a situation in which clubs are flotsam on the swirling currents of geopolitics and the world economy? Chelsea alone in the past four years have had a Russian oligarch forced to sell the club after falling under UK government sanctions, while a subsequent American co-owner has been forced to sell his minority stake after his insurance business came under federal investigation in the US. It’s a curious world in which the professional gamblers feel like a welcome breath of fresh air.

View image in fullscreen Chelsea fans hold banner during a peaceful, fan-led protest calling for accountability and structural change at Chelsea Football Club in January. Fans criticised the club’s ownership model, recruitment strategy, and overall leadership since the takeover, urging an end to micromanagement and a return to long-term ambition at the top level of English and European football. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images

The days of the local businessmen, the owners of mines, shipyards and factories, the hauliers and scrap-metal dealers, are gone. Some invested because they genuinely wanted to give back to their communities or liked the sport. Others did so because it was easier to fund a local football club than to improve working conditions or pay a proper wage. And some did so because, wrongly in most cases, they thought there may be money to be made.

But nobody should think those were days of purity. The decrepitude of English stadiums in the 1980s should caution anybody who thinks football was uncomplicatedly better then.

The contradiction has always lain at the heart of English football. Clubs represent their communities and for fans support becomes an aspect of identity, a link to family and place and past, a role that has only become more significant as the influence of traditional institutions – the church, the workplace, the social club – has faded. Yet fans in England have almost never owned their club, which in part underlies the present crisis.

That is not to say fan ownership is a panacea. There is much to be admired about the German 50+1 model which, to oversimplify, ensures outside investors can never own a majority of the club. But it has not prevented Bayern Munich from winning 13 of the past 14 Bundesliga titles. Some sort of recognition that a club is not just a business, that it has a community function might, though, have prevented the free-for-all that has led to this mess.

At least when most owners were local, there was some understanding of what the club meant to its area, and a recognition that exploitation or neglect could have direct consequences. No owner wanted demonstrations at the directors’ entrance, or to be jeered as he drove the streets in his Rolls-Royce, or to have his car showroom boycotted because he put up ticket prices then sold a popular centre-forward at a knockdown price. The distant majority shareholder in his boardroom in Los Angeles, his penthouse in Monte Carlo or his luxury villa on the Gulf feels the sting less keenly.

Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League, who did more to shape the modern competition, for good and for ill, than any other individual always spoke of being “neutral about ownership models”. Essentially that meant taking the money without worrying too much about where it came from. The current Premier League is the consequence: a gleaming, world-leading edifice, but built on what?

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Perhaps it’s not fair to be too harsh on the Premier League. This is not just modern football; it is modern Britain. As Miguel Delaney and Jack Pitt-Brooke argued on the Libero podcast this week, the Premier League is a direct outcome of Blairite economic policy, a point made clear in Oliver Bullough’s Butler to the World In the book he described the classic New Labour approach as “allowing something, making money from it and attempting to solve the problems it causes after they’ve occurred”.

But how do you solve those problems in football? How can football extricate itself from the clutches of the mega-rich? Regulation, up to a point, helps – and there may at least now be a sense that there can be enforcement. Whatever the flaws of the profitability and sustainability rules, or the squad cost ratio that has replaced them, it may be useful if football could accept the basic premise that the game shouldn’t just be about how rich your owner happens to be. But that can only go so far; a door open to the world has admitted a world of problems.

Short of some sort of financial crash in football, the sort of apocalyptic event that would make the sport unappealing to big finance and require the game to be built anew, with a fresh spirit that might recategorise football clubs as community assets rather than simple businesses, we’re probably stuck with it.

How, after all, could football ever escape the society that produced it?

Sports.title: Henderson and João Pedro lead Chelsea charge against Bournemouth
Sports.content:
Watch and learn, kids. The day began with one for the youth audience, Cole Palmer appearing on a live stream to explain the thinking behind his latest contract extension. It finished with the oldest player to join Chelsea during the BlueCo era stealing the show with an all-action midfield display.

Even Palmer was happy to step aside as Jordan Henderson used his right foot to curl home a free-kick that drew comparisons with one of David Beckham’s specials. It was Henderson’s second spectacular strike – he marked his home debut by opening the scoring with a bending effort from 20 yards and also laid on an assist for Morgan Rogers to make it 2-0 – although it is fair to assume that Xabi Alonso did not bring the veteran to Stamford Bridge for his goalscoring prowess.

The idea was more to lift standards in the dressing room. Chelsea needed experience and are surely better off now a 36-year-old starting for them in midfield is no longer a laughable notion.

“We signed him for everything,” Alonso said of Henderson. “If he’s able to score two beauties as today, we are more than happy for him. But apart from the goals he’s done many good things. He’s always involved in the action, always giving solutions to teammates.”

Henderson set the tone for Chelsea, driving into tackles and raising the tempo with the urgency of his passing. He joined from Brentford in the summer and is keen to do more than make up the numbers. Chelsea, up to fifth after their first win in four league games, were more stable with Henderson alongside Moisés Caicedo, who lasted 72 minutes on his long-awaited return from a calf injury.

View image in fullscreen Moisés Caicedo (left) returned to the Chelsea team after a spell on the sidelines due to injury. Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

Alonso, who was without Reece James after the captain picked up a knee injury in training on Friday, was still disappointed his side have now gone 22 league games without a clean sheet. They were 3-0 up when Evanilson pulled a goal back for Bournemouth, who are finding the transition from Andoni Iraola to Marco Rose trickier than anticipated and must manage games better.

Even so, Alonso was pleased with Chelsea’s level. They have scored in the first 10 minutes in five of their six league games this season and are a match for anyone when the front three of Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro take full flight.

Palmer had a point to prove after having his desire to play for England questioned by Thomas Tuchel last month. His impact was immediate, although it owed much to Bournemouth’s naivety. The visitors lined up in a flat 4-4-2 formation and gave Palmer far too much space when he sauntered down the right in the first minute.

It was encouraging to see Palmer moving freely, especially after Alonso’s admission that the playmaker’s decision to sit out the international break was related to last season’s groin pain, but Bournemouth were a soft touch. There was no challenge on the 24-year-old, who has displayed his commitment to Chelsea by signing on until 2034.

Palmer floated into the area, turned and rolled the ball to Henderson, who hit it first time with the inside of his right foot and saw his bending effort go in off the inside of the right post.

View image in fullscreen Jordan Henderson (centre) give Chelsea an early lead with a fine finish. Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/Reuters

There were 68 seconds on the clock when Henderson became Chelsea’s oldest scorer in the Premier League since John Terry in May 2017. “We knew Chelsea are a team that starts well,” Rose said. “It was our responsibility that we didn’t react the right way with this information.”

Bournemouth were overwhelmed. Chelsea pushed again in the third minute, Palmer’s flick freeing Pedro Neto to test Djordje Petrovic. The ball broke loose and Henderson swept a pass to Rogers, who cut in from the left and his shot flew in via a deflection off Antonio Silva.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The focus switched to Bournemouth’s long list of absentees. Justin Kluivert and Eli Junior Kroupi are big losses in attack. Alex Scott, the subject of multiple bids from Chelsea in the summer, exacerbated a thigh problem during a scintillating display for England against Croatia last Saturday.

These are worrying times for Bournemouth, who are winless after six league games. Goal difference is keeping them out of the bottom three and they struggled without Scott’s energy and quality in midfield. Ryan Christie and Tyler Adams were overrun and Silva had a nightmare at the back, his error at the start of the second half allowing Neto to nip in and set up João Pedro to make it 3-0 with an emphatic shot.

Bournemouth had chances during the first half, Christie, Rayan and Silva drawing saves from Emiliano Martínez, but it suited Chelsea for a basketball game to develop.

View image in fullscreen A tidy finish from close range gave João Pedro a second goal of the game and Chelsea a fourth. Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty Images

There were echoes of past battles between Alonso and Rose in the Bundesliga. Rose, who ended Alonso’s 35-game unbeaten run with Bayer Leverkusen when he was RB Leipzig’s manager, was a distinct second-best this time. Evanilson bundled in from a corner, but Chelsea were rampant.

The fourth goal arrived when Rogers found the overlapping Pep Chavarria, whose low cross was gobbled up by João Pedro. Alonso, who had become increasingly frantic on the touchline, relaxed. He was a great midfielder in his day and will have appreciated the technique when Henderson’s free-kick flew beyond the reach of Petrovic.

Sports.title: Bruno Guimarães completes Arsenal comeback to end Leeds’ unbeaten run
Sports.content:
Arsenal built the foundations of their new success on a desire for competition, an appetite for battle. But what happens when that spirit is insufficient, when your opponents play just as hard as you do? Well, then you bring on Bruno Guimarães and you play even harder.

Arsenal had just snatched an equaliser against a dominant Leeds side when Mikel Arteta introduced his key summer signing. The former Newcastle captain has been having to bide his time but when he entered the field just after the hour, he turned the game on its head.

Arsenal had been ponderous until this point, even uncertain at times. The passing had been intricate, not incisive, and echoes of familiar weaknesses had put the crowd on edge. Guimarães put paid to all that. Not only snapping into tackles, not only moving the ball at pace, he was desperate for everything to go faster, more aggressively, with sharper intention. Nine minutes after coming on, he scored the winner.

It was a goal that deserved to decide the contest and reflected the best of what the home side had been trying to achieve. Play developed down the left where Noni Madueke had shone, but here it was Bukayo Saka playing a one-two with Martin Ødegaard. The captain then poked a short pass to Declan Rice who – with Guimarães now covering him – had burst into the opposition area. Rice back-heeled the ball to the edge of the area and there was the Brazilian waiting, poised, to steer the ball unerringly into the corner of James Trafford’s goal.

In the time between Leeds’ opener and the winner, Arsenal had five efforts on goal, the same as in the preceding 55 minutes. Once the lead was established, they should have had at least two more goals, with Ødegaard somehow missing from two yards out and Trafford denying Saka in a one-on-one in the final move of the match. Leeds did not feature as an attacking threat in the final half hour, so decisive was the switch in momentum.

View image in fullscreen Riccardo Calafiori equalises for Arsenal against Leeds. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

Arteta said his team had to “pinch our desire to win” to overcome a visiting side who appear no longer to be punching above their weight, but rather have moved up a class.

“We had to face the challenge because [Leeds] are a team that hadn’t lost in the Premier League,” he said. “They’re in a great position because they fully deserve it. They are incredibly dangerous and we got into a situation, [a goal down] after that defeat against Brighton, 12:30 kick-off.

“It is a bad mixture and we got out of it through … pinching our desire to win, by showing the personality and courage that we have in this team.”

Arteta will be able to take satisfaction from the way his team managed the result, the effectiveness of his substitutes and other smaller details such as the continuing creative contributions of Rice – now with three assists to his name – and a second goal for Riccardo Calafiori, whose buccaneering inside runs have been a feature of the season.

On the other hand, his midfield was outmuscled and outplayed in the first hour, with the opening 10 minutes of the second half a period of dominance for the visitors that deservedly delivered a goal when James Justin finished Gabriel Gudmundsson’s cross after the Swede had run off the back of Ben White.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen James Justin (centre) fires Leeds ahead. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/Reuters

Arsenal’s centre-halves, are looking like less of the sum of their parts, with Ezri Konsa and Gabriel uncertain when faced with the accuracy and variation of Leeds’ deliveries.

“It’s a credit to the mentality that Mikel Arteta has created, that even on a tough day they found a way to win”, said Daniel Farke. The German bemoaned the Arsenal equaliser, bundled home by Calafiori after White had knocked down a Madueke cross, believing that if Trafford had got a hand to it, “we would have gone on to take three points.”

With the proviso that there can be no back-slapping in defeat, however, Farke said the match showed his team’s improvement since returning to the Premier League. “We have developed in all aspects,” he said. “You can speak about game management, you can speak about pressing, about compactness against the ball, or quality in possession, or in counterattacks. We were able to compete much better with set pieces.

“Today we came very close to winning an away game against one of the best sides in the world and we played exactly on their level, more or less.”

Sports.title: Real Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior sent off for hair-pulling in victory over Villarreal
Sports.content:
Yan Diomandé earned Real Madrid a tight 1-0 victory over Villarreal to keep them six points behind La Liga leaders Barcelona, even though winger Vinícius Júnior was sent off for hair pulling.

Vinícius, on as a substitute, scored but his goal was disallowed and then he was dismissed after a VAR review showed he had pulled the hair of Villarreal’s Nathan Saliba.

José Mourinho’s side battled through the final stages with 10 men, holding on to win and provisionally going third. But the red card left a bitter taste for Real, with Vinícius running the risk of a potential ban which could keep him out of El Clásico on 25 October.

“I don’t know what’s going on with the referees, with this red card, I don’t understand,” said the Madrid midfielder Aurélien Tchouaméni. “But the most important thing is the victory.”

Kylian Mbappé was fit to start the match for Madrid after suffering a knee problem playing for France during the international break. There were a smattering of whistles for the superstar forward, with some fans believing he has been unprofessional in recent weeks, but also applause from others.

Mbappé, a candidate for the Ballon d’Or trophy later this month, was Madrid’s most threatening player in the first half, although he had little competition.

View image in fullscreen Players react as the referee, Isidro Díaz de Mera Escuderos, sends off Vinícius Júnior. Photograph: Denis Doyle/Getty Images

Mourinho started with out-of-form Vinícius on the bench, following his trips to Australia and India with Brazil during the international break.

Madrid improved defensively, giving Villarreal few chances of note, but struggled to build much in attack themselves in a drab opening half.

Mbappé struck the post from Álvaro Carreras’s lay-off as Madrid pushed Villarreal back early on. Villarreal soon gained a foothold and restricted Madrid’s opportunities, until Mbappé forced a good save from Peter Gulacsi.

There was some more mild whistling for Madrid’s display from their fans at half-time, but soon they were able to celebrate summer arrival Diomandé’s first goal for the club. The Ivorian winger, Madrid’s record signing, produced a sharp low finish into the far corner after good work from Federico Valverde to play him in.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Yan Diomandé scores the only goal of the game at the Bernabéu. Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty Images

Vinícius thought he had doubled Madrid’s lead after Jude Bellingham charged in down the left and cut the ball back for him. However the winger’s joy turned to anger after the referee, Isidro Díaz de Mera Escuderos, was called to watch Vinícius’s hair pull on Saliba in the buildup by VAR and sent off the Brazilian, disallowing his goal.

Madrid’s Belgian goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois, who had made a couple of smart saves earlier in the half, then produced an acrobatic stop to thwart Carlos Romero.

Mbappé was denied again by the Hungarian goalkeeper Gulasci as the forward left the Bernabéu frustrated in his hunt for goals, although his team were able to clinch three important points to stay on Barcelona’s trail.

Sports.title: Ten-man Brighton continue fine form with battling win at Sunderland
Sports.content:
When Jaouen Hadjam lashed Brighton’s second goal low beyond Robin Roefs, it sparked a mass exodus. With a smattering of boos, the Stadium of Light emptied at a speed of knots and frown lines creased the forehead of Sunderland’s manager, Régis Le Bris.

Undaunted by Pascal Struijk’s second-half red card, Brighton had not merely cemented their hold on third place but boosted an already healthy points tally to 13.

This was not quite as fluent as Brighton’s 3-0 deconstruction of Arsenal before the international break, but no one can possibly underestimate their supreme defensive organisation now.

“It wasn’t easy but we always had this belief we could get something here,” said the Brighton manager, Fabian Hürzeler. “We keep clean sheets and we always have chances to score. We’ve always played good football, but I don’t want us just to be known as a nice team anymore.”

Sunderland are stuck on four points with a solitary Premier League victory to their name this season. They head to central Portugal for Thursday’s Europa League meeting with Torreense in introspective mode.

View image in fullscreen Jaouen Hadjam sealed the win for Brighton at the Stadium of Light. Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Ed Sykes/Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Sportsphoto

As a cagey first half unfolded, Kyril Louis-Dreyfus looked on anxiously from the directors’ box. Sunderland’s owner and chair has added the title chief executive to his club portfolio after Tom Burwell’s abrupt departure just five months into the role of interim CEO.

Among the 29-year-old’s more pressing tasks in this hands-on role is to secure a front-of-shirt sponsor after the collapse of a deal with Visit Ghana.

At the interval, Louis-Dreyfus was probably relieved the scoreboard read 0-0. Deep in stoppage time at the end of the first period, Struijk had headed against an upright with Roefs beaten.

View image in fullscreen Enzo Le Fee shows his disappointment after Sunderland’s defeat to Brighton. Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty Images

It was the best chance of a half low on clearcut chances and only really enlivened by some beautiful calibrated deliveries from Enzo Le Fée. Sunderland’s attacking playmaker created decent early openings for Wilson Isidor – deputising for the hamstrung Brian Brobbey – and Thomas Meunier. Significantly, though, Le Fée faded badly in the second half.

In the 53rd minute, a home defence missing the hamstrung Dan Ballard paid the price for a failure to clear a long throw when Pascal Gross’ clever through ball cued up Maxim De Cuyper to slide the crispest of low first-time shots between Roefs and a post. It was the 35-year-old Gross’s seventh direct goal involvement in a Brighton goal in his last six Premier League appearances, but his team were soon reduced to 10 men.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

When a poorly positioned Struijk felled Isidor as he accelerated towards the area the £20m summer signing from Leeds denied a clear goalcoring opportunity, but initially the referee, Tom Bramall, did not see it that way. The video assistant referee urged Bramall to visit the pitchside monitor, which prompted a change of heart and a red card for Struijk.

View image in fullscreen Brighton defender Pascal Struijk was shown a red card after a VAR review for this challenge on Sunderland's Wilson Isidor. Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty Images

Despite their numerical disadvantage, Brighton continued to look comfortable. It did not help Sunderland’s cause that, unusually, Granit Xhaka proved untypically slapdash in possession. Perhaps the strain of admitting to obtaining a fake Covid vaccination certificate during the pandemic – the authorities in Lucerne issued Switzerland’s captain with a suspended £136,000 fine last week – took its toll.

Recent social media footage shows Xhaka demonstrating commendable restraint in the face of jibes from Newcastle fans while out shopping with his wife near their home in Gosforth, but he could have perhaps done with a little more trademark aggression here. In its absence, the visiting substitutes Georginio Rutter and Hadjam combined for the Algeria left-back to strip the shine expertly from Sunderland’s Portuguese trip.

“It was a tight, intense game,” said Le Bris. “But we weren’t at our best. It’s a question of composure. We have to change the momentum.”

Sports.title: Ipswich stun Fulham with last-gasp comeback to increase heat on Arbeloa
Sports.content:
Álvaro Arbeloa bristled at suggestions he cannot handle the pressure after Fulham’s at Ipswich extended their winless start in the Premier League to six matches. The former Real Madrid manager was minutes away from a first managerial victory in the competition after Ryan Sessegnon’s brilliant 55th-minute strike, but the visitors collapsed late on in abject fashion.

Abdoul Ouattara produced a thunderbolt from 30 yards to level for Ipswich after 88 minutes and Dara O’Shea headed home Jack Clarke’s free-kick in the second minute of stoppage time to consign the visitors to a painful loss. Tottenham securing a point at Manchester United pushed Fulham to the bottom of the table.

With his side facing another week in the relegation zone, Arbeloa pushed back at suggestions he is feeling the scrutiny, saying: “I never worry about my position.

“I don’t feel fear. You cannot be a coach if you feel it. You have to work, take the decision and you need to show confidence to your players. I am so happy with many things they are doing. I know it is not easy for them.

“It’s not about my position, it is about Fulham’s position. That is the most important thing. It is just six games, but it is true we need points.”

View image in fullscreen Álvaro Arbeloa reacts during Fulham’s defeat at Ipswich. Photograph: MB Media/Getty Images

Arbeloa walked straight down the tunnel at full-time after shaking hands with his opposite number, Gary O’Neil. Fulham are seven points behind promoted Ipswich as they switch focus to Saturday’s visit of Hull.

Asked how he would block out the noise, Arbeloa said: “Maybe you don’t know me, but I played for the best team in world. I have coached the best team in the world. Maybe you don’t know, but just to let you know, that pressure is part of my life since I was a kid.

View image in fullscreen Dara O’Shea (centre) scores Ipswich’s dramatic late winner at Portman Road. Photograph: Ben Whitley/PA

“It is normal in football. It is normal for players, it is normal for coaches and everybody that is around a team. Pressure is something that is important for me and I like it.”

This defeat made it four league losses this season for Fulham and they have conceded after 75 minutes in matches with Sunderland, Crystal Palace, Manchester United and now Ipswich.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

O’Neil struck a different tone after he celebrated a third victory of the campaign with substitutes Chuba Akpom and Clarke able to make telling contributions during a dramatic finale.

“On the result, I’m proud of the players and proud of the way we finished the game,” O’Neil said. “They showed exactly what they are – together, hard-working, have quality, never going to stop.

“Looked fitter than the opposition, I thought. The last 20 minutes, it looked like they were starting to tire and we were able to keep pushing. The subs helped with that.

“That Fulham side have been in the Premier League for a while now and for us to be able to compete with them the way we did was impressive.”

Sports.title: USWNT exposed by ruthless Spain as early goals settle heavyweight friendly
Sports.content:
In less than a year’s time, the United States and Spain will almost certainly arrive in Brazil as the top two contenders to win the Women’s World Cup. Spain, holders of the top spot in Fifa’s rankings for the past 60 weeks, are the defending champions; the second-ranked US won gold at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

This month’s pair of friendlies between the two sides are taking place with caveats. Both sides are missing several of their most important players to injuries. The opening match in Brazil is 258 days away. Spain have booked their place, but the US still have to actually qualify for the World Cup, through a regional tournament that begins next month.

Even without full-strength rosters, a meeting between these two teams is a compelling bill. And in their first of two friendlies, on Saturday in Washington DC, Spain had the upper hand, scoring twice in the first 14 minutes of a 2-0 win.

“You can’t afford to go 2-0 down against the best team in the world, especially the way we conceded those goals,” US coach Emma Hayes said. “That’s the learning.”

In just the fifth meeting between the two sides and the first since 11 October 2022 – before Spain broke through to win the 2023 World Cup – the reigning champions took advantage of defensive lapses and the US midfield’s struggles. After trailing by two goals for the first time under Emma Hayes, the Americans played a much-improved second half, but failures to convert chances and a stopped penalty kept them scoreless.

In many ways, Saturday’s game and the rematch on Tuesday in Chester, Pennsylvania, are more stress tests than clashes of titans – or causes for alarm bells. Hayes has intentionally crafted this year’s calendar to pit the US against elite competition. The Americans played Japan three times in April, winning twice and losing once, and split a pair of away friendlies against Brazil in June. Saturday was the first time the US ever played the world No 1 in Fifa’s rankings on home soil.

“There’s going to be games like that, and I’m happy it’s not the World Cup right now,” forward Trinity Rodman said. “You take what you can from this game and go into the next game.”

View image in fullscreen Trinity Rodman controls the ball during the United States’ international friendly against Spain at Audi Field in Washington DC on Saturday. Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty Images

A matchup with both sides closer to full strength would have perhaps been more instructive as a preview of a potential World Cup meeting, but such a clash had been ruled out this week. Center-back Naomi Girma and midfielder Sam Coffey, the two players most vital to the US defensive spine, are out with injuries. Spain are missing two-time Ballon d’Or winner Aitana Bonmatí, Vicky Lopez, Mariona Caldentey and Cata Coll with injuries; Clàudia Pina and Mapi León withdrew from camp on Friday.

If the lengthy list of absentees affected Spain, it didn’t show. They went ahead in the third minute on a 20-yard screamer by Patri Guijarro. The US struggled to assemble their shape after a turnover and left the Barcelona midfielder with significant space.

The second goal came just 11 minutes later, the result of another defensive breakdown. Salma Paralluelo isolated Tierna Davidson on the left side and sent a cross to a wide-open Eva Navarro, who fired it for a one-touch finish on the run. All 11 US players huddled above the box for several minutes after conceding.

The US’s connections looked off throughout the first half, from giveaways to overhit clearances. Rose Lavelle attempted to lay off a forward pass with Sophia Wilson and Alyssa Thompson on the break, but both players mistimed their runs and the ball rolled out of bounds to a groan from the Audi Field crowd. Wilson’s best attempts of the half hit the post and rolled wide. The issues in the midfield – for the first 65 minutes, Lavelle, Lily Yohannes and Lindsey Heaps – that predate the Hayes era were evident again.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Spain’s Natalia Ramos reacts during Saturday’s international friendly against the United States at Audi Field. Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty Images

The Americans looked improved and composed in the second half after adjusting their high press. Spain did not produce a shot on target in the second half, and the US outshot them 13-6 on the day. Wilson thought she had scored the US’s first goal in the 53rd minute, but it was waved for offside after video review.

The US earned a penalty in the 67th minute after Wilson drew a foul by Natalia Ramos in the box. The taker was Yohannes – a surprise choice, given the 19-year-old has never attempted a penalty in four seasons at Ajax and OL Lyonnes. Wilson, a regular taker for the Portland Thorns, is a perfect 11 for 11 on penalties in the NWSL. (Yohannes told reporters after the game she was second on the US’s list of takers, behind Heaps.) Adriana Nanclares saved Yohannes’s stutter-step attempt and the Americans remained off the board.

Forward Mallory Swanson and midfielder Ashley Sanchez were among the second-half substitutes. Swanson, who was out for all of 2025 on maternity leave, made her first game appearance in 710 days. Sanchez was recalled to the national team amid a strong NWSL season with the North Carolina Courage and earned her first US minutes since October 2023. She nearly scored off a cross in the 88th minute but slid as her foot connected with the ball.

Spain increased the physicality for the final quarter-hour. They committed 12 fouls to the US’s four and went down to 10 players in stoppage time after Athenea del Castillo saw red for a hair pull.

The US will have a chance to remedy their finishing issues in Tuesday’s rematch in Pennsylvania. They have not gone consecutive games without scoring since the 2023 World Cup.

Sports.title: Cole Palmer casually announces his new Chelsea contract on awkward mock livestream just HOURS before clash with Bournemouth - as Blues star returns to Twitch after being banned for streaming EA FC27 too early
Sports.content:
Cole Palmer has claimed Chelsea are 'going in the right direction' after signing a new long-term contract until 2034. The Chelsea star announced his new deal on a mock Twitch livestream, which saw him respond to fake questions from fans. Palmer read out the question 'How long are you staying at Chelsea then?', with the attacker responding: 'Well, I've just signed a new contract about 20 minutes ago.' 'So I'm staying for about eight more years. 'So hopefully you can sing that song a bit more that you all sing.' The mock Twitch stream comes after Palmer was temporarily suspended from the platform last month after playing EA Sports FC 27 before the game's release, leading to the midfielder appealing for them to lift his ban. Cole Palmer has signed a new long-term deal committing him to Chelsea until 2034 Palmer announced his new contract on a mock Twitch live stream before an official announcement Palmer has insisted Chelsea are heading in the right direction in their pursuit of major trophies Palmer had seven years left to run on his previous deal, but has agreed improved terms with the new contract extending his commitment by a further 12 months. The 24-year-old expressed his belief the Blues are making progress and will be in contention to win major trophies. 'Chelsea means a lot to me and I think the club is going in the right direction, so I'm delighted to sign and I'm obviously very happy,' Palmer said. 'Speaking to the owners, to the sporting directors and obviously the manager, they gave me a lot of confidence so it was only right to sign. 'Speaking to players as well, everyone has the same ambitions. I feel like we can win major trophies here consistently and I want to be a part of that and play a big role in it too.' Palmer has scored 58 goals and provided 34 assists in 138 appearances for Chelsea since joining from Man City in 2023. The attacking midfielder has played a key role in helping the Blues win the FIFA Club World Cup and Conference League in 2025. Palmer has enjoyed a strong start to the season having scored four goals and provided two assists in seven matches. He now boasts one of the longest contracts in the Premier League, with team-mates Joao Pedro and Geovany Quenda also on deals until 2034. Erling Haaland's long-term Manchester City contract also runs until 2034. Despite his performances for Chelsea, Palmer has made just 14 appearances for England. Palmer has enjoyed a strong start to the season, scoring four goals in seven matches Palmer withdrew from the England squad during the recent international break, with Three Lions boss Thomas Tuchel stating he 'misses way too many camps' and that this was 'another missed opportunity'. Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso defended Palmer, with his withdrawal through injury related to the groin problem which has previously plagued him 'We were cautious, and he was cautious as well, he wanted to be,' Alonso said of Palmer. 'He wouldn't have played the way he wants to play. It's sometimes better to take a step back and wait until you feel better and do it the right way. 'There is always a risk. With Morgan (Rogers), there was a risk. Nothing happened. With Jamie (Gittens), there was a risk. We've lost him for a few weeks. With Cole, it was the right decision.'

Sports.title: Christian McCaffrey and Olivia Culpo welcome their second child in the midst of NFL season as they reveal baby boy's adorable name
Sports.content:
Christian McCaffrey and Olivia Culpo welcome their second child in the midst of NFL season as they reveal baby boy's adorable name

San Francisco 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey and wife Olivia Culpo have welcomed their second child, a baby boy named Roman Augustus.

Culpo, a former Miss Universe, revealed the name and Roman's birthday, September 29, in a Saturday post on Instagram. The slides included shots of both her and McCaffrey holding the infant, as well as a photo of Roman meeting his big sister, Colette, who was born in July of 2025. Another slide shows Culpo smiling alongside McCaffrey as she prepares for a C-section birth.

It's unclear if the couple has a particular affinity for Roman history or their young boy's namesake, the emperor born Octavian in 63 BC.

McCaffrey, the son of three-time Super Bowl champion Ed McCaffrey, and his model-influencer wife tied the knot in June 2024 in her native Rhode Island.

Previously, Culpo said she wanted to wait to have another child, but realized she was four months pregnant just six months after giving birth to Colette.

'I did not think that this was going to happen the way that it did,' she said on TikTok in May. 'I am so fortunate to be able to bring another child into the world. Few things that have been running through my mind, 'cause I just really didn't plan on this at all. … Well, I hope that this baby is healthy.'

Christian McCaffrey and wife Olivia Culpo have welcomed their second child, a baby boy

McCaffrey, the son of three-time Super Bowl champion Ed McCaffrey, and his model-influencer wife Olivia Culpo tied the knot in June 2024 in her native Rhode Island

She did note that she was 'definitely not totally healed' from her previous C-section.

'In the beginning, I was like, 'Oh, my God, can I even do this? Is this allowed? Like, what's gonna happen?' she recalled. 'I just wish that I had planned a little better.'

Culpo first made her pregnancy announcement on her 34th birthday with a series of adorable family snapshots from a photoshoot with their daughter Colette and their puppy.

McCaffrey has enjoyed becoming a father, as he told Us Magazine in February.

'It's the best, man,' McCaffrey said. 'Good day or bad day, you come home and seeing her smile takes all the pressure off. It takes all the worries of life away. It's been the biggest blessing in our life.

Culpo shared a photo of her daughter Colette, while pregnant with her new son, Roman

It's unclear if the couple has a particular affinity for Roman history or their young boy's namesake, the emperor born Octavian in 63 BC and later immortalized in countless statues

'Watching Olivia become a mom has been so cool. We had [Colette] in July, which was right before training camp so I was kind of in go-mode and went through the whole season. There's challenges that come with that. So, to now take a breath and be able to be a dad has been really, really fun.'

Since welcoming Colette, the couple have been adapting to their new role as parents while also juggling McCaffrey's commitments on the football field.

She lifted the lid on how fatherhood has changed McCaffrey's perspective on losses in an interview with the New York Post in January while discussing his playoff loss to the Seattle Seahawks.

'Well, first and foremost, I have always been worried about his health and safety,' she told the New York Post. 'If he's feeling good and if I notice, "Okay, he's walking okay or he doesn't look too banged up." I'm really excited and happy. And he feels that way too.

'I think ultimately it's just such a physical sport that you just want to be healthy enough to reach the goals that you have for yourself,' she continued. 'I think just being there for him and definitely being sensitive to the fact that it does mean a lot and sometimes he will be upset.

Last summer, the couple announced the birth of Colette, their first baby together

In addition to their two children, the couple also shares a small dog named Oliver Sprinkles

'Having a baby there really has changed that and made everything feel a little bit more grounded and light — and just have a better perspective because… win or lose, you still have to show up for her.'

Culpo continued: 'I always knew he would be a really good dad because he's just a really good person. And his parents [Lisa and former NFL wideout Ed McCaffrey] are just a great example.

'But I feel like I'm happy for the perspective that it's able to give him, especially with his career,' she said. 'So I'm very grateful for that.'

A three-time All-Pro now in his 10th NFL season, McCaffrey had a successful campaign in 2025 after becoming a father, rushing for 1,202 yards and 10 touchdowns to go with 924 yards and seven more scores through the passing game.

Most importantly, he appeared in all 17 games for the 49ers, who fell to the eventual Super Bowl-champion Seahawks in the Divisional Round of the playoffs.

This year, the 49ers are off to a 4-0 start thanks to 340 yards from scrimmage and four touchdowns from McCaffrey.

Sports.title: 'Worried' Gary Neville tells struggling Man United stars to 'get a grip' after Spurs draw ahead of tough run - as he warns midfield duo CAN'T play together and calls out lack of fight in Michael Carrick's men
Sports.content:
A frustrated Gary Neville has again accused Manchester United's players of lacking effort in their draw with Tottenham and warned they risk being 'eaten alive' by Atletico Madrid in midweek if they don't buck their ideas up.

The Red Devils were twice booed off at Old Trafford on Saturday evening as they conceded a late equaliser against ten-man Spurs to take their winless run to four games in all competitions.

But there seems to be a lack of fight from the team, according to Neville, with fans already questioning the side's desire to run after Youri Tielemans said they didn't do much work in that area of the game over pre-season.

Coupled with United's poor running numbers so far this season, and there are serious questions around the team's play – and Neville has once again taken aim.

'What United fans won't accept is what they deem as a lack of effort and the reality is they're not running enough, they're not showing enough tenacity, determination and fighting spirit,' he said on The Gary Neville Podcast. 'The boos tell you they are really despondent with what they are watching.

'What we are seeing at the moment is a team that looks like they are curling up in a ball and the club, for some of them right now, is getting a bit big for them.

Gary Neville has told Manchester United's players to 'get a grip' following their draw with Tottenham on Saturday

United are winless in four and were poor against 10-man Spurs, who scored a last-minute goal

'The shake of Carrick's head will be... are they doing it for me? What's happening with that lot? Have they lost their confidence? Have they switched off? Are they going under? What is going on? Because these aren't the players I was working with last season.'

United will face Atletico in midweek in the Champions League and face the prospect of a tough task at the Metropolitano despite a win in their first match of the Champions League league phase.

Atletico are second in LaLiga and beat Real Madrid in the Madrid derby the week before the international break.

There is also, meanwhile, concern around United's personnel – particularly in midfield. Something that Neville thinks needs to be looked at.

'With (Youri) Tielemans and (Kobbie) Mainoo, I think we've seen enough of it now,' Neville said. 'I'm not calling time on it because I think that's probably too drastic - but I've seen enough of it to think it's not dynamic enough to play at this football club in the Premier League. They are both good players individually but sometimes you have players who just don't quite knit together and suit each other.

'When (Carlos) Baleba came on with Mainoo, that certainly looked more like there was more energy but there is going to have to be something done in there and the rest of them are going to have to get a grip.

'They're going to Atletico and then to Elland Road, and if you're not quite right there mentally and physically, you're going to get found out. If they don't get going, it's going to be a worrying few weeks.'

Neville also said it's time for United to stop playing Youri Tielemans (left) and Kobbie Mainoo (right) in midfield together

Michael Carrick's side will head to Spain to take on Atletico Madrid in the Champions League this week

Speaking on United's lack of apparent effort, he added: 'It is a real concern, going into a slog where you are playing every three days and the Champions League is going to hit you hard.

'You've got tough matches and all of the games coming up are going to need real personality and character, and it needs a group of players who are resilient and at the moment you do worry about them going into that run of matches and how they are going to come out of it.

'That three-week break was supposed to be a reset moment. But how you can perform like that in the first 20 minutes is really difficult to understand.'

Sports.title: Feckless Man United were dreadful and embarrassing at times in Spurs draw: Play like this in a week of reckoning and Michael Carrick will be clinging to his job, writes IAN LADYMAN
Sports.content:
Feckless Man United were dreadful and embarrassing at times in Spurs draw: Play like this in a week of reckoning and Michael Carrick will be clinging to his job, writes IAN LADYMAN

At Old Trafford they revelled in what they believe will be the imminent downfall of their neighbours at Manchester City. They sang their songs about cheats and about relegation. They dragged old banners down from the loft and repurposed them. They bedded in for what they believe and hope will be a long and tortuous decline for the team from the east part of town.

But then they watched their own team play and reality came crashing in like a hangover after a good night out. It’s hard to revel in the problems of others when your own team is as bad and as feckless as this.

Manchester United almost got away with it here. They were largely dreadful – embarrassingly and shamefully so in the first half – but looked set to win after a Bryan Mbeumo goal was followed by the sending off of Tottenham substitute Rodrigo Bentancur.

The Uruguayan’s headbutt on Luke Shaw stands out as one of the most stunning acts of self-harm in a Spurs season that has had a few. What an idiot.

Before that Spurs had dominated but missed chances. We have seen this gory movie from Roberto de Zerbi’s team a few times already this season. As such United looked to somehow go home with only their second Premier League win of the season. Huge cracks looked set to be covered by three points on this occasion at least.

Dominic Solanke's late leveller rescued Tottenham a point at Old Trafford

For the second home league game running, United could not manage to beat ten men

The boos at the end at Old Trafford were loud and long and thoroughly deserved

But for the second home league game running, United could not manage to beat ten men. Last time it was City and a 1-0 defeat here after Phil Foden’s red card. This time it was an injury time Dominic Solanke goal that did for them. The boos at the end were loud and long and thoroughly deserved.

United have a heck of a week ahead now. Atletico Madrid in the Champions League on Tuesday and Leeds United next Sunday. Both away. If they play anything like this they lose both and Michael Carrick will be clinging on to his job before we have even bought our fireworks.

Worryingly for the United manager, his team don’t look particularly well coached and in a first half that Tottenham dominated didn’t look that keen to run around very much either.

Remember when Gary Neville had them for not trying hard enough in that 1-1 draw at Fulham before the international break? Well, this was worse.

United should have been two goals down after 25 minutes. The reason they weren’t lay in the identity of the opposition. Spurs were impressive for large parts of this game. Conor Gallagher was magnificent while Archie Gray was not far behind. But they have forgotten how to win so once again they didn’t.

Rodrigo Bentancur’s headbutt on Luke Shaw stands out as one of the most stunning acts of self-harm in a Spurs season that has had a few

Bentancur was fortunate his act of stupidity didn't cost his side

Still it’s not hard to see how Tottenham get out of the mess they are in down the near the foot of the table. Their results feel as though they will turn. United? They just don’t look good enough.

Carrick and his staff had three weeks to think about this game, to work out how to correct the problems of early-season. Yet United’s first-half football was moribund. They were outplayed by Tottenham from the opening minute and, more damningly, they were outrun too.

We have seen this before from Spurs this season. Good football and no goals. Here they did everything but score.

Solanke, later to be the hero, was the most obvious culprit of the first half. In just the third minute, United goalkeeper Senne Lammens passed the ball straight to Lucas Bergvall and when he played Solanke through, he allowed Lammens to save when he should have been given no chance.

That set the tone for the half. Spurs – with key players on the bench for a variety of reasons – were organised and purposeful and energetic. Gallagher was excellent while Savio and Mohammed Kudus carried threat if not always the right end product.

United, by contrast, were lame. They seemed content to let Spurs come on to them and only started to muster some kind of momentum on the break in the final ten minutes of the half.

Spurs were particularly progressive down their left where United’s emergency right-back Leny Yoro had a difficult time. A goal should have come from there in the 21st minute when a nice combination allowed Savio to feed Kudus only for the shot on the turn to fly by the post.

Bryan Mbeumo's clever strike had given the hosts the lead

There was also a shot over the bar from Bergvall and a break into the box by Gallagher that was halted by a desperate but timely toe-poke from the retreating Youri Tielemans.

On the touchline De Zerbi looked grimly frustrated and no wonder.

Early in the second half Savio was again away down the left and once again his low cross almost led to something for his team but didn’t. Then, a minute later, the Brazilian did find Solanke in the middle only for another good chance to go begging, this time over the bar.

Later on a misdirected Harry Maguire interception allowed Savio in only for Kobbie Mainoo to divert the shot over. In between all that United had shown some belated promise.

New signing Carlos Baleba was rapturously welcomed when he emerged as a substitute and his first contribution was to control the ball beautifully and send Fernandes away down the left.

But it was another substitute, Joshua Zirkzee, who impacted the game more significantly. The Dutch forward started to link play better and hold up the ball. It enabled United to get up the pitch more regularly and, with eighteen minutes left, they somehow took the lead.

Mbeumo is a reliable finisher and he took this one well. Turning on to his left foot in the penalty area, he shot low across Antonin Kinsky and into the far corner after taking a pass from Matheus Cunha. But with at least five Spurs players in the vicinity, he simply should not have been given that amount of time.

For Spurs, another disaster loomed. And things soon got an awful lot harder.

Bentancur’s lunging tackle at Fernandes was not clever but the headbutt he planted on Shaw after the United player arrived to shove him in the chest was just stupid. Briefly chaos reigned by the near touchline. Players, coaches. They were all in. When it settled down, Spurs were a man down and a goal down.

Now United boss Michael Carrick faces a huge week which may define his future

United just had to manage the game now. Given what we have seen from them this season, it was far from a given that they would. And, perhaps quite predictably, they didn’t.

Two minutes into eight minutes of time added, Sandro Tonali – by now playing at left-back – crossed to the far post for Solanke to head in.

It was a marvellous effort by a striker with something to prove. Why United defender Lisandro Martinez attempted to wrestle him instead of looking at the ball, maybe only he will know.

As his team celebrated in the corner, De Zerbi clutched a spare ball and appeared to try and eat it. The Italian may feel his luck is about to change. It should do. His team looked well coached here. By contrast, United continue to exist on a mixture of vague hope and sense of history. Neither will be good enough in the long term.

Sports.title: 'Hurt' Michael Carrick rues Man United's failure to kill game against 10-man Spurs - as Roberto De Zerbi reveals Rodrigo Bentancur's red card inspired his side
Sports.content:
'Hurt' Michael Carrick rues Man United's failure to kill game against 10-man Spurs - as Roberto De Zerbi reveals Rodrigo Bentancur's red card inspired his side

Michael Carrick was left to rue Manchester United's failure to kill off 10-man Tottenham after Rodrigo Bentancur was sent off for headbutting Luke Shaw at Old Trafford.

Carrick admitted it 'hurt' to be booed by fans after Dominic Solanke struck in injury-time to give Spurs a 1-1 draw and leave United with six points from six league games – their worst start in 40 years since Sir Alex Ferguson replaced Ron Atkinson in November 1986.

It was the second Premier League game in a row at home that United – who also conceded a late equaliser at Everton last month – couldn't beat 10 men after losing the Old Trafford derby to Manchester City.

'When things aren't quite going to plan, I understand the reaction at times,' said Carrick of the boos at the end of both halves. 'Obviously, it hurts, you know. It hurts a lot. It's not nice to go through, but sometimes you have to go through it.

'I care as much as anybody about this club. But it's coming from a good place really, and so I understand it.

'I'm not happy with the amount of points we've had so far. There's no hiding from that. I'm not hiding. That's the reality and we've got to accept it. We need to put things in a positive direction quite quickly, that's pretty plain.

Michael Carrick was left frustrated at his Man United side's 1-1 draw with Spurs on Saturday

'That's two late, late goals against us to throw away two wins. So that changes a lot of things. It changes the feelings among ourselves and it changes the points.

'We need to do better with seeing out games once we get ourselves in a good position, that's for sure. We're more than capable of doing that. We've just got to be a little bit more streetwise in the moments and a little bit more stubborn and strong.

'It's definitely something where, 10 men or not 10 men, if we're ahead in games, we've got to see them out.'

Tottenham are still without a win in their six Premier League games this season, but the manner of their performance and fightback gave Roberto De Zerbi plenty of reason to feel positive.

The Italian admitted that Bentancur's reaction to being pushed by Shaw was the wrong one, but bizarrely revealed that he kissed the player in the dressing-room afterwards because he showed some fighting spirit.

'I kissed Rodrigo and say thanks,' revealed De Zerbi. 'It is clearly a mistake from Rodrigo, it is not the right reaction in football.

'But now Tottenham needs to react. Sometimes the reaction is not nice, not positive for the team, but in that moment maybe with 10 players we played with more courage more energy.

'For a long time Tottenham played without this blood and this character. Now I am the coach and I want to see this character every game. With the qualities and the character and the right energy, we are going to win many games and score many goals.'

Sports.title: 'Stupid' Rodrigo Bentancur sparks mass brawl after HEADBUTTING Luke Shaw as Spurs star is sent off in clash with Man United
Sports.content:
'Stupid' Rodrigo Bentancur sparks mass brawl after HEADBUTTING Luke Shaw as Spurs star is sent off in clash with Man United

Tottenham midfielder Rodrigo Bentancur was branded 'stupid' by Gary Neville after headbutting Luke Shaw and seeing red against Manchester United.

Bentancur had only been on the pitch for 12 minutes as a second-half substitute, but lost his cool in the 78th minute when he lashed out at Shaw and was given his marching orders.

He appeared to put a high tackle in on the left back, who was left fuming and chased his opponent down before pushing him to the ground.

Bentancur responded by rushing to his feet and headbutting Shaw, resulting in a brawl between the players.

'Madness from Bentancur,' Neville said on Sky Sports. 'Lack of discipline is not what he (Roberto De Zerbi) needs.

'It's stupidity. It really is.'

Rodrigo Bentancur is sent off... and here's why ⬇️ pic.twitter.com/3ahzz5iUbg — Sky Sports Premier League (@SkySportsPL) October 10, 2026

Rodrigo Bentancur (left) was sent off for Tottenham against Manchester United after headbutting Luke Shaw

The Uruguay international had to be pulled away from Shaw, who was booked, by United defender Lisandro Martinez.

A member of Tottenham's coaching staff had to eventually escort him down the Old Trafford tunnel.

Tottenham were already 1-0 down at the time, after dominating the first-half but failing to find the back of the net – a problem they have had regularly this season.

Tottenham boss Roberto De Zerbi, meanwhile, said after the game: 'I kissed Bentancur in the dressing room. We need this type of character. Football is character.'

United got their act together in the second period and went 1-0 up through Bryan Mbeumo, and Bentancur's actions made it a near-impossible task for Roberto De Zerbi's side to come back.

They did, though, manage to do just that in stoppage time when Dominic Solanke converted a cross to leave Old Trafford stunned.

Spurs are, though, still without a win this season. They did, however, move from bottom to 18th in the table.

More to follow.

Sports.title: Man United 1-1 Tottenham PLAYER RATINGS: Who has lacked composure all season? And which summer signing put in his best display in a Spurs shirt? Now have YOUR say
Sports.content:
In a game neither side could afford to lose, Manchester United and Tottenham played out a 1-1 draw – though the match was short of anything but drama. Spurs dominated the first-half at Old Trafford but, as has been the case for them so often this season, failed to find the back of the net. United regrouped after the break and took the lead through Bryan Mbeumo, and it looked as though it would be tough for Spurs to come back when they were reduced to ten men. Rodrigo Bentancur saw red when he headbutted Luke Shaw in the 78th minute but that didn't deter the away side. Dominic Solanke got in front of Lisandro Martinez to head in an equaliser, and it was enough for Spurs to take a point back to north London. Daily Mail Sport's CHRIS WHEELER and MATT BARLOW were at Old Trafford to rate the players. Manchester United conceded a late equaliser to throw away three points against Tottenham Man United (4-2-3-1) SENNE LAMMENS – 5 Has lacked the same composure since his mistake for Belgium at the World Cup. Poor pass out to Mainoo almost cost United early on but at least he made amends with a smart save from Solanke. LENY YORO – 5 Played out of position again at right back and Spurs focussed on that side of United’s defence but produced two fine interception tackles on Van Hecke and Udogie. HARRY MAGUIRE – 6 It said much about United’s lack of creativity that the big defender decided to try his luck from 30 yards towards the end. Otherwise looked solid up against the physical challenge from Solanke. LISANDRO MARTINEZ – 4 Put just enough pressure on Solanke to force him to fire over in front of goal early in the second-half but was outmuscled by the Spurs striker when he equalised to such an extent that Martinez’s back was facing the ball as it came over. LUKE SHAW – 6 Kept Kudus in check on United’s left and was involved in the main flashpoint of the game towards the end when he reacted angrily to a wild challenge from Bentancur who was sent off for aiming a headbutt at him. YOURI TIELEMANS – 4 Struggled against the energy of Bergvall and Tonali in midfield. Did well to track back and get a vital touch to deny Gallagher a one-on-one chance before half-time. KOBBIE MAINOO – 5 Carrick said the England midfielder had done a little bit of training since pulling out of international duty but not enough on this evidence. Vital block to divert Savio’s close-range shot over in the second half. AMAD DIALLO – 6 Available for the first time this season and went straight into the starting line-up. Probably United’s most dangerous player during his hour on the pitch, but fired tamely at Kinsky with their only chance of the first half and skied another effort into the Stretford End. Amad Diallo was available for the first time this season for United and was United's most dangerous player while he was on the pitch BRUNO FERNANDES – 5 Carried a knock playing for Portugal in the international break and looked like it was still affecting him. Very subdued performance by his standards. MATHEUS CUNHA – 5 The Brazilian has been more effective off the left than as a false nine, and had a hand in the goal. But struggled for much of the game and spent too much time on the floor moaning at the officials. BRYAN MBEUMO – 7 Amad’s return allowed him to play through the middle, as he did in pre-season, but came to life after reverting to the right before the hour mark as he scored a goal and went close to a second. Subs DIOGO DALOT (for Yoro 59) – 6 Booked late on and part of a treble change that was dearly needed. CARLOS BALEBA (for Tielemans 59) – 6 What a boost it is for United to have him available. United were better with him on the field. JOSHUA ZIRKZEE (for Diallo 59) – 7 Provided a different option for his side and may find himself being used more than expected depending on Benjamin Sesko's injury status. MARCUS RASHFORD (for Cunha 90+5) Manager MICHAEL CARRICK – 6 A big game for him. Always stone-faced, but will surely be feeling the pressure. Had to cop a lot of stick at various times during the game, and will be livid with how his side finished proceedings. Still under the cosh. Bryan Mbeumo, meanwhile, scored United's goal but was best when he moved to the right Tottenham (4-2-3-1) ANTONIN KINSKY – 6 A complete bystander for the first half hour and very little to do overall. Not a lot he could do when beaten by Mbeumo. Save to deny the United goalscorer a second priceless when Solanke levelled in stoppage time. ARCHIE GRAY – 6 Solid and determined. Does not always look entirely comfortable at right back but his greatest asset is that he keeps going and refuses to buckle. Kept Cunha quiet for most of the first half forcing Carrick to switch him and Fernandes. Booked. JAN PAUL VAN HECKE – 5 Sometimes erratic on the ball. Won headers albeit against an attack with little aerial threat. Made tackles on the edge of the penalty box but easily turned by Mbeumo for the United goal. Booked. MARCOS SENESI – 7 Exuded calm, read the game and used the ball well. Forged a good understanding with Van Hecke. Replaced in the closing stages when De Zerbi wanted Fernandes on. DESTINY UDOGIE – 7 Kept Amad quiet and drove forward to dovetail well with Savio in the first half. Alert on the cover to make a couple of vital clearances in the second half. Jan Paul van Hecke (right) was erratic on the ball and found himself spun for United's goal LUCAS BERGVALL – 6 Terrific energy in opening phase when Spurs took control. Won the ball for early Solanke chance. More vertical drive than Bentancur and fewer mistakes in possession. Faded and replaced. SANDRO TONALI – 6 Perhaps his best display in a Spurs shirt. Read the game, shielded his centre halves and covered the ground effectively. Still expect more quality on the ball and eventually it came. He was operating as a left back when he produced the cross for Solanke’s goal. MOHAMMED KUDUS – 5 Bright opening on his first start since January. Got on the ball and tried to create. Good chance squandered in the first half when he fired wide. Faded and withdrawn on 66 minutes. CONOR GALLAGHER – 7 Exceptional work-rate and effective in the first half. Glimpse of goal denied by an excellent recovery by Tielemans just before half-time. Less influential after half time but still industrious. Booked. SAVIO – 6 Playing on the left, where his pace off the mark brought early successes one-v-one against Yoro. Quick on the break, good chance created for Solanke second half. Switched to the right when Marmoush came on. DOMINIC SOLANKE – 6 Surprise captain, showed strength to lead the line and occupied United’s centre halves. Wasted glorious chances at the start of each half but kept going and equalised with a glancing header in stoppage time. Dominic Solanke (right) was Tottenham's surprise captian for the day and did well tohead a late equaliser for his side SUBS OMAR MARMOUSH (on for Kudus 66 mins) – 4 Made little impact as the game slipped away from Spurs. RODRIGO BENTANCUR (on for Bergvall 66 mins) – 3 Ruined any hopes of a real fightback. First, a reckless tackle and then up to headbutt Shaw sparking a mass skirmish and leaving Spurs to finish the game with ten men. JAMES MADDISON – (on for Gallagher 74 mins) – 5 United scored as he was waiting to come on and the game changed again with the red card soon after. Tried to get on the ball and make things happen. MICKY VAN DE VEN (on for Udogie 74 mins) – 5 Came on at left back and ended up back in the middle after Senesi’s late exit. MATEUS FERNANDES (on for Senesi 90 mins) MANAGER ROBERTO DE ZERBI – 6 Rewarded for his faith in the front four he has been working with over the international break. They started at an impressive tempo but could not capitalise. Subs backfired when Bentancur was sent off but will love the spirit shown to fight back.
