World.title: The Kennedy Center names new artistic director, amid concerns
World.content:
The Kennedy Center names new artistic director, amid concerns

toggle caption i Saul Loeb/AFP/via Getty Images

The Kennedy Center has named Rick Canny, a talent manager who has worked with acts including ZZ Top and former Mötley Crüe drummer Tommy Lee, as its new artistic director. His appointment came despite complaints from staff about his business practices as a consultant for the arts institution.

According to an email obtained by NPR sent to high-level staff Thursday, Matt Floca, the center's executive director and chief operating officer, announced that Canny would be the center's new artistic director. Canny has served as a consultant to the Kennedy Center since shortly after President Trump became the institution's chairman in February 2025.

Sponsor Message

Floca has no background in arts administration, programming or fundraising, in contrast to chief administrators at similar performing arts venues around the country. He was previously head of facilities at the Kennedy Center before being promoted in March , and holds a degree in construction management.

Floca wrote: "Rick will advise me and the broader leadership team on artistic strategy, business practices, presenting and talent curation, ticketing and pricing models, media opportunities, and programming sponsorships."

Floca also wrote: "Since April 2025, Rick has worked with the Center as a consultant through his firm, Favor the Artist, including serving as creative lead for the Kennedy Center Honors and the Mark Twain Prize. He will continue in this capacity while serving as the Center's Artistic Director."

Concerns about fees and expense

The Kennedy Center is mostly closed, but it says it will maintain a small amount of public and educational programming, while the entire closure is being contested in federal court. The previous head of programming came and left within two weeks in January .

Arts administrators around the country have told NPR that booking performances for performing arts centers is done years in advance.

The Kennedy Center did not respond to NPR's requests for comment on Canny's appointment, but confirmed the contents of the email. Canny also did not respond to multiple requests for comment.

Sponsor Message

Favor the Artist 's website does not include any information about its client roster or about the firm's history. The published lists of his professional background indicate that Canny has little experience in programming the kinds of performers more typically booked at a venue such as the Kennedy Center, including marquee contemporary solo performers and groups, orchestras, and dance and theater troupes.

NPR has obtained an internal memo written in March by the center's then-senior director of music programming, Sammy Miller, raising concerns about fees and expenses charged by Canny. NPR has reached out to Miller for comment, but did not receive a reply.

In that memo, sent to Floca and the Kennedy Center's human resources department, Miller said that during one month in early 2026, Canny had charged the center $30,000 in consulting fees. And in another month, Canny had charged over $28,000 in fees and travel expenses, including two first-class round-trip flights between Los Angeles and Washington, D.C.

The Kennedy Center did not reply to NPR's request for comment regarding staff concerns about Canny. In a statement to The New York Times on Friday, the center said that the $30,000 fee "did not reflect Mr. Canny's current agreement," but did not provide specifics. The institution also told the Times that Canny's travel expenses had been reviewed.

Miller wrote that he had previously tried to resolve his concerns through the center's general counsel and its finance office, but "both offices appear to be protecting Mr. Canny."

In its recent public statements and court filings, the Kennedy Center has repeatedly claimed to be on the verge of bankruptcy . Last month, Trump said that the arts institution has lost "hundreds of millions" of dollars. Trump has not offered evidence to support that claim.

World.title: At least 2 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama
World.content:
At least 2 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama

toggle caption i Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images

Emergency crews in Florida and Alabama are surveying damage wrought by Hurricane Isaias, after the storm bashed into the Gulf Coast as a Category 2 storm Friday night. At least two people have died from storm-related incidents, NPR has confirmed.

Isaias brought 105 mph winds onshore, snapping trees and knocking out electricity. Officials warn that flash flood threats persist, but further inland.

One death occurred in Escambia County, in the far west of the Florida Panhandle. Shortly before 9 p.m. local time Friday, a rescue team found a person pinned under a large tree, according to Sgt. Melony Peterson of the Escambia County Sheriff's Office.

"The victim was inside the home when the tree collapsed," Peterson said via email.

Another death was reported in Jefferson County, Ala., which includes Birmingham.

"We did have a storm-related fatality overnight," Jefferson County Emergency Management Agency Director Jim Coker told NPR. "A tree did fall on the house," Coker added. "It was a single-family residence."

toggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images

As of 11:50 a.m. ET Saturday, about 780,000 power customers remained without power in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, according to the monitoring site Poweroutage.us . That figure had been closer to 900,000 earlier Saturday.

Sponsor Message

In Florida, the worst outages were in counties such as Santa Rosa; Holmes; Washington; and Walton – all of which had more than 80% of their residents without power, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference.

The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners.

"Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges.

toggle caption i Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to the National Hurricane Center . It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if landfall coincided with peak high tide. It arrived roughly two hours before high tide in Destin.

Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. By 5 a.m. local time on Saturday, its sustained winds had dropped to 35 mph, as the system sped its way through Alabama.

"Multiple trees and power lines are down across the county," tweeted the emergency management agency in Jefferson County, Ala. It told residents to "avoid unnecessary travel if possible while crews clear roads and restore service."

World.title: Opinion: Can I keep the baseball I caught?
World.content:
Opinion: Can I keep the baseball I caught?

toggle caption i Colin Hubbard/AP

This week, an ethical question, of all things, intruded into the baseball playoffs.

Tuesday night, Dodgers versus Braves, in Atlanta. A young man in a Dodger jersey caught a foul ball in the stands. As so often happens these days, someone seated nearby captured it on video, and then felt compelled to instruct the man, "Give it to the kid! Give it to the kid!"

And indeed there was a small boy, maybe preschool-aged, a few rows back in a Braves jersey.

But the Dodgers fan looked into the man's camera and told what turned out to be millions of viewers on social media, "I'm sorry, I can't! I'm not giving it to the kid! I feel bad, but I'm not giving it to the kid!"

Sponsor Message

Some commenters denounced the man for keeping the ball. Some others have inveighed against the little boy for looking disappointed.

Before we criticize anyone's ethics, we ought to ask ourselves: what would we do if a baseball fell into our hands at a playoff game? Keep it, or give it to the nearest child?

Because I am a father, I'm pretty certain I would give it to a child. But also because I'm a father, I know that within a few days, the ball so tenderly bequeathed might have rolled, abandoned, under a bed, surrounded by lost socks and forgotten Labubus.

Also, a foul ball hit by almost any player would be a nice souvenir. But what if it had been a home run struck by, say, Shohei Ohtani? That ball could be as much of an investment as a Picasso!

We sought ethical advice from Nancy Sherman, a Professor of Philosophy at Georgetown University, who told us, "Manners are not morals."

The professor said she was mostly alarmed by the public shaming of both man and boy, who, after all, were not aware that their instinctive, personal reactions would soon be turned into some kind of moral exercise for the digital age.

Sponsor Message

"The young guy who caught the ball says, 'I'm sorry…I feel bad, but I'm not giving it to the kid'"… says Professor Sherman. "I think that's a healthy, honest response."

So the next time you go to a game - if a fly ball seems to be arcing your way, you might pause before you reach for it to ask yourself, "Do I really want this ethical dilemma?"

World.title: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often
World.content:
Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often

toggle caption i The Engel family

Todd Engel had operated heavy machinery, like forklifts and rubber-tire loaders, around warehouses and highways in suburban Maryland for four decades.

In early 2023, Engel's doctor put him on Ozempic, a GLP-1, for diabetes. That winter, on New Year's Eve, Engel woke up feeling as if a patch covered his right eye: "I couldn't see anything. It was all dark. It was black."

The doctor told Engel and his wife Shelley it was a form of optic neuropathy — NAION, for short – an inoperable condition caused by tiny strokes that cut off blood flow to his eye. When the doctor listed all known causes, Shelley Engel specifically asked about Ozempic. "'We have heard nothing about that,'" she recalls the doctor telling her.

Sponsor Message

Seven months later, the journal JAMA Ophthalmology did publish research showing higher rates of NAION among diabetic patients taking Ozempic, or semaglutide, as the active ingredient name is known. But neither Engel nor his doctor were aware, so Engel kept taking weekly shots until his left eye went black, just as the other had done the year prior.

More than one in 10 Americans are taking a GLP-1 drug for weight loss, according to a recent Gallup analysis, and one in seven has taken them at some point. The drugs are prescribed for a growing number of conditions and come with a range of side effects.

Engel has filed a lawsuit alleging the maker of Ozempic, Novo Nordisk, failed to warn patients and doctors about the risk of NAION.

His suit is part of two main ongoing consolidated lawsuits alleging life-threatening or life-altering harm from GLP-1 drugs.

In a statement to NPR, spokespeople for Novo Nordisk pointed to subsequent research casting doubt on whether their GLP-1 drug causes NAION, for example, and said the cases are without merit.

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

The legal question before the courts hinges in part on whether the GLP-1 drugs caused the harm. Observational data can show correlation — that people taking GLP-1s were perhaps more likely to have this eye complication occur — but not causation. For that, more detailed investigation is needed.

Sponsor Message

When the JAMA Ophthalmology study came out showing the correlation between NAION and diabetic patients on Ozempic or semaglutide, two medical groups critiqued it. The American Academy of Ophthalmology and the North American Neuro-Ophthalmology Society issued their own consumer clarification saying, in part: "This is not the type of study that can show the treatment caused NAION." The groups did acknowledge there is a potential link, but further research would be necessary to determine that. For now, they don't recommend that patients stop taking their GLP-1s.

A partial database

The Food and Drug Administration keeps a database tracking adverse events. It's one of the only mechanisms for doctors, patients and drug companies to submit reports of complications possibly linked to pharmaceuticals. Reporting is mostly voluntary and the agency does not verify the reports, but it is a crucial first step to prompt regulators to do further research and eventually decide, for example, if labels need updating.

In this database, NPR found more than 1,000 reports of optic neuropathy linked to GLP-1s since 2024. That's out of nearly 190,000 reports made about the drug over that period, most of which included minor gastrointestinal issues, dosing errors or injection site redness.

Spokespeople for Novo Nordisk — maker of Ozempic and Wegovy — say NAION and other serious conditions are exceedingly rare in clinical trials. The company continues to collect and share data with the FDA about the side effects reported with the drug since going to market, but the agency has not requested warning-label changes. The FDA said in an email to NPR it has undertaken its own study to assess NAION risks, and is assessing claims and will "determine the need for regulatory action" once its assessment is complete.

The legal challenge

That is not sufficient for patients today, says attorney Jonathan Orent, a lead court-appointed attorney on the two major multi-district litigation lawsuits alleging harms from GLP-1 drugs. He says drug makers ought to update warnings to doctors and patients — as they have in Europe — even if the conditions are rare.

Sponsor Message

It's necessary, Orent says, because "you're never going to have the population size to detect rarer events in a clinical trial; you're also never going to have the diversity of your real world population."

Orent's cases include 247 plaintiffs with NAION, and more than 4,000 with other serious digestive conditions like pancreatitis or gall stones. "These warnings would have made a difference in the lives of real people," he argues. In an emailed statement, Eli Lilly, whose GLP-1 drug brands Mounjaro and Zepbound contain the active ingredient tirzepatide said it will "vigorously defend against these claims."

NPR's analysis of the FDA's adverse events data show 1,928 reports of pancreatitis since 2024. (Other forms of pancreatitis are also listed, including 135 cases of necrotizing pancreatitis.)

Engel says he would've stopped taking Ozempic had he known that it might have put him at risk for blindness. Now, he mourns all he's lost, including the ability to work or walk the beach unaided. "Being able to play ball … with my grandchildren, I can't do these things anymore," he says. "I will never, never be able to see my wife's beautiful face every day."

Uncertainty in reporting

Obesity and diabetes are complex metabolic diseases that affect many organs, and increase risks for other ailments. That's part of what makes it hard to pinpoint whether problems that patients encounter on GLP-1 drugs are caused by the drugs themselves.

That's part of why Emory University diabetes specialist Mohammed Ali, for example, did not report any of the three patients he's treated who developed serious problems, like pancreatitis or gallstones, while taking GLP-1s, to the FDA's adverse events database.

He says he wasn't certain those problems were caused by the drugs themselves, even if the timing was suspicious.

"They may have had subclinical disease," Ali says. "In other words, we didn't know they had preexisting pancreatitis or preexisting gallstones."

Sponsor Message

Calls to poison control

The boom in online sales, where GLP-1s are heavily marketed, also adds to the challenge, says pharmacist Robert Miller at the West Texas Poison Control Center.

Buying drugs on Instagram? "That's definitely a new thing," Miller says, and many sites offer little to no medical supervision of patients. That's why, he says, more calls are coming into poison-control centers like his, with patients reporting vomiting or other GLP-1 side effects.

"So is there even a physician who's motivated to report side effects or someone the patient feels they can report those side effects to?" he says.

These questions are playing out now in court, where plaintiffs like the Engels are seeking damages from drugmakers.

But Shelley Engel also wants more side-effect warnings, which she says might've helped her husband avoid blindness. She says her husband's outgoing, vivacious personality has changed

"This could have been prevented, if we only knew," she says.



NPR correspondent Sydney Lupkin contributed to this report.

World.title: Saudi-led coalition vows retaliation after deadly Houthi attack on Riyadh airport
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The latest attack on Riyadh's international airport killed at least 12 people, officials said Saturday, as a Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen. The third attack this week on King Khalid International Airport also left more than 300 others injured.

The third attack this week on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday left at least 12 people dead and more than 300 ‌wounded, Saudi authorities said, as Yemen's Houthis escalated the campaign they launched this summer against the kingdom.

The dead included four Saudis, two people from Bangladesh and one person each from the U.S., Jordan, Palestine, Syria, Sudan and Egypt, the Saudi civil aviation authority said. At the latest count, officials said, 309 were wounded.

Hospitals were flooded with wounded brought by ambulance and helicopter, people briefed on the matter said. Some were in critical condition.

Saturday's attack, the ​deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade, occurred without warning, with no alert issued ​by Saudi Arabia's threat warning system. This week's two previous attacks on King Khalid International Airport left four people dead and caused heavy damage to a Saudi commercial plane parked on the tarmac.

The deadly strikes exposed vulnerabilities in the kingdom's defence capabilities as it wages an ​air campaign against the Houthis to support a ground war by the Yemeni government against the Iran-backed group.

This image from video, obtained and verified by Reuters, shows thick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Thursday. It was attacked again on Saturday. (Reuters)

A Saudi-led military coalition vowed ⁠to respond to the attack.

Saudi Arabia and the ⁠Yemeni government have claimed hundreds of strikes on targets in Houthi-held territory. The Houthis have ‌said these killed civilians including women and children. Reuters could not independently verify those claims.

All flights were diverted from Riyadh on Saturday, and operations at the airport that serves a city of roughly 8 million people were temporarily suspended, the Saudi civil aviation authority said.

The head of the Houthi media office said in a post on X after the attack that the group had "shut down Riyadh international airport." The Houthis have said airliners should avoid ⁠Saudi airspace, declaring it a zone of military operations after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government launched an offensive against the group on Monday.

WATCH | How the Houthis could further disrupt global trade: How Yemen’s Houthis could supercharge global trade disruptions | Duration closed caption 5:37 Houthi rebels have taken control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline and the strategic strait of Bab al-Mandeb, threatening to further destabilize global trade. For The National, CBC’s Margaret Evans breaks down the militia’s gains and how it could offer Iran more leverage in its war with the U.S.

U.S. President Donald Trump, speaking to reporters outside the White House, was asked whether Washington planned to join Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

"We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so ‌we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," he said.

One eyewitness at the airport on Saturday reported seeing an explosion and then multiple people lying injured on the ground inside. More than a dozen ambulances were seen rushing towards the facility. A video verified by Reuters showed ambulances at the airport.

An injured traveller told Reuters they saw something fly across the sky outside the airport before part of the ceiling near a ​departure gate collapsed.

The U.S. embassy in Riyadh said it was "aware of attacks" and "strongly recommends all U.S. citizens avoid this airport and surrounding areas."

The Canadian Embassy in Saudi Arabia published a statement advising Canadians to avoid all travel to King Khalid International Airport due to the security situation.

Saudi Arabia entered the Yemen war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition ⁠to try to force the Houthis out of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. The Houthis had stormed Sanaa the previous year, pushing out government forces.

The war was fought to ⁠a bloody stalemate, with hundreds of thousands of Yemenis killed by fighting and famine. Saudi Arabia struck a 2022 deal with the Houthis, freezing the conflict.

That ⁠ceasefire unravelled ⁠over the summer, culminating in a lightning Houthi advance that took ​the Red Sea chokepoint of Bab el-Mandeb from Saudi-backed government forces.

WATCH | Houthis expand control in Bab el-Mandeb: Houthi rebel control expands over key oil shipping lane | Duration closed caption 2:05 Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen are expanding their control over a key Middle Eastern shipping route, adding further pressure to global oil supplies and prices.

The Saudi-backed Yemeni government began an offensive this week to try to retake that territory, which has so far ​made slow gains, even as the Houthis put ⁠the country's third-largest city, Taiz, under siege.

Flight-tracking site Flightradar24 showed all flights to Riyadh had either been diverted or cancelled, with only a helicopter hovering over the airport at one point.

Houthi attacks on Thursday and earlier in the week had already prompted a number of carriers to suspend or cancel services to the Saudi capital, shortly before Riyadh is due to host major energy and investment conferences.

Organizers of those conferences said ahead of the strikes on Saturday they would go ahead as planned.

World.title: How some separatists are responding to Smith’s pledge against 2nd referendum if remain vote wins
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Premier Danielle Smith’s pledge that she won’t hold another referendum on separation if the remain vote wins this month — at least as long as she is premier — is getting pushback from some prominent Alberta separatists.

“Well, I guess it depends on how long she plans to be premier,” said Cory Morgan, who heads the third-party advertiser Pathway to Independence.

“I'm not saying that as a threat sort of thing, you know, they’d kick her out if she didn't support it,” Morgan told CBC News Saturday.

“I'm just saying, you're quite a crystal ball if you would say that it would never be in the cards. I mean, what if she were premier six years still from now, and the winds had changed?”

Smith made the comment during a one-on-one interview with CBC News’ chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault Friday.

WATCH | Premier Danielle Smith rules out 2nd referendum if Albertans vote to remain: Smith rules out 2nd Alberta referendum: 'Not as long as I'm premier' | Duration closed caption 1:35 In an interview with CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she would not hold another referendum on separation should a majority of Albertans vote to remain in Canada on Oct. 19.

On Oct. 19, Albertans will choose either Option 1, to remain in Canada, or Option 2, to begin the process to hold a second, binding referendum on separation.

Morgan said he sees Smith's statement as the premier “trying to make what appears to be a stronger stance during the tail end of this campaign.”

“To set it out saying that there would never be one as long as she's premier, well that means that she doesn't respect the principles of direct democracy she said she does,” Morgan said.

“If there were another referendum within a few years and Albertans said they wanted it, I believe that's her obligation to allow that to happen.”

Cory Morgan speaks to supporters during an Alberta independence rally in Taber, Alta., on Sunday, June 28, 2026. (Matthew Bruce/The Canadian Press)

Morgan says if Option 2 is unsuccessful, he understands another referendum is unlikely for at least a couple of years. But the movement is not going to go away, he said.

Alberta Prosperity Project CEO Mitch Sylvestre has agreed on that point.

He told CBC News Saturday that he does not think Smith’s stance on a second referendum “could go very well for her,” given the number of people in her party in favour of Alberta independence.

A recent Janet Brown Opinion Research Poll for CBC News suggested 53 per cent of respondents who would vote for the United Conservative Party would also vote in favour of the separation option in the upcoming referendum.

Party members could have a chance to voice their opinions on the matter next month, when the UCP holds its annual general meeting.

With just over a week of campaigning left until the referendum, Sylvestre described himself as “cautiously optimistic” about his side’s chances.

“A lot of people I talk to are basically closet separatists. And hopefully they’re gonna come out and vote, and if that's the case, then there's a chance that we can win.” he said.

Morgan says he’s seeing more people “flirt with” the idea of voting Option 2, but says those in favour of independence still have their work cut out to win a majority vote.

Advance polling runs from Oct. 13 to 17, with polling stations on referendum day Oct. 19 open from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m.

World.title: Trump says Ukraine should get a new president, blames Zelenskyy for U.S. diesel prices
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump says it's time for Ukraine to get a new president, suggesting current Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end his country's war with Russia.

Speaking at the White House Saturday, Trump said, "I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,″ adding that "for some reason [Zelenskyy] never does."

Trump also suggested that if he had been U.S. president in 2022, "that war would have never started. There was no reason that that war with Ukraine and Russia started. It started due to incompetence."

Zelenskyy has "lost 30 per cent of your country and you've had over a million people go between the two of them, over two million people killed. That's a war that should have never started. And I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."

Trump's comments come after Russian strikes killed at least 17 people in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, Ukrainian officials said Saturday, one day after the U.S. president announced a deal to buy Russian diesel that Kyiv warned would help bankroll Moscow’s war in Ukraine.

Three children were among those killed when Russian aerial bombs hit residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said Saturday. At least 16 people were wounded in the attack.

WATCH | Trump strikes deal with Putin on diesel: Trump reverses course on Russian oil sanctions | Duration closed caption 2:08 U.S. President Donald Trump has announced a deal to import Russian diesel as fuel prices soar, reversing course on sanctions against Moscow. Ukraine is condemning the move, warning it will directly benefit Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Missiles also struck Kyiv in a daytime attack Saturday. Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said four people were wounded.

Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4½ years since Moscow's full-scale invasion. Ukraine is struggling to counter escalating Russian bombardments that have killed more than 60 people over the past four days.

Trump said Friday he had struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

Anger in Kyiv over diesel deal

"Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote Saturday on X.

He said the attacks show Moscow understands "any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities."

Zelenskyy and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrive for a news conference on Oct. 4. Zelenskyy on Saturday criticized the new U.S.-Russia diesel deal. (Thomas Peter/Reuters)

"Russia’s choice is war," Zelenskyy said in a later Telegram post, after drone attacks on energy facilities and a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv.

He said every additional billion dollars Russia earns from exports would help pay for weapons components, drone upgrades, missile production and the recruitment of mercenaries, and that Moscow would only be ready to stop when its ability to fight diminished.

Zelenskyy added the diesel deal signalled to Moscow that "it is apparently permissible to continue attacking. And this needs to be corrected."

He urged the U.S., Europe and other partners to limit Russia’s capacity to wage war.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine was co-ordinating steps to counter the extra revenue Russia will receive, and that he had spoken to French President Emmanuel Macron about shoring up air defences, warning of an increased risk of further missile strikes in the coming days.

He also said he had discussed the developments with Finnish President Alexander Stubb, adding that Ukraine would receive ammunition in the coming days for the F-16s it uses to intercept Shahed drones.

Trump was set to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia with President Vladimir Putin in a phone call.

Instead, the American leader announced Friday that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons (272,100 tonnes) of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons (453,500 tonnes) in November and one million tons (907,000 tonnes) "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional three million tons (2.7 million tonnes) "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.

European allies question U.S.-Russia deal

Ukraine’s European allies expressed dismay at the deal and said they stood by their commitment to sanctions.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said Stockholm regretted the agreement, �“as energy revenues are central to the Russian war chest,” and noted that the European Union would adopt its most comprehensive sanctions package yet on Monday, with 1,600 listings targeting Russia’s military-industrial complex.

The German government "remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions," spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said, adding that support for Ukraine "remains unwavering.”

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski questioned whether Russia could deliver at all. Citing his embassy’s reports of fuel shortages even in Moscow, and “serious sources” saying Ukraine has damaged about half of Russia’s refining capacity, he asked on X: “So where will the surpluses for export come from?”

WATCH | Rubio says Ukraine war reaching dangerous 'stalemate': War in Ukraine is at a dangerous stalemate, says U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio | Duration closed caption 5:25 A Russian bomb attack on the eastern Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people, authorities said Thursday. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is warning that the war could escalate to a broader regional conflict involving NATO countries.

Trump’s shocking announcement was in stark contrast to a sweeping Russia sanctions law he signed last month that aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenues that fuel Russia's war against Ukraine.

In a lengthy post online reacting to the deal on Friday, Zelenskyy said Russia would repay it "with further terror and perfidy." He framed it as an investment in the war that could prolong it.

"It plays into Russia’s hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world," he said.

According to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington, Zelenskyy called it "a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners."

Trump announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war.

"I believe our team is simply being used as a smoke screen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other," Zelenskyy said.

World.title: What is your seafood eating? Investigation traces problems in global feed supply
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The following story is part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C.

In 2020, a team of government investigators in Goa, India, arrived at a factory named United Marine Products to find out how it was disposing of its toxic wastewater.

For years, local residents had complained that the factory was making their air unbreathable and their drinking water deadly. This factory produces fish meal, a protein-rich powder used to feed farmed fish, which is made by pulverizing and cooking wild-caught fish.

Soon enough, the inspectors discovered that the plant operators had employed a new and illegal way to dispose of the facility's wastewater, drilling bore holes into the ground in a field behind the plant. The authorities later concluded these holes likely contaminated groundwater and sickened villagers and livestock.

The United Marine Products plant in Councolim, Goa, India. In 2020, investigators determined the plant had drilled holes into the ground behind the plant to illegally dispose of wastewater from fish meal processing. (Changing Markets Foundation)

The plant owner denied wrongdoing.

Seafood consumers in Canada might think they have no connection to these sorts of far-away problems.

But this factory in India supplied Skretting, a major feed producer used by dozens of fish farms in Canada — so its product may feed the salmon from British Columbia and New Brunswick or trout from Quebec you see on store shelves.

A five-year investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C., uncovered a variety of similar hidden costs involved in producing this feed, including the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, and violent protests spurred by the horrid stench from fish meal factories.

These social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury types of seafood are eaten.

A worker unloads a crate of anchovies from the holding area of a boat at the port of El Callao, Peru. The world’s largest producer of fishmeal, Peru faces growing concern about overfishing and pollution from its fishmeal industry. (Rodrigo Abd/The Associated Press)

Whether domestically raised or imported, the most popular types of farmed seafood consumed in Canada – salmon, shrimp, trout, sea bass, sea bream – are fed fish meal, which is made from the very kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving , thereby accelerating ocean de pletion, say fisheries scientists.

“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of B.C. in Vancouver.

“And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”

LISTEN | Stench, pollution and civil unrest: Ian Urbina unpacks the investigation: The Current 23:57 The hidden costs of fish feed

Canada’s reliance on global fish meal

Since 2022, more than half of the seafood eaten globally has come from fish farms rather than wild catch, according to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization . Aquaculture is a $444-billion industry and the fastest-growing segment of global food production. Most of these fish farms are powered by fish meal and fish oil, made from wild fish pulled from the ocean.

Unlike growing bivalves such as oysters, clams, and mussels, which do not typically require external feed, the toughest challenge to raising carnivorous seafood, such as salmon and trout, is feeding them.

A worker drives a tractor past mounds of fish meal made from menhaden fish to be used as animal feed supplements in Reedville, Va., in 2015. (Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP/Getty Images)

Canada has more than 200 fish farms, most of which rely on fish meal or fish oil that, when made domestically, comes primarily from Pacific anchoveta, chub mackerel, herring, haddock, pollock, sardines, and frigate tuna.

Canada prohibits boats targeting fish for the sole purpose of making fish meal or fish oil, so domestic fish meal is typically made using skin, bones and other byproducts of processing that would otherwise be thrown away. That’s widely viewed as a more sustainable way to produce feed protein than using whole human-edible fish.

However, at least two-thirds of the fish meal used in Canada, primarily by aquaculture farms – roughly 53,000 tonnes in 2023 – is sourced from abroad, which ties Canadian consumers to these hidden and overseas social costs. Canada also imports more than $4 billion in seafood annually, of which a third is primarily farmed salmon and shrimp, which rely heavily on fish meal and fish oil.

Food for Feed investigation

The Outlaw Ocean Project’s five-year investigation mapped roughly the entire global fish meal industry, including more than 1,400 fish meal factories across 64 countries, tracing supply chains from fishing vessels to processing plants, feed mills, fish farms and seafood retailers.

The reporting effort involved dozens of journalists from as many countries who visited factories and farms and boarded fish meal ships at sea.

In Gambia and Mauritania, the investigation documented how the industry drives food insecurity as fish that once sustained local communities are diverted into fish meal factories for export.

Workers sort catch aboard the China-flagged Lu Lao Yuan Yu 010 in Gambian waters in 2019. When Outlaw Ocean reporters boarded vessels, they documented widespread complaints about poor living and working conditions. (Fábio Nascimento/The Outlaw Ocean Project)

In India and Peru, the industry was tied to at least 80 protests, some violent, in the form of labour strikes and demonstrations sparked by the water pollution or the stench from factories cooking thousands of tonnes of decomposing fish. Canada is the largest importer of fish oil from Peru.

In China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labour on fish farms.

The investigation mapped more than 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang and Tibet — two regions subjected to severe state repression — that produce an estimated half-billion dollars’ worth of farmed seafood annually, some of which is exported to the United States and Canada.

A worker tosses fishmeal pellets into pens at a fish farm in Thailand in 2021. Over half of the seafood eaten worldwide comes from fish farms. (Mako Kurokawa)

‘Overexploited’ or worse

The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fish meal production in at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency , a guide created by ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets.

For example, less than 30 per cent of the fleet had publicly available location information and less than 25 per cent had a unique vessel identification number (or ship licence plate). Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.

At least half of the species landed by the assessed fish meal vessels were classified by scientific studies as “overexploited” or worse — including flat and round sardinella in Senegal, oil sardines in India, and anchoveta in Chile.

Most of the vessels in the global fish meal fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish, which can indiscriminately sweep in bycatch and non-target species.

At least 165 of the ships in the fleet were bottom trawlers, a destructive gear type that scrapes the ocean floor with weighted nets.

Fish meal reliance declining, industry says

In response to questions from The Outlaw Ocean Project about the sustainability of fish meal, the IFFO , which is the international fish meal association, emphasized that its “role is not to advise which markets should use fish meal and fish oil.”

Véronique Jamin, a spokesperson from the organization, said that fish farming is “the most efficient animal protein system” and is becoming more efficient over time.

Sacks of fish meal stored at a factory in Lima on December 3, 2009. While the aquaculture industry says it has decreased its reliance on fish meal overall, some companies have increased demand as they grow. (Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty Images)

In response to a question about overfishing by the fish meal industry, Jamin said, “Because small pelagics are fast-renewing stocks, their sustainable harvest threshold is much higher than for slow-growing species like cod, tuna, or deep-sea fish.”

The feed and aquaculture industries have emphasized that they are decreasing their reliance on fish meal and fish oil by adding other ingredients to the mix, such as insects, algae, and krill. Between 2000 and 2020, the share of fish meal in global aquaculture feed fell from 23 per cent to eight per cent, according to the IFFO .

Producers of salmon, which typically requires larger amounts of fish meal and oil to thrive, say they have made progress, too. Members of the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance, which includes large producers like Cermaq and Mowi, reduced the proportion of these ingredients in salmon feed to less than 20 per cent, according to a November 2025 press release .

“These results show salmon farming companies have adopted science-based methods that have improved the standard of salmon farm sustainability overall in Canada,” said Timothy Kennedy, president of the Canadian Aquaculture Industry Alliance, in the release.

A salmon farm near Campbell River, B.C., is shown during a routine health inspection in 2018. (Jonathan Hayward/The Canadian Press)

However, as aquaculture overall grows so too has demand for fish meal.

For example, to meet demand, five of the world’s largest salmon companies increased their absolute use of fish meal or fish oil made from whole wild fish by as much as 39 percent between 2020 and 2024, according to a report from the Farm Animal Investment Risk and Return Initiative.

Two of the salmon companies that increased their absolute use of fish meal have a presence in Canada: Mowi, which announced in June 2025 that it was selling its Canadian farms to Cooke; and Grieg Seafood, whose Canadian farms have since been acquired by Cermaq. (Mowi, Cermaq, Cooke, and Grieg Seafood did not respond to a request for comment.)

Skretting opens investigation

As of 2025, there were at least seven factories processing fish meal and fish oil in Canada, and these plants are not without problems.

Between 2021 and 2024, at least two of the plants were tied to pollution or unsustainable fishing practices, according to Bait to Plate , an online tool created by The Outlaw Ocean Project that tracks the fishing and seafood industries. Neither company responded to the project’s request for comment.

However, the far greater burden of food insecurity, collapsed fish stocks, social unrest, and air and water pollution is borne by the poorer countries that produce the fish meal or farmed seafood that Canada imports.

For example, Canada imports over a third of its shrimp from India, where the investigation found explosions, fires, and worker asphyxiations at factories producing fish meal that supplies the country’s shrimp farms.

Freshly caught live shrimp are seen on a shrimp farm in India, April 11, 2025. (Sahiba Chawdhary/Reuters)

As recently as 2022, United Marine Products, the Goan fish meal plant that was found to be illegally dumping wastewater, supplied fish meal to Skretting Canada, which produces feed for many of Canada’s fish farms.

At another factory called Bismi Aquatic Products in 2021, a migrant worker died while he was cleaning a wastewater tank and passed out from the fumes. Major shrimp brands like IFC and AZ Gems, which source much of their shrimp from India, are sold across Canada at major supermarket chains like Metro Canada, Loblaws, and Costco Canada.

Skretting has a “zero-tolerance policy” for breaches of its policies that clearly state business partners abide by all applicable laws and regulations that govern their business activities, said the company’s Sustainability and Communications Director, Jorge Diaz, and has opened an investigation to verify the information found in this reporting.

In response to questions from Outlaw Ocean, Metro spokesperson Stephanie Bonk wrote : “All Metro suppliers are required to respect working conditions across the supply chain as outlined in our Supplier Code of Conduct for responsible procurement.”

World.title: Stelco says Hamilton layoffs still happening despite Ottawa's threats of legal action
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hamilton-based steelmaker Stelco says it will proceed with hundreds of layoffs, despite threats of legal action from the federal government.

In a letter obtained by CBC News, Stelco Inc., which is owned by Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs, says it rejects allegations from Ottawa that it is violating binding employment commitments under the Investment Canada Act (ICA).

"Your representation that Stelco's planned layoffs cause it to breach its undertakings is false," says a letter written to Industry Minister Mélanie Joly by Paul Simon, president and general counsel at Stelco Inc.

Citing the ICA's guidelines, Simon went on to write that "the undertakings do not stipulate a commitment to avoid layoffs, nor do they include a requirement that employment levels be above a certain amount on each day of the five years of the undertakings."

The letter comes after Joly issued an ultimatum last week to the company: share a plan to save the up to 500 jobs that could be impacted at the Hamilton plant or face potential legal action.

WATCH | Up to 500 Stelco employees impacted by layoffs: Stelco layoffs start despite Ottawa's legal threats | Duration closed caption 2:24 Stelco started laying off steelworkers at its Hamilton plant despite government demands that it reveal a jobs-saving plan within five days or face potential legal action.

In a statement to CBC News, Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, said he was "not surprised with Stelco's convoluted response."

"The bigger problem is that the union, which represents the affected workers, was not privy to the agreement in the first place," he said. "As the group with the most at risk, we weren't consulted or [given] a chance to review the undertakings."

Cleveland-Cliffs acquired Stelco in a $3.4-billion cash-and-stock deal that, according to a news release at the time, kept "national interests at the forefront" and recognized the "importance of the workforce."

According to Joly's letter, this includes "undertakings to continue to employ at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees as were employed when the transaction was announced."

In a statement to CBC News on Saturday, Joly's office said the federal government still expects Steclo to "meet its legally binding commitments to employees."

"These commitments were agreed upon as undertakings under the Investment Canada Act and do not cease to apply because of changing business strategy or market conditions," the statement said. "As our legal team reviews the Stelco letter, all options are on the table."

WATCH | Carney says feds will pursue legal action if needed against Stelco: Stelco 'betrayed' Ontario workers with layoffs, Carney says | Duration closed caption 1:16 Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada will 'use all the powers that we have' to ensure that Stelco meets its 'legal obligations for employment.' The company, which is owned by U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs, announced plans on Monday to idle some production at its Hamilton plant, putting hundreds of workers out of a ‌job.

Prime Minister Mark Carney also said last week that Ottawa will "use all powers that we have" against Cleveland-Cliffs as it pursues the Ohio-based company to the "fullest extent of the law."

In 2009, Industry Canada sued Stelco's previous owner, U.S. Steel, over job protection. The matter was settled out of court in 2011.

Stelco alleges Ottawa knew of its intentions

In its letter to Joly, the company emphasized "Stelco’s situation is a result of factors beyond its control" — citing the impact of U.S. President Donald Trump's 50 per cent tariffs and the ongoing trade war.

The federal government has said that Stelco refused offers of financial support before choosing to announce it was idling its Hamilton plant.

Stelco's letter alleges that "the government's offers of financial assistance were not responsive to the issues at hand and did not address the root cause for Stelco's decision to indefinitely idle its Hamilton Works finishing lines."

The company goes on to allege that the industry minister was "inaccurate and misleading to the Canadian public" when she said Ottawa only recently learned of Stelco's intentions.

Stelco alleges that it was in constant communication with the federal government about its financial concerns. "By failing to mention or acknowledge these regular communications, your letter created the false impression that we have not been co-operative and transparent."

Stelco did present a plan to comply with ICA job commitments in its letter, as requested by Joly.

The company reaffirmed that it will proceed with its Hamilton layoffs, again citing "exenstive external factors" that make it difficult to produce and profit off of those steel products.

It said laid off workers could be given the opportunity to fill open positions at its Lake Erie plant. Stelco said it would continue to engage with the federal government.

In terms of what the company wants to see from Ottawa, it wrote: "The most important step the government could take would be to impose further restrictions on imports of cold-rolled and coated steel products into Canada, limit import substitution, and eliminate remissions for steel products that Canadian producers, including Stelco, can supply."

World.title: This loaf of rye bread is selling for $60 in New York. Is it worth it?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | 'There were people who were coming in and buying 10 loaves': The Current 7:56 Would you buy a $60 loaf of bread?

A bakery in New York is selling a loaf of rye bread for $60 US ($85 Cdn). But while many have criticized the price as exorbitant, a food critic who tried it says it tells a more complex story.

“Is the bread delicious? The answer is yes. Is the bread worth it? [That] I think is a much more complicated question,” said Elazar Sontag, a food critic for the Washington Post.

Austrian baker Martin Auer opened Rye in Manhattan last month, making the titular loaf from water, imported rye flour and salt. The fourth ingredient, according to the bakery, is time: 24 hours for the dough to rest, ferment and develop, then 70 minutes in the oven. The loaf weighs about 1.5 kilograms, and is also sold in smaller portions.

Auer’s family have been in the bread business since 1936, and offer the same loaf in Vienna for a fraction of the price, just over €14 ($22 Cdn). The New York loaf’s price tag caught the attention of many on social media, with one TikToker describing Auer as either “a criminal or an evil genius” for capitalizing on New York’s taste for hype.

The Current contacted Rye with questions, but did not receive a response. The bakery previously told Sontag that the New York pricing reflects rent, wages and transportation, as well as costs related to development, design, packaging and the work of making the bread itself.

Sontag tried the loaf and wrote about it in the Washington Post. He spoke to The Current’s Matt Galloway about what he thought. Here is part of their conversation.

I'm really glad to have you here, in part because you have had the bread. What is it like?

I can confirm the tab, it is very expensive. Even knowing exactly what I was going for, when I saw that number come up on the little screen before I tapped my phone, it is kind of an eyebrow-raising moment.

The bread itself is delicious … people aren't really talking about the taste of the bread because to most people it's kind of beside the point. But if what you really are wondering is, is the bread delicious? The answer is yes. Is the bread worth it? [That] I think is a much more complicated question.

Part of it is the experience of going to the bakery, right? You said it's like an Apple store in some ways?

It has this very stern, but also sort of aspirational feel that I think will be familiar to anyone who shops at designer clothing stores … [or] people who buy their technology from Apple.

Apple similarly is sort of going for a certain kind of aspirational living, very clean, very minimal. It's not necessarily what you expect from a bakery. There's so many kinds of signifiers in there about lifestyle, right? You feel like you're walking into a place that's telling you how you should want to live, as opposed to necessarily just selling you a loaf of bread.

WATCH | 'I'll buy what I have to buy ... how does it feel? Awful': Persistent high food costs felt by shoppers | Duration closed caption 2:38 New Statistics Canada figures show that while food prices have gone down compared to last month, the cost of putting food on the table has outpaced other basic living expenses for 17 consecutive months.

Who is buying a $60 loaf of bread?

Well, the short answer is, at the moment, a lot of people, because of this discourse and how far it has travelled.

But I actually asked one of the employees … and he said that a lot of people were coming just because they were curious. But he also said that it should be noted it's in a very wealthy New York neighbourhood. And that there were people who were coming in and buying 10 loaves. Now, that's about $600 of bread.

The owner has admitted that the same loaf sells for much less in Austria. You heard one of those people from social media at the beginning. Is this person a criminal or an evil genius?

I mean, probably neither. I think really this person is sort of just fitting into the long and storied tradition of kind of outlandish New York businesses.

I think the idea that people have latched onto — that this is really a sign of some new awful era of New York and a time when Americans can just sort of be hoodwinked and cheated — there's something there. I think the way that social media amplifies these sorts of conversations can make our culture feel very, very bleak.

Rye bakery in New York. Food critic Elazar Sontag says the store has a 'very stern but also sort of aspirational feel.' (Submitted by Elazar Sontag)

But, you know, as I pointed out in my column when I was writing about the bread , New York is a city of ridiculous contradictions. The idea that a $60 loaf of bread is so novel in a city where you could get a sushi dinner for one that costs a thousand? It's a little silly to me. Of course, the bread is also totally ridiculous, but I don't know that it's an indicator of some evil genius. It's certainly not criminal, as long as people are willing to 

Bloomberg called this a K-shaped loaf of bread, pointing to the idea of the K-shape economy, which has this huge gap between the rich and the poor. What do you make of that? The bread is stamped, so if you buy the loaf of bread, everybody knows that it's not just a normal loaf of bread — this is the $60 loaf. Is this just about conspicuous consumption?

The shortest, shortest answer is probably yes. But it's not about the loaf of bread and I think people understand … that the loaf of bread is a symbol, right.

People are getting on the internet and saying, I think one of the most common lines right now is: bread is supposed to be a food of the working class, and the poor. It's flour and water — and how are we making something that is about access and about nourishment a symbol of this just sort of disgusting, offensive level of wealth. I take that, but I think it's important to remember that this is not a bakery that dropped into a working-class, under-resourced neighbourhood, and now suddenly the only option people have is this $60 bread.

I think that the tension and the anxiety is that it does point to something very real in America, certainly very real in New York, about this K-shaped economy. It's ostentatious, it comes in this bag that's printed with big blocky RYE letters. And you know, it does feel like a status symbol, and I think it does say something a little foreboding about our culture right now, that bread is a status symbol. But avocado toast was a status symbol 10 or 15 years ago.

What do you do with a $60 loaf of bread? Do you make avocado toast with it? Is it a sandwich? Do you just dip it in olive oil?

You savour it … you eat it very slowly.

World.title: AI photos are making it harder to know what you're booking on Airbnb. Here's what to look out for
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | When Airbnb photos don't match reality: Cost of Living 5:19 Can you believe what you see on Airbnb?

Josh Wells, a college student from Iowa, was excited to explore Montreal on his first trip outside the U.S. But as he scrolled through Airbnb listings in search of a place to stay, he began to notice something that didn't seem quite right.

Several of the hosts renting out their properties had profile pictures that Wells suspected were generated by artificial intelligence.

"Your average person taking an iPhone photo, there's obviously like a little bit of imperfections," Wells told the CBC's Cost of Living. "The AI photos, they just looked too perfect."

Still, Wells kept browsing. He was even close to booking one of the properties when a final look at the listing's photos raised another red flag.

He zoomed in on a piece of wall art depicting two halves of faces joined together. At the top, the artwork appeared to read "Picasso." But in another photo of the same room, taken from a different angle, the artwork looked different.

"The text was all warped and funky," he said. "I'm just like, 'Yeah, OK, this is AI."

When booking his trip to Montreal, Wells found extremely polished-looking photos of hosts appeared in numerous Airbnb listings, leading him to suspect they had been generated using AI. Short-term rentals in that city are subject to strict rules aimed in part at protecting the city's housing supply. (Josh Wells/Reddit)

That was enough to put Wells off the listing — and ultimately using Airbnb for this trip. Unable to tell whether the photos showed a real place or an AI-generated version of one, he opted for an apartment-style hotel instead.

"The fake profile picture is one thing, but listings of the actual place that you're staying at and spending thousands of dollars was an immediate no for me," Wells said.

Wells isn't the only traveller to question whether the photos found on Airbnb or similar short-term rental-style platforms accurately reflect reality.

In July, an Ottawa family reported that their daughter arrived at a Toronto Airbnb to find a room that looked significantly different from the listing photos, which they suspected had been generated or heavily altered using AI.

The family provided side-by-side photos showing differences in the room and bathroom. Airbnb said the listing did not match the property and refunded the guest, but did not confirm whether artificial intelligence had been used.

As AI makes it easier to alter photos, experts say travellers may find it increasingly difficult to know whether Airbnb-style listings accurately reflect reality, raising questions about consumer trust and protections in Canada.

When a photo makeover goes too far

The proliferation of free, quick and easy-to-use AI tools is making photo editing increasingly tempting, said Francis Syms, associate dean in the faculty of applied sciences and technology at Humber Polytechnic in Toronto.

Beyond the major AI platforms, such as ChatGPT, Claude by Anthropic and Google's Gemini, countless other websites offer free tools for modifying images, said Syms. Hugging Face, for example, hosts thousands of AI tools that let users upload and edit photos.

"In a matter of 10 seconds, you can upload a picture to one of these sites and ask it to remove all the smudges or to change the furniture," he said. "You'll get that image back maybe 30 to 60 seconds later."

Artificial intelligence platforms like ChatGPT allows users to quickly and easily edit photos. (Marco Bertorello/AFP via Getty Images)

It's difficult to know where AI editing crosses into deception, said Daniel Guttentag, an associate professor of hospitality and tourism management at the College of Charleston in South Carolina.

"If you put in a fake hot tub on the back patio, I think basically everyone would agree that that is a blatant misrepresentation of what one's unit offers," he said. "Whereas if you just start to play with the lighting a little bit … I think most people would be comfortable with that.

"But then there's a whole lot of space in between, when it crosses that line into, 'Wait, this isn't what I signed up for.'"

Guttentag said another concern is the use of AI-edited images to make it appear that guests have damaged a property, potentially leading to compensation claims.

In 2025, a guest from London, U.K., booked an Airbnb in Manhattan and was accused of causing more than £12,000 ($22, 665) in damage .

She disputed the claim after noticing inconsistencies in photos of a supposedly cracked coffee table, which she suspected had been digitally manipulated or generated by AI.

Airbnb initially said she owed more than £5,000 ($9,444), but later fully refunded her after the case drew media attention.

Can you trust what you see online?

Relying on listing photos to decide which property to book makes trust particularly important for Airbnb guests, said Guttentag.

"You can't try it on in advance, like a pair of shoes," he said. "You have to have the confidence and the trust that it's going to live up to your expectations."

Although AI-altered photos might help hosts attract bookings in the short term, guests who arrive to find something different than what was advertised may leave negative reviews, Guttentag said. If people feel misled "one too many times," he said, it could prompt them to stop using the platform altogether.

Daniel Guttentag is an associate professor of hospitality and tourism management at the College of Charleston in South Carolina with research interests in Airbnb and artificial intelligence. (Submitted by Daniel Guttentag)

In a statement to CBC News, Airbnb says its rules require listings to be "accurately represented" and that the company may ask hosts to remove content that uses AI or other digital technology to "edit flaws, hide damage, add amenities or attributes that are not part of a listing, or otherwise materially misrepresent the listing."

The company further said it encourages guests to report misleading listings and that those who find a property that doesn't match its description can contact its 24/7 community support team. Under AirCover, Airbnb added, it may help guests find a similar place or provide a refund if the host can't resolve the issue.

In August, California's Artificial Intelligence Transparency Act (CAITA) took effect, requiring AI-generated images, videos and audio to carry information that can help consumers identify whether digital content was created or altered using AI.

A figurine in front of the logo of the AI assistant "Claude" built by the US artificial intelligence safety and research company Anthropic during a photo session in Paris on February 13, 2026. (Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images)

Canada doesn't yet have AI-specific legislation addressing misleading advertising, said Steve Szentesi, a Toronto-based competition and advertising lawyer. But he said existing laws can already apply to deceptive AI-generated images.

The federal Competition Act prohibits misleading advertising, whether the claims are made through text, photos, audio or other forms of media. Provincial and territorial consumer protection laws offer similar safeguards.

While AI-generated images are relatively novel, the underlying issue is not, Szentesi said. Courts have dealt with disputes over real estate listings for decades, including cases where photos of a property didn’t match the home itself or contradicted descriptions in the listing.

For consumers who believe a short-term rental listing misrepresents a property, Szentesi suggests first raising it with the rental platform. They can also file a complaint with the Competition Bureau or their provincial or territorial consumer protection act.

In the meantime, Syms suggests would-be bookers look for possible signs of AI-generated images in listing photos, such as crooked door frames, tile lines and countertops, oddly shaped furniture, inconsistent shadows or reflections, and blurry or jumbled words on books or wall art.

Travellers can also use a tool like Google Lens, he said, to search for the same image online and check whether it has been taken from another website rather than showing the actual property.

For Wells, the experience hasn't ruled out him using Airbnb altogether — he had a positive experience booking with the platform in Kansas City in March. But his search for a place in Montreal has made him more wary, he said.

"I am open to it again as long as there's just no fake AI listings involved."

World.title: Children, pregnant woman among 9 dead in Pennsylvania shooting
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A shooting in a residential area of Erie, Pa., left nine people dead, including the suspected shooter, and rocked the city. Police said two children and a pregnant woman were among the dead.

Erie police Chief Rick Lorah said the 45-year-old male gunman was related to seven of the victims in Friday's shooting, while the eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman.

Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators showed two "distressed" women arriving at the home shortly before 5 p.m. and pounding on the door, he said. The gunman then came out and shot them before returning inside.

Police arrived to find the two women dead outside. Inside they found the bodies of a five-year-old boy, a one-year-old girl, two more women, two young men and the shooter.

Lorah declined to discuss motive but said investigators would talk to other relatives and examine the cellphones of the women who were killed outside the home.

"They knew something was going on at that house," he said. "We have to figure out what that is."

Officers arrived within minutes of receiving an alert via ShotSpotter, a controversial gunshot detection system that relies on artificial intelligence and a network of microphones to identify gunshots. All nine deaths occurred before officers arrived, the city said, and no additional shots were fired after that.

"Sounds heard during the police response that may have been mistaken for gunfire were flash bangs associated with law enforcement's tactical response," the city said.

"I have not seen anything like this in my 28-plus years," Lorah told a local news station earlier in the day. "I'm not sure that the city of Erie has ever seen the loss of life and the devastation that we just witnessed."

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he offered his administration's "full support" to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin.

Erie is located about 190 kilometres north of Pittsburgh.
