“Providing a platform where civil society representatives can participate and engage with OSCE participating States and executive structures is one of the OSCE’s core values. They must be able to do so without facing any negative consequences.

This is essential for the OSCE’s mechanisms to function. We are concerned about comments made in connection with the participation of Georgian civil society representatives in this conference, as well as reports received from various human rights defenders attending the OSCE Human Dimension Conference in Warsaw. We reiterate the importance of ensuring safe participation in OSCE events, without any reprisals.”

Incident at the conference

The conference in Warsaw is attended by Baia Pataraia, head of the Georgian NGO Sapari, and Tamar Oniani, head of the Georgian Young Lawyers’ Association.

On 5 October, during a speech by a representative of the Georgian delegation, Pataraia held up a banner reading: “Free all Georgian political prisoners.”

Pataraia says her protest was peaceful and silent, and that she had arranged it in advance in accordance with OSCE rules.

“Wherever I find myself alongside the [Georgian] government, I will remind them that prisons are full of political prisoners and that the Georgian people will never accept this,” she says.

Pataraia adds that Germany, Slovenia and other countries have urged Georgia to implement the recommendations of the Moscow Mechanism and stop persecuting media representatives, politicians and civil society members.

In this context, she also criticised the Georgian authorities’ bid to make Georgia the OSCE chair in 2027.

“They want benefits, money, prestige and power from everyone, but they themselves fulfil none of their obligations,” Pataraia said indignantly.

The ruling Georgian Dream party is seeking to secure the OSCE chairpersonship for 2027. Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili says the country has already submitted its application to the OSCE and hopes to win the support of participating States. However, according to the publication Rapporteur, EU member states do not support Georgia’s bid.



OSCE conference in Warsaw

World.title: Abkhazia plans pension reform, new law to take work history into account
World.content:
The government of Abkhazia has drafted a pension reform bill aimed at streamlining pension legislation, taking employment history into account when calculating pension payments and introducing specific support measures for socially vulnerable groups.

The draft pension law was prepared by the Ministry of Social Welfare and Demographic Policy. According to Minister Kama Adzynba, the bill aims to streamline regulations governing employment-related, insurance-based and funded pensions, as well as payments for special services to the country.

One of the key principles of the proposed reform is to take individuals’ employment history into account when determining pension payments. Currently, pensions in Abkhazia stand at 6,000 roubles [approximately $70], a standard amount paid to everyone, regardless of whether they have worked for many years or have never been formally employed.

Pensioners who hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship and also receive a Russian pension have their Abkhaz pension reduced to a largely symbolic 500 roubles [around $6].

The new system is intended to address this “injustice”. It also provides for survivor’s pensions and other social benefits, which are expected to exceed the basic social pension.

The bill also introduces special pensions for distinguished service to the country. Recipients of state orders and veterans of the 1992-93 Georgian-Abkhaz war are among those proposed for inclusion in this category.

The draft law will be submitted to parliament for consideration.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s $90bn reserves draw criticism from former opposition leader
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s foreign currency reserves

Ilgar Mammadov, former chairman of Azerbaijan’s Republican Alternative (ReAl) party, has criticised the country’s accumulation of $90bn in foreign currency reserves. In a Facebook post, he argued that there was little reason to take pride in such substantial reserves when some elderly citizens were forced to survive on modest social benefits.

Mammadov proposed using part of the reserves to improve living standards while expanding economic freedoms.

“There are no reasonable grounds for a country like Azerbaijan to hold $90bn in foreign currency reserves,” the politician wrote.

What makes up Azerbaijan’s $90bn in foreign currency reserves?

Azerbaijan’s strategic foreign currency reserves comprise the Central Bank’s foreign exchange reserves and the assets of the State Oil Fund (SOFAZ). According to figures published by the State Statistical Committee, their combined value stood at $90.77bn as of 1 September 2026. This represents the total value of funds held in various financial assets.

The two institutions’ reserves serve different purposes. The Central Bank’s reserves are used to maintain stability in the foreign exchange market and mitigate risks associated with external payments.

The State Oil Fund accumulates revenues from oil and gas production, invests them, makes transfers to the state budget and builds up savings for future generations. Its assets are invested in bonds, equities, gold and property.

The authorities regard the substantial reserves as an indicator of the country’s financial resilience. Speaking at the Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in September, President Ilham Aliyev stressed that the reserves were approximately 20 times greater than the country’s external public debt.

According to Aliyev, this demonstrates the strength of Azerbaijan’s financial system and the stability of its national currency.

‘These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace’

Mammadov also approaches the issue from the perspective of public welfare. He argues that elderly citizens have contributed to the creation of national wealth not only through formal employment but also through domestic and agricultural work.

“Only the government of the New Azerbaijan Party (YAP) can proudly boast of having $90bn in foreign currency reserves in a country where 180,000 elderly citizens receive no retirement pension and are forced to make do with an old-age allowance of $130. This is simply shameful.

“People over the age of 65 have contributed to society throughout their lives through their labour and their role as consumers in the economy, helping to create the conditions for accumulating $90bn in foreign currency reserves.

“Whether it was a housewife who spent years supporting her husband as he worked as a labourer or engineer, or a man who worked in the fields for a pittance, supplying city residents with fresh fruit and vegetables, they all contributed to building up these reserves.

“This is a hardworking generation that the YAP authorities have left with virtually no means of subsistence in old age, while continuing to boast about the country’s foreign currency reserves.”

Mammadov argues that taking pride in growing reserves while this generation faces financial hardship is also morally unacceptable.

“Viewed from this perspective, even the question of economic efficiency becomes secondary. These $90bn have become a symbol of shame and disgrace.”

Assets held abroad and dependence on oil

Mammadov also argues that holding substantial foreign currency reserves abroad carries political risks. He cites Iraq and Libya as examples, pointing to the depletion of their financial resources during wars and the freezing of their assets. He links these events to the interests of external powers and suggests that Azerbaijan could face similar risks.

“By maintaining foreign currency reserves on this scale, Azerbaijan is merely provoking major players in the current world order, who are accustomed to playing by their own rules. It is like putting on our most expensive jacket, stuffing its pockets with bundles of cash and going for a walk at night down the most crime-ridden street in the city.

“There are plenty of historical examples. In 1980, Iraq’s foreign currency reserves stood at 36bn–40bn. In today’s money, that is just over $90bn. And what happened? A war with Iran was soon orchestrated, partly for the sake of that money, though not exclusively. As a result, all the money was spent on purchasing weapons from abroad, and the reserves were exhausted. Who benefited? The arms dealers.

“In 2011, Libya’s foreign currency reserves had barely reached $150bn when the country was plunged into turmoil. Some of the money was spent on arming the sides in the civil war, while around a third of the assets were frozen in foreign financial institutions (and someone is still profiting from them). The rest has never been traced.

“In today’s world, where the law of the jungle prevails, there is no point in keeping such substantial foreign currency reserves abroad. One day, a provocation could be staged against us too, and the money could be seized,” he wrote.

Mammadov also sees a potential collapse in financial markets as a serious threat. He believes securities are significantly overvalued and that a sharp fall in their prices could result in substantial losses for Azerbaijan.

Another of his arguments concerns the economy’s dependence on oil. Recalling the currency devaluations of 2015, he notes that the country’s foreign currency reserves failed to prevent the sharp depreciation of the manat.

“The reason reserves are rapidly depleted during a crisis and cannot serve as a financial safety net lies in the unhealthy state of our economy and its dependence on oil.”

According to Mammadov, if oil prices remain low for a prolonged period, substantial foreign currency reserves alone cannot guarantee economic security.

What does Mammadov propose?

Mammadov is not calling for Azerbaijan to spend all its foreign currency reserves. He believes some funds should be retained to deal with economic crises and natural disasters, although he does not specify how much should be set aside.

“There is an urgent need to improve people’s living standards, particularly those of the elderly. At the same time, economic freedoms must be expanded without delay so that citizens can realise their creative and entrepreneurial potential and generate new wealth,” the politician wrote.

Mammadov sees the rule of law as a fundamental prerequisite for these reforms. He concluded his post by urging voters to support the Republican Alternative (ReAl) party.

World.title: Pashinyan on extradition of Azerbaijani soldier, meeting Aliyev and Medvedev’s statement
World.content:
Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

The extradition of Azerbaijani serviceman Nasimi Musayev is not under discussion, and Baku has not made such a request. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists this during his traditional hour-long briefing.

“What extradition are you talking about? There is no such issue, and we are not discussing it. Azerbaijan has made no request,” he said.

At the same time, he stressed that Armenia would have returned Musayev on the same day if he had not committed a crime.

Pashinyan described the Azerbaijani serviceman, who illegally crossed into Armenia and shot a resident of the village of Shaki, as having committed an “ordinary crime”. The prime minister drew parallels with other forms of cross-border crime:

“We also have other cases of cross-border crime. Drugs are constantly exported to Armenia and transported through Armenia in transit. There is no need to turn this into an apocalypse.”

The prime minister does not believe the incident in Shaki could threaten the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

He considers the peace that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established an achievement that requires protection. He warns that they could destroy it in a day, while reaching the current state of relations could take another 30 years. For this reason, he does not consider it appropriate to make statements that could threaten the peace process.

On 1 October 2026, Nasimi Musayev illegally entered the village of Shaki in Armenia’s Syunik Province. Local residents found him inside a house, where he opened fire with an assault rifle and wounded a 39-year-old woman. Her three children witnessed the incident. Her two sons also suffered injuries, while her daughter has yet to recover psychologically.

Musayev fled after the shooting, but authorities detained him shortly afterwards in another house. The Armenian Prosecutor’s Office brought criminal charges under five articles of the Criminal Code. The charges include illegally crossing the border, causing serious bodily harm to a local resident and violating the inviolability of a home. A court ordered his detention for two months.

During the briefing, the prime minister also addressed Dmitry Medvedev’s controversial statement about turning Armenia into a “new Ukraine”, a possible meeting with Aliyev at the CIS summit and the issue of missing persons.

“No official meetings are planned”: on contacts with Putin and Aliyev

On 8-9 October, Pashinyan will attend the CIS summit in Turkmenistan. Asked about possible meetings with the presidents of Russia and Azerbaijan, he recalled that his latest meetings with Putin and Aliyev took place in Bishkek last month. He also spoke to the Russian president by phone the day before.

“The format is such that contacts with the president of Russia and the president of Azerbaijan will certainly take place. We will be in the same place today and tomorrow. No official meeting is planned. If it turns out that such a meeting is necessary, it may take place,” he said.

“Armenia has already faced such a threat”: response to Medvedev

People in Armenia continue to discuss Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev’s statement. He said that Armenia’s leadership had decided to change the country’s course and that this would not lead to anything good.

“The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” Medvedev said.

Journalists asked Pashinyan whether Armenia could face such a threat. He replied:

“Armenia has already faced a similar danger and situation. In September 2022, [during the Azerbaijani armed forces’ invasion of Armenia’s sovereign territory], the CSTO failed to fulfil its obligations.”

The Collective Security Treaty Organisation is a military alliance led by Russia. Armenia is a member of the CSTO. Under the organisation’s charter, its allies had to provide military assistance to a member state, but that did not happen.

The Armenian prime minister could not explain why Medvedev was making such statements and threats:

“Following the same logic, someone else could say: ‘We do not want Armenia to turn into a “new Russia”, given that explosions can be heard in various parts of Russia.’ This is an unfortunate genre.”

He assured that Armenia would not turn into anything else and would instead become an even more independent state.

“Some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes”: on missing persons

Azerbaijan periodically demands that Armenia provide information about the fate of missing Azerbaijanis and the locations of their graves. President Ilham Aliyev repeated the demand at an international conference on missing persons in Baku.

According to Armenia’s prime minister, both sides should make joint efforts to establish the fate of missing people:

“We have stated that we are ready to cooperate. The problem is that some circles in Azerbaijan use this issue for political purposes, including to generate hostile rhetoric and pursue other aims.”

According to figures Pashinyan presented, the whereabouts of around 1,000 people who went missing during wars since the 1990s remain unknown in Armenia.

He says the wording itself — “their whereabouts are unknown” — shows how little information the authorities have about these people:

“Some circles in Azerbaijan sometimes try to create the impression that we know where these people are and refuse to share the information. But that is not the case.”

Pashinyan believes the two sides should resolve the issue through cooperation and close this chapter. He said that in Bishkek, he and the Azerbaijani president also discussed stepping up joint efforts by the relevant commissions of the two countries.

Pashinyan on Azerbaijani serviceman’s extradition and other issues

World.title: ‘Light rosè’, or why claim that Abkhazia has no good wine is outdated. VIDEO
World.content:
Wine in Abkhazia

For a long time, Abkhazia was known mainly for its basic range of wines. The region’s unpredictable climate, with annual rainfall of up to 2,000 mm, was seen as a challenge, as was the popularity of mass-produced semi-sweet wines.

However, modern winemaking practices have challenged this perception. Today, Abkhaz wine producers are shifting their focus towards premium wines.

The Association of Winemakers is actively reviving local indigenous grape varieties. It says fermentation control and modern scientific methods now make it possible to produce delicate, dry and fresh rosé wines.

World.title: European Parliament resolution on banning opposition parties in Georgia: what it says
World.content:
On 8 October, the European Parliament adopted its latest — and seventh — critical resolution on Georgia. This time, it focuses on the ruling Georgian Dream party’s attempts to ban five opposition parties and political groups.

In the resolution, the European Parliament strongly condemns the attempts to outlaw these opposition parties and calls for the immediate withdrawal of the constitutional lawsuit against them.

The draft resolution also once again calls for the release of political prisoners and sanctions against those responsible for Georgia’s democratic backsliding. It specifically names Georgian Dream founder and honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili, party secretary-general Kakha Kaladze, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili.

The document says that the actions of Georgian Dream have caused the situation in Georgia to deteriorate further. Democracy and media freedom have declined, while human rights and the rule of law face growing violations. The document says this increasingly conflicts with Georgia’s international obligations and responsibilities, including the Copenhagen criteria.

The draft resolution also notes that two German foundations — the Konrad Adenauer Foundation and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation — had to close their offices in Tbilisi after the authorities rejected their funding applications under the grants law.

The draft resolution also again refers to the persecution of journalists in Georgia who covered the authorities’ repression of the opposition and civil society.

According to the draft resolution, the European Parliament:

Strongly condemns the attempt to outlaw Georgia’s opposition parties and calls for the immediate withdrawal of the constitutional lawsuit against them. It stresses that a functioning political opposition is an indispensable pillar of democracy and that using judicial mechanisms to eliminate legitimate political opposition is incompatible with democracy. It notes that banning the only opposition party represented in the Georgian parliament undermines the government’s previous narrative that it targeted only parties “under boycott”;

Timeline of European Parliament resolutions on Georgia

Since October 2024, the European Parliament has adopted six critical resolutions concerning the Georgian government. In these documents, MEPs have criticised Georgian Dream’s policies on democracy, the rule of law, human rights and the country’s European integration.

World.title: Today, six years ago: Armenia hit its fourth missile attack on Azerbaijan's Ganja (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 11. Today marks the sixth anniversary of Armenia's missile strike on Ganja, which occurred at approximately 2:00 a.m. on October 11, 2020, Trend reports.

Ten innocent people lost their lives and forty more were injured when a ballistic missile attack hit the heart of the city.

This fourth missile strike on Ganja exemplified Armenia's military-political leadership's policy of terror against civilians, in gross violation of the Geneva Convention, UN resolutions, the Hague Convention, UNESCO, and other international and regional obligations to which Armenia was bound.

Throughout the conflict, Ganja endured a total of five missile and heavy artillery attacks, which claimed 26 lives, injured 175 people, and caused severe damage to civilian infrastructure and vehicles.

The war, which began on September 27, 2020, and lasted 44 days, saw the deaths of 93 Azerbaijani civilians, including 54 men, 27 women, and 12 children. Additionally, 444 people were injured, including 268 men, 109 women, and 67 children, as a result of Armenia's military actions.

Notably, the former so-called “president” of the Karabakh separatists, Arayik Harutyunyan, who was accused of orchestrating terrorist attacks on Ganja's civilian population during the Second Karabakh War, has been detained by the State Security Service and transferred to Baku.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 11, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 11. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020 in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 15th day of the Second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev in connection with the shelling of Ganja: the Azerbaijani side will give a worthy answer to all this!

- President Ilham Aliyev: The missile attack on Ganja was carried out from the Vardenis region of Armenia.

- President Ilham Aliyev: These dishonorable deeds of Armenia can never break thewill of Azerbaijani people.

- First VP Mehriban Aliyeva: I call upon the international community not to remain indifferent to all happened.

- The Ministry of Defense issued a statement that the information disseminated by the Armenian side about the alleged killing of civilians in Hadrut by Azerbaijani servicemen - a woman and her disabled son - is groundless, not supported by facts and is aimed at misleading the international community.

- The Ministry of Defense issued a statement that the information disseminated by the Armenian side about the missile strikes allegedly inflicted by the Azerbaijani army on settlements in the occupied territories is a lie and disinformation.

- Azerbaijani Ganja city once again under fire.

- As a result of the next shelling of Ganja by the Armenian Armed Forces, 5 people were killed and 27 were injured.

- Information about the shelling of Baku does not correspond to reality.

- Armenian armed forces launch missile attacks on Azerbaijani Mingachevir.

- Azerbaijani army delivers fire strikes against the Armenian Armed Forces.

- Deputy regiment commander of the Armed Forces of Armenia destroyed.

- A large number of forces and equipment of the Armenian army destroyed.

- On October 11, around 08.00, an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) of Armenia, which attempted to fly in the Mingachevir direction, was destroyed by the air defense units of Azerbaijan.

- The forces and means of the Armenian Armed Forces, which tried to go on the offensive, were destroyed.

- The Prosecutor General's Office of Azerbaijan reported that as a result of the shelling of Ganja by the Armenian Armed Forces, 7 people were killed and 34 were injured.

- The Armenian Armed Forces fired at an ambulance with a white flag on it, which was picking up the bodies of the Armenian military.

- The death toll in Ganja as a result of rocket attacks from the Armenian Armed Forces has reached 9.

- The Prosecutor General's Office of Azerbaijan reported that since the beginning of the attacks of the Armenian Armed Forces, 41 civilians were killed and 205 civilians were wounded.

- The Azerbaijani Defense Ministry stated that the responsibility for the aggravation of the situation in the region lies entirely with the leadership of Armenia.

- Video of the moment of the missile strike on Ganja released.

World.content:
Emergency services including paramedics and multiple police have responded to an incident in Melbourne's city centre.

Witnesses have told the ABC there was a car driving erratically down Flinders Street and Elizabeth Street, with police remaining at the scene.

The chaos unfolded very close to the Melbourne marathon event, where thousands of people were running a route that passed by Flinders Street Station at the Swanston Street end.

World.title: Pre-COP push leaves Australia's remotest territory feeling forgotten
World.content:
Residents of Australia's remotest territory say they feel forgotten by the government's global climate change efforts ahead of the major COP31 forum in Türkiye.

The federal government hosted pre-COP meetings in Tuvalu and Fiji this week in a bid to raise the voices of Pacific Island nations.

But on the far opposite side of Australia's recognised territory, and 8,900km from this week's Pacific meetings, residents of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands (CKI) feel they have been left in the lurch.

Tuvalu (pictured) and Cocos (Keeling) Islands face similar climate threats like flooding and coastal erosion. (Supplied)

Faced with coastal erosion, flooding and other climate-driven issues mirroring those of Pacific nations, the Cocos Islanders made a bid to be represented at COP31.

Their application was approved by the United Nations, but not selected for funding by the Australian government, with the delegation informed they had been unsuccessful just before this week's talks.

Their panel proposal, submitted by the University of Western Australia's Oceans Institute, would have featured the challenges faced by the Cocos (Keeling) Islands as a low-lying island community.

The Cocos (Keeling) Islands are facing coastal erosion and flooding, like their Pacific Island counterparts. (Supplied: Chris Bray)

Residents rue missed opportunity

Home Island resident Luluk Sloan said COP31 presented an opportunity to bring global awareness to the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.

With a coastal hazard management plan suggesting retreat slammed by the islands' residents, they had hoped attendance would have allowed them to learn how other island communities were dealing with climate-driven challenges.

"A council delegation was actually looking at visiting the Pacific Islands just to see what sort of mitigation they've got planned in terms of not retreating," she said.

"I think it's a disappointment that we don't have that link; we can't really tell our story globally."

Luluk Sloan lives on Home Island. (Supplied: Luluk Sloan)

Ms Sloan said it felt like the islands were being left behind.

" We are an Australian territory, who's voicing for us? Who's vouching for us? No-one. "

West Island resident Rose Cummins also would have attended the conference.

"I certainly applaud the Pacific Islands. I think they've done an incredible job in raising the profile of climate change and how it's directly impacting them," Ms Cummins said.

"I guess we would just like the same opportunity."

Rose Cummins lives on West Island. (Supplied: Rose Cummins)

A spokesperson for the Department of Climate Change, Energy and Water acknowledged the impact climate change was having on the Islands.

But the department rejected suggestions that the focus on the Pacific came at the expense of Australian communities.

"Engagement with Pacific partners complements, rather than replaces, our support for Australian communities facing climate risks," the spokesperson said.

The Oceans Institute said it remained committed to working with the islands' community to help address the ongoing challenges posed by climate change.

Community not heard

Residents say there has been a lack of meaningful consultation on the plan to manage the islands' ongoing coastal risks.

"I think a lot of people felt that it's another consultation," Ms Sloan said.

"What are they going to do about it? Possibly, probably, nothing."

Cocos (Keeling) Islands residents say they have seen metres of shoreline vanish. (Supplied: Luluk Sloan)

Ms Cummins said expressions of interest for a community reference group, promised since the start of the year, were only issued last month.

"There's no decision-making abilities; it won't affect any policy or anything like that," she said.

"That will still be done by experts who don't live here."

The Climate Change Department spokesperson said the Coastal Hazard Risk Management and Adaptation Plan (CHRMAP) was a key step in supporting CKI to respond and adapt to climate change.

"The [plan] gives us a clear picture of the coastal hazards facing the islands and will help guide the work we do together to strengthen preparedness and improve community safety," the spokesperson said.

But Ms Sloan remained sceptical.

"I think people are slowly realising that … the delivery of services is on the decline," she said.

"And that's probably because they're thinking: 'Oh yeah, 50 years from now, the islands are going to go under.'"

World.title: Pro surfer swaps California waves for life in the outback
World.content:
Last month, Brazilian professional surfer Caio Ibelli was riding barrelling waves at the Surfing Champions Trophy in the Maldives.

Today, he's at home, in the outback, almost 1,000 kilometres from the east coast.

The 32-year-old is one of Mount Isa's newest residents, swapping surf and sand for the red dirt plains of north-west Queensland.

Caio Ibelli's days are now spent wrangling his toddler in the outback town of Mount Isa. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"After living in so many different places, this is the best place in the world to live," Ibelli said.

Originally from Brazil, Ibelli moved to Australia after a stint in California.

First picking up a surfboard when he was three years old, he said by the time he was seven, his talent was being noticed.

Caio Ibelli was three years old when he started surfing in Brazil. (Supplied: Caio Ibelli)

By 23, Ibelli had qualified for the World Surf League tour, kicking off a nine-year professional career.

"After that, I kind of retired … I wanted to have kids and a family," he said.

Ibelli said although a move to the outback wasn't always planned, he was proud to be raising his son in the city, despite knowing little about what to expect.

One-year-old Thomas Ibelli is spending his first years in the outback, despite his dad's professional surfing career. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"It is getting a little bit too hot. It's about 38 degrees right now, and I heard it goes all the way to 46 … I've never felt that in my life," he said.

It was his wife's career that brought the family, including their one-year-old son, Thomas, to the region after completing her medical degree.

"Every time I speak with my friends in the hospital and say that my husband is a professional surfer, everybody has the same reaction… 'Oh, how?'" Talie Ibelli laughed.

"We actually love it here. We love the community, and it's a great opportunity for my son to be raised here … this is the real Australia."

Caio Ibelli won the World Surfing Championships in the Maldives last month. (Supplied: Caio Ibelli)

The family have only been to the beach about six times since moving to the bush, which makes his recent win in the Maldives all the more impressive.

"I was playing with my son and then my phone rang and I'm like, 'What? Go to the Maldives in 10 days? I'm smelling the dirt here right now,'" he said.

He said muscle memory along with his new-found "outback attitude" helped him snag the overall win.

"The event was cool. Winning it was amazing, it was awesome," he said.

Caio Ibelli spent about a decade travelling the world surfing circuit. (Supplied: Caio Ibelli)

"Seeing my son playing on the blue water, watching the sharks all day, it was just super special."

Mount Isa has its fair share of athletic prowess, with tennis star Pat Rafter, golfer Greg Norman and AFL player Charlie Cameron all born in the city.

It's unclear yet whether Caio Ibelli's son, Thomas, will follow in his father's footsteps. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Ibelli said it was a privilege to be among the mining city's claims to fame, including perhaps being its most famous surfer.

"After I won the contest in the Maldives, coming back to Mount Isa, I've been going around in places, and people are like, 'Are you the surfer?' And I'm like, 'Yeah', and people are kind of tripping," he said.

The Ibelli family have found a home in north-west Queensland, living in the mining city of Mount Isa. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"I feel so fortunate to be here, Australia is such a good place, and Mount Isa is amazing."

Even with the positives, he admits it is tough to be a surfer with no surf.

"I'm really missing some kind of water, so sometimes I go to swim, or I'm just hoping Mount Isa Council will build us a wave pool sometime soon," he laughed.

Ibelli's next dream is teaching bush kids how to surf.

Caio and Talie Ibelli plan on raising Thomas as an "Aussie kid". (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"I'm so grateful for being here with my family, and I feel like the least I could do is like giving back, and I would love to some day take local people to the beach and surf," he said.

" Who knows, like one day we can bring like a Mount Isa Surf Club on a competition. "

World.title: Taylor says he would welcome return of Frydenberg to politics
World.content:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says he would welcome the return of former Liberal treasurer Josh Frydenberg to politics, as he continues to defend the Coalition's newly released migration policy.

On Saturday, Mr Frydenberg released excerpts of his upcoming memoir A Grateful Son, published in The Australian, which included details of his election defeat four years ago.

The former Kooyong MP, who was a leadership frontrunner, fuelled speculation he may contest a seat in the next election as he outlined his vision for Australia.

He urged the Liberal Party to "reclaim" the centre of politics, arguing there was a lack of political courage in Canberra.

Mr Frydenberg proposed several policy changes across energy and AI and a pitch to leverage a portion of state GST revenue based on how many homes were built.

Josh Frydenberg says Canberra lacks political courage. (AAP: James Ross)

When asked whether he would welcome or fear his former colleague's return, Mr Taylor said he needed "every good leader" heading into the next federal election.

"People will play different roles … whether it's just liking Facebook and Instagram posts all the way through to being a candidate," he told Insiders on Sunday.

"But we've all got to mobilise, and I welcome Josh playing whatever role he's able to play."

Coalition policy for 100,000 NOM The Coalition would cut net overseas migration to 100,000 for two years.

Mr Taylor immediately added that the Coalition would not adopt Mr Frydenberg's suggestion of raising the GST.

"We will not be raising the GST in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis. That we won't do," he said.

"We'll put Australia and Australians first, but we won't be raising taxes.



"I'm a fiscal conservative. I believe in lower taxes, and that's why we'll be giving the tax-back guarantee, lower income taxes for Australians without raising the GST."

Taylor defends budget neutrality of Coalition's migration cuts

Despite economic concerns raised by the business, aged care, education and construction sectors about the Coalition's migration policy, the opposition leader maintained it would be "budget neutral".

Mr Taylor said the policy had not been officially costed by the Parliamentary Budget Office, due to "constraints".

"In terms of analysis, there are limitations on what the parliamentary office can do because of its legislation. It cannot model directly on Labor's policies so we had to give it assumptions to work with," he said.

"That is a constraint, but as we approach the election, we won't have that constraint."

The policy proposes slashing temporary migration by 650,000 places over four years and offsetting the lost tax revenue with 100,000 additional skilled migrants, who would be higher-paid and therefore pay more tax.

Compare Labor, the Coalition and One Nation's migration cuts One Nation wants negative migration in its first years, the Coalition has promised to more than halve it, while Labor has announced measures to ensure migration actually falls to its target of 225,000.

He reiterated that aged care, which heavily relies on temporary visas, would be subject to a transitional arrangement that allowed these workers to stay on existing visas for a longer period of time.

"If you cut numbers and raise standards, you can maintain budget neutrality. And you can strengthen the economy because the average income, the average productivity of the person coming into this country rises," he said.

"What's happening under Labor is they are driving economic growth through population growth alone."

Australia's net overseas migration, or NOM, fell to 292,100 people in the year to March, with Labor pursuing a target of 245,000 for this financial year and 225,000 the year after.

World.title: Man charged with attempted murder after Barossa Valley hinterland stabbing
World.content:
SA Police are investigating an incident in the Barossa Valley hinterland after a 30-year-old man sustained multiple stab wounds yesterday evening.

Police said emergency crews were called to a private property on Pine Creek Road at Bethel.

The victim, who is from Kapunda, was flown to hospital in a critical condition.

"His condition is now considered stable," police said in a statement.

"A 22-year-old Nuriootpa man was arrested at the scene by police without incident."

Police said the 22-year-old was charged with attempted murder and refused police bail.

"Police wish to reassure the local community that this was not a random incident and the men involved are known to each other," police said.

The man is expected to appear in court on Monday.

Police are asking anyone who witnessed the incident and has not yet spoken to police to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: Sense of pride for group who unveils WA's next big thing
World.content:
From the Big Pineapple in Queensland to the Big Prawn in New South Wales, the next "big thing" will be unveiled in the West Australian town of Moora.

A group of conservationists has worked tirelessly for seven years to launch two 11.5-metre Carnaby's cockatoos in the wheatbelt town, 180 kilometres north of Perth.

Those spearheading the project say they hope the sculptures will be a tourism drawcard and bring awareness to the endangered icon of the region.

A 'local icon'

The Kerkhoff Carnaby Group came up with the idea in 2019 in an effort to put Moora on the map and highlight the town as an important place for the cockatoos' conservation.

The group's namesake, 84-year-old Moora conservationist Wally Kerkhoff, has built and installed nesting hollows for the local Carnaby's population throughout the area for more than 40 years.

The critically endangered birds are found in Moora between July and February, when they breed in the hollows of old salmon gums and wandoo trees.

Carnaby's cockatoos landed on the sculptures on the day of installation, giving their tick of approval. (Supplied: Kerkhoff Carnaby Group)

Moore Catchment Council community landcare officer Rachel Walmsley has worked alongside Mr Kerkhoff for 14 years and described the conservationist as a "legend".

"If it wasn't for Wally, we wouldn't have Carnaby's in Moora anymore," she said.

Ms Walmsley said she hoped the new installation would inspire the next generation of Carnaby's cockatoo conservers.

"Wally has done his job. He won't be around forever," she said.

"We need to carry on the fight to keep these birds alive and thriving."

Fittingly, the Kerkhoff Group voted to name the male Carnaby figure Wally, with Mr Kerkhoff given the rights to pick a name for his female counterpart, settling on Mrs Carnaby.

A community effort

The COVID-19 pandemic and rising fuel prices made completing the project challenging.

The project cost $540,000, with 74 per cent from community donations.

There are 240 named donors, many of whom live in Moora and surrounding towns.

Kerkhoff Carnaby Group secretary Topsy De Vries said the community support behind the project meant the giant birds belonged to the residents.

"As we would encounter more roadblocks, say we needed more money to bring the project to life, I would have neighbours come over wanting to give what they described as 'a bit of money', then handing over cheques of $10,000," she said.

"We did feel like giving up a couple of times, but we couldn't because people trusted us.

"People really believed in us."

Erich Juhren volunteered his time to travel to Queensland and back to retrieve the cockatoos. (Supplied: Kerkhoff Carnaby Group)

One of those residents who went "above and beyond" was retired truck driver Erich Juhren.

Mr Juhren drove the sculptures, in sections, several thousand kilometres from Queensland to their new home, where they were put together piece by piece and "perched" on a branch.

Another 'big thing'

Official measuring of the sculpture by manufacturer Natureworks Australia confirm the birds stand as tall as the Big Tractor in the nearby town of Carnamah.

The Big Carnaby's Cockatoo project was a collaboration between the Kerkhoff Carnaby Group, Moore Catchment Council and the Shire of Moora. (Supplied: Kerkhoff Carnaby Group)

"People have asked us, 'Why so big?' And I always say, 'It's no good building a small, big thing,'" Ms De Vries said.

Ms De Vries said there was an air of disbelief that the day of the unveiling had arrived.

"My family have seen me go through this for the past seven years and they can't believe it's nearly over," she said.

" You sit there, you look at them and you get a feeling of, 'We've done it.' "

A tourism 'must-see'

Ms De Vries said the sculptures had already lured tourists from around the state to watch them being erected and the finishing touches being applied.

"One of the local cafes is already benefiting because we now have to wait 30 minutes for our morning coffee," she said.

Moora Shire President Ken Seymour said the local government welcomed the new attraction.

"I look forward to seeing these sculptures attracting more people to the regions, getting people out of the city and enjoying what we have to offer," he said.

Ownership and maintenance of the Carnaby's cockatoo sculptures will be transferred to the Shire of Moora as of the launch day.

World.title: Pregnant woman among eight killed in Pennsylvania shooting
World.content:
A pregnant woman, children and other relatives are among eight victims gunned down by a man at a home in Pennsylvania.

Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said the 45-year-old man was related to seven of the victims, while the eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman.

Video and audio evidence recovered by investigators included muffled gunshot sounds coming from inside the home just before two "distressed" women arrived and began pounding on the door shortly before 5pm on Friday, local time, Mr Lorah said.

The gunman then came out and shot them as they ran toward him, before returning inside.

Police arrived to find the two women dead outside.

Bystanders gather near a house where nine people were confirmed dead. (Reuters: Greg Wohlford/USA Today)

After deploying a drone and robot, police went inside the home and found the bodies of a five-year-old boy; a one-year-old girl on the first floor; two more women and two young men in a stairwell; and the shooter on the second floor.

"Out of respect for the victims and the families, I will not discuss the details of what our officers encountered inside that home," Mr Lorah said at a news conference.

"But I want our community to understand the gravity of what happened and the profound impact this tragedy has had on those involved and on our community as a whole."

Mr Lorah declined to discuss motive but said investigators would talk to other relatives and examine the mobile phones of the women who were killed outside the home.

"They knew something was going on at that house," he said.

"We have to figure out what that is."

Mr Lorah said officers arrived within minutes of receiving an alert via ShotSpotter, a controversial gunshot detection system that relies on artificial intelligence and a network of microphones to identify gunshots.

No additional shots were fired after that.

"Sounds that may have been mistaken for gunfire came from flashbang devices, chemical munitions, used by SWAT officers," he said.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said he offered his administration's "full support" to Erie Mayor Daria Devlin, who spoke directly to the victims' families during the news conference.

"I am so deeply sorry. What happened to you was horrific, and there is nothing that any of us can say today that will make this any easier," she said.

"But you do need to know that our entire community is with you, we're grieving with you. And we are here to support you."

District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz urged the public to refrain from speculation as the investigation continued.

"Please do not allow rumours, speculation or unverified information to add to the pain that these families are already experiencing," she said.

Erie is about 190 kilometres north of Pittsburgh.

Speaking at a campaign rally outside Philadelphia, Mr Shapiro mentioned both the Erie killings and the shooting of two Philadelphia police officers early Saturday.

"Today has been a dark day across this commonwealth," he said.

AP

World.title: More than 70 stranded as Solomon Islands ferry drifts for days
World.content:
More than 70 passengers have been stranded aboard a drifting ferry in Solomon Islands waters since Friday, as an international operation scrambles to get supplies to the vessel.

The ferry was sailing between the remote islands of Anuta and Vanikoro in Temotu Province when its engine failed on Friday, leaving it adrift at sea.

A Panama-registered bulk carrier reached MV Awka on Sunday morning and began transferring water and food, passenger John Tua said.

Mr Tua, a nurse with the provincial government, said the engine was overheating when it broke down about 100 nautical miles from its destination.

"Everyone is OK, no-one panicked, passengers were calm … we're just waiting for the rescue ships to come," he said.

While the seas have been mostly calm, Mr Tua said the ship had also experienced rough swells.

A distress call was issued on Friday, with the Solomon Islands enlisting help from the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) and New Caledonian government.

John Tua with communication equipment dropped from an Australian aircraft. (Supplied: John Tua)

An AMSA spokesperson said its Cairns-based rescue jet made several drops of critical items including food, water, medical supplies and communications equipment.

A French aircraft from New Caledonia was first on the scene on Saturday, dropping life rafts and desalination equipment.

"The urgent need was water. We've run out of water onboard … the ship's water supply was used to cool the engine down when it was heating up," Mr Tua said.

"We have lots of brown coconuts on board to drink, but our water is finished."

On Sunday morning, the Panama-registered bulk carrier Sunnine 3 reached the vessel early and began transferring water and food, which was lifestreamed online by Mr Tua.

Loading...

Passengers have stayed in touch with families using the ship's Starlink internet, while Mr Tua has been the main source of news for worried relatives.

Temotu Premier Stanley Tehiahua said a police patrol boat was on its way from Honiara.

"To all relatives, families and friends anxiously awaiting news of their loved ones, we recognise the emotional distress and uncertainty you are experiencing," he said in a statement.

"We call on everyone to remain calm, united and prayerful during this difficult time," Mr Tehiahua said.

The ABC has requested comment from the Solomon Islands Maritime Safety Administration and the country's Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre.

The incident comes three weeks after the inter-island ferry MV Matui sank in rough seas in neighbouring Vanuatu with more than 50 people onboard. More than 30 people from the MV Matui are still missing.

There have been calls for Australia and New Zealand to invest more in maritime safety, including from Peter Nuttall, a sustainable researcher at the University of the South Pacific, who told the ABC after the Matui sinking that Australia could easily invest in better vessels for the Pacific.

"We could have built 40 to 60 safe, brand new, low-carbon ferries for the same budget as we've spent on 20-something patrol boats, several which have already been scrapped," Dr Nuttall said.

World.title: This athletics great says the Melbourne Marathon track was the ‘best ever’
World.content:
SportAthleticsMelbourne Marathon This athletics great says the Melbourne Marathon track was the ‘best ever’ Michael Gleeson October 11, 2026 — 12:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Eliud Kipchoge might be the greatest marathon runner of all time, a two-time world record holder and dual Olympic gold medallist, but he’s also 42 and hadn’t won a marathon in three years. When he came for this year’s Melbourne Marathon, it felt like he was here to run, not race, a sort of grand farewell world tour, an exhibition run around the world. Seven marathons on seven continents. Oceania? That’ll be Melbourne. Tick. Eliud Kipchoge, winner of the men’s Melbourne Marathon. Luis Enrique Ascui On Sunday, the best we have seen won his first marathon since Berlin in 2023. The field in Melbourne might not have been the strength of Berlin, but his time was a sharp 2:09.08, a Melbourne Marathon race record. (As distinct from a course record, as the course changes a bit.) “I want to celebrate with the people of Melbourne. I want to celebrate with the people of the world. You know, to show people that sport is about actually crossing the finishing line and coming together,” Kipchoge said once he got his head clear of a mob of cameras that closed in on the diminutive Kenyan at the line.



His hardest push might not have been the killer last 10 kilometres so much as getting from the finish line clear of a camera pack to reach the thousands of fans in the stands of the MCG. “After three years, I’ve never won, but this is my first win. I believe that my body is still [good], still able to compete with the next generation. I am the oldest athlete still competing, but I am happy to run with the Gen Zs – those who are under 30, yes,” he said. A young fan meets Kipchoge after the race. Luis Enrique Ascui “My best message to Melbourne is that please, let us all be one. Let us come out in line. Let us run every day. You know, let us run for health. Let us run for education. Let us run for environment. Thank you, everybody. Thank you very much.” Jimmy Webster, the former pro cyclist, was on Kipchoge’s shoulder for 20 kilometres with a lead pack, but by the 30-kilometre mark, Kipchoge had opened up a 30-second gap. At 32 kilometres, Webster blew up and faded back, but Kipchoge was not completely right either.



At that point, he was on track to run 2.05 or 2.06, but had a side or abdominal problem that seemed to hamper him and ease him back for a couple of kilometres. The question was whether, at his age, he would flag. But with age comes experience; instead, Kipchoge knew to pull his stride for a couple of kilometres, reset and he went again. He cruised into the MCG to thousands of fans in the northern stands, fireworks and Jess Hull and Cam Myers holding the ribbon at the line. Tom De Canto came in second, 1.26 behind Kipchoge. Kipchoge celebrates after the race. Luis Enrique Ascui “Actually, the crowd is wonderful. I have never seen a crowd like this,” Kipchoge said. “Melbourne is really, really a sporting city. I know it’s more than a sporting city because as the people take their culture is wonderful. It’s above everything as far as sport is concerned. “With the tennis [the race started outside the tennis centre], finishing at cricket where Olympics was actually there in 1956, ran on the Formula 1 track, so it was four sporting events in one competition.



“So I’m happy. I will come back to Melbourne, you know, to watch tennis, to watch Formula 1 next year, to see, you know, people of Melbourne playing cricket. This is the best track ever.” New Zealand’s Camille French won the women’s marathon in 2:28.25, 23 seconds ahead of Australian Olympian Sinead Diver. World.content:
CultureLive reviewsMelbourne live reviews Old world charm abounds in this classic telling of a fairytale Tony Way Andrew Fuhrmann and October 11, 2026 — 12:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Key points DANCE: The Stuttgart Ballet bring The Sleeping Beauty to Regent Theatre

MUSIC: Isata Kanneh-Mason peforms at the Melbourne Recital Centre

MUSIC: Pekka Kuusisto performs with the ACO at Legends and Luminaries

DANCE

The Sleeping Beauty ★★★★

Regent Theatre, until October 18 The Stuttgart Ballet is in town, offering a rare chance to see a major European company dance one of its signature storybook ballets – with all the old-world charm and seriousness you could want. It’s also a chance to see a handful of genuine international ballet stars. First among them is Elisa Badenes, who danced Aurora on opening night, a dancer with exceptional composure and the silkiest of turns. The Stuttgart Ballet is in town. Kate Longley Her Prince Désiré was Henrik Erikson: neat as a folded napkin in everything he does. His partnering with Badenes was compelling throughout, culminating in an exquisite grand pas de deux during the marriage festivities. The highlight was a diagonal of supported turns and plunging fish dives where, for one blissful moment, the two dancers appeared so connected, so entirely at one, that it was unclear who was supporting who. The wicked fairy Carabosse was danced by Jason Reilly, a veteran dramatic dynamo. He has a distinctive presence: quick, harassed, mocking, but earnest even when parodying the classical steps of the others.



Carabosse has an elevated significance in Marcia Haydée’s version of the ballet. Haydée has transformed the contest between Carabosse and the Lilac Fairy into a sort of epic contest between good and evil. It can seem a little absurd – too much drama for the fey conceit – but this is a production that is very much of its time. Created in 1987, it’s essentially a Cold War fairy tale, showing a world dominated by two great powers. Mizuki Amemiya of The Stuttgart Ballet. Kate Longley Abigail Willson-Heisel brought unflappable presence to the Lilac Fairy, while among the other dancers, Brazilian-born Adhonay Soares drew the eye with the height and energy of his leaps as the bare-chested Ali Baba. It’s a long way to travel just to perform The Sleeping Beauty, even if it is a defining production. Once upon a time, they might have brought a second ballet to show another side of their repertoire. But visits by international companies of this stature – any stature, really – are few and far between these days.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann



MUSIC

Isata Kanneh-Mason ★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, October 9 Navigating a journey from darkness to light, pianist Isata Kanneh-Mason’s Australian debut recital offered plenty of familiar music. Bookended by two of Beethoven’s most popular sonatas, the “Moonlight” and the “Waldstein”, it also included Ravel’s astoundingly imaginative but fiendishly difficult Gaspard de la nuit. Two works by Bulgarian-English composer Dobrinka Tabakova provided a contrasting contemporary aesthetic. Isata Kanneh-Mason performs at Melbourne Recital Centre on October 9, 2026 Laura Manariti In Beethoven’s famous moonlit opening, Kanneh-Mason’s striking ability for extremely restrained dynamics and tone colour might have suggested a burgeoning sense of drama, yet this remained unrealised. The blazing finale displayed her prodigious technique, even if greater detail could have been revealed with lighter pedalling. In Ravel’s brightly hued triptych, the water sprite Ondine splashed around in a luxurious aqueous soundscape while Kanneh-Mason’s trademark restraint lent the scene of the scaffold appropriate eeriness. She also convincingly captured Scarbo’s caprice, mischief and malevolence.



After a symbolic change from dark evening gown to shorter pale blue dress, Kanneh-Mason turned to two works by Tabakova, containing the nucleus of the program. Nocturne, an attractive minimalist miniature summoned up night. Using harmonics and repeated notes, Halo effectively evoked a lunar halo which becomes increasingly bright. Editor's pick Melbourne live reviews Jealousy, friendship and love take centre-stage in this story Clearly close to her heart, Kanneh-Mason played the “Waldstein” with great devotion, ensuring that the finale’s beginning did point to the dawn (an alternative nickname for the work). The blazing sunshine of the closing pages, however, were clouded over by some heavy pedalling. Impressive as Kanneh-Mason’s playing is, trading some technical brilliance for a wider tonal palette and greater emotional abandon would have taken the performance to a higher level. An over-the-top arrangement of the 1960s hit I Say a Little Prayer for You provided a buoyant encore for the enthusiastic audience.

Reviewed by Tony Way



MUSIC

Pekka Kuusisto: Legends and Luminaries ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, October 10 Ebullience is at the heart of Pekka Kuusisto’s artistic DNA. Joy, passion, commitment and a sense of fun are among the enviable qualities the Finnish violinist and composer brought to his latest collaboration with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Pekka Kuusisto (left) performs with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Nic Walker As guest leader, Kuusisto helmed the orchestra through a program of contrasting styles, all with their own aural appeal. In Kuusisto’s thoughtful arrangement of excerpts from Mozart’s The Magic Flute, a little messiness was the price paid for an overture that ran at bullet train speed. Once the high-octane excitement subsided, beautifully shaped lyrical moments emerged before leading into the Queen of the Night’s aria. Written for Kuusisto and premiered with the ACO Collective in 2019, American composer Nico Muhly’s Shrink: Concerto for Violin and Strings is a tour de force that is a perfect fit for the dedicatee’s mercurial personality.



Across the work’s 22 minutes, Muhly weaves an intricate, compelling tapestry of textures, while the soloist jumps through every technical hoop imaginable. Kuusisto clearly thrives on such challenges, bringing unflagging zeal and a wealth of colour and emotion to the cleverly constructed score that exploits narrowing intervals alluded to in the title. Editor's pick Melbourne Fringe Festival Not just red noses and creepy characters: Why it’s time to give clowning another chance Receiving its first Australian performances on this tour, Pulitzer Prize-winning composer Ellen Reid’s “paean to the Californian landscape”, West Coast Sky Eternal elicited an empathetic performance. Its shifting textural perspectives are intriguing at first before an extended pizzicato passage tends to unbalance its structure. Clearly revelling in Kuusisto’s leadership, an arrangement of Mendelssohn’s String Quintet No. 2 in B-flat, Op. 87 received classic ACO treatment. Ebullience certainly radiated through the outer movements, while an elegant second-movement scherzando preceded an exquisite, heart-tugging slow movement. A superbly judged encore came with Reger’s arrangement of one of Bach’s most intimately rhapsodic works for organ, the chorale prelude O Mensch, bewein’.

Reviewed by Tony Way The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Ben Roberts-Smith joins 600 veterans as Albanese marks Australia’s 25 years in Afghanistan
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAustralian War Memorial Ben Roberts-Smith joins 600 veterans as Albanese marks Australia’s 25 years in Afghanistan Rob Harris October 11, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anthony Albanese has paid tribute to Australian troops who endured a battlefield where every footstep could conceal an explosive and threats could come from within their own ranks, as about 600 veterans gathered to mark 25 years since the beginning of Australia’s longest war. Among those attending Sunday’s national commemoration at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra was Victoria Cross recipient Ben Roberts-Smith, who faces five charges of war crime murder over the alleged executions of Afghan detainees. He strongly denies the allegations. Ben Roberts-Smith arrives for a National Commemorative Service recognising the 25th anniversary of Australian service in Afghanistan. Alex Ellinghausen The prime minister honoured those who served in Afghanistan, the 47 Australian personnel who died as a result of their service and the families who continue to live with their loss. “It was an environment in which vigilance had to be as relentless as the dust that we saw depicted in the video that began today’s solemn ceremony,” the prime minister said.



“Where every footstep could feel heavy in a landscape sown with explosives, where any crowd might hold a suicide bomber, and where the threats came from without, and sometimes devastatingly from within.” Front row: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Minister for Veterans’ Affairs and Minister for Defence Personnel Matt Keogh, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Opposition Spokesman for Veterans’ Affairs Michael McCormack, at the Australian War Memorial on Sunday. Alex Ellinghausen He paid tribute to Afghan soldiers and interpreters who risked their lives to assist Australian forces, many of whom attended the ceremony. “What shone brightly amid all of this was the courage of so many Afghans, the soldiers, the interpreters, all who stood against their oppressors and put their own safety on the line to help,” he said. Albanese also recognised those who returned wounded in body or mind, and the families who endured the pride and pain of military service.



“We honour all who went and all who fell,” he said. Former Prime Minister Tony Abbott and Opposition Spokesman for Industry and Sovereign Capability Andrew Hastie ahead of the service. Alex Ellinghausen The gathering marked a quarter of a century since Australian forces deployed to Afghanistan following the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States. The conflict became Australia’s longest military engagement, spanning operations against al-Qaeda and the Taliban, counter-insurgency campaigns and efforts to train Afghan security forces. About 26,000 to 30,000 Australians served under Operations Slipper and Highroad, with 263 wounded. The Taliban’s return to power in August 2021, following the withdrawal of international forces, left many veterans questioning the outcome of the two-decade campaign.



Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, former Prime Minister John Howard, former Prime Minister Scott Morrison and Opposition spokesman for Veterans’ Affairs Michael McCormack. Alex Ellinghausen Kahlil Fegan, who served on multiple operational deployments and led multinational teams in Afghanistan, including Mentoring Task Force 4, reflected on the fall of Kabul and the questions it raised for those who served. “Was it worth it? What did we achieve, and how will we be remembered?” he said. Fegan said wars were often judged by their endings, but the meaning of military service could not be measured solely by political outcomes. “It is measured in such things as duty, courage, sacrifice, and by standing by your mates when it matters,” he said.



Roberts-Smith, a former Special Air Service Regiment corporal, sat in the front row alongside his partner, Sarah Matulin. He was granted permission by a judge last month to travel from Brisbane to Canberra for the service, subject to strict bail conditions. His prosecution has become a focus of debate over alleged unlawful killings by Australian special forces and the investigation of veterans accused of war crimes. No trial date has been set. Ben Roberts-Smith (2nd from left) during the National Commemorative Service. Alex Ellinghausen Fellow Victoria Cross recipient Dan Keighran also attended, alongside former prime ministers John Howard, Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison. Liberal MP Andrew Hastie, a former SAS captain who served in Afghanistan and gave evidence in Roberts-Smith’s defamation trial, sat behind the former prime ministers with his children.



Chief or Defence Force, Admiral Mark Hammond laid a wreath alongside chief of airforce, Air Marshal Stephen Chappell and Lieutenant General Susan Coyle, the chief of army. Janny Poate, whose son Robert was killed at 23, in a “green on blue” attack, also read a tribute. Hugh and Janny Poate at their home in Canberra with a photograph of their son Private Robert Poate. Janny Poate paid tribute at the service. Alex Ellinghausen “We remember a human story that includes the families who waited, worried, endured separation, and who suffered loss? Most of all, we remember this: their strength and resilience.” Albanese said the service of Australian personnel demonstrated what was worth fighting for, regardless of the eventual outcome of the conflict. “What Australians serving in Afghanistan embody is something that we must never lose,” he said.

World.title: Apple’s big question: will customers rush to buy its $3500 foldable phone?
World.content:
TechnologyPhones Opinion Apple’s big question: will customers rush to buy its $3500 foldable phone?

Dave Lee October 11, 2026 — 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A big question Apple analysts are asking is: how many consumers are waiting for the iPhone Duo? The answer is hugely important to Apple’s stock this year and beyond. The new iPhone Pro range has been out for nearly three weeks, and from the get-go analysts noted somewhat flat consumer interest compared with last year’s Pro models. Apple’s new chief John Ternus is desperate for a breakout hit to begin his tenure. Bloomberg One theory is that a significant number of would-be buyers are waiting for Apple’s new foldable model, which doesn’t come out until October 23. If that’s true, then it’s good news for Apple, its investors and the company’s new chief executive officer, John Ternus – who would love a breakout hit to begin his tenure. At a starting price of $3499 in Australia, the Duo would boost the iPhone’s average selling price – a key metric watched by Wall Street. Add the signal that Duo’s success would suggest Apple still has the innovative “juice,” as they say, and the stock could build on what’s already been a banner 12 months – up 22 per cent since the start of the year.



Related Article Opinion

Phones I’d pay $3500 for an iPhone. So should you David Swan Technology editor But if it’s not the case, and consumers are just holding off on an upgrade altogether, Apple’s bold attempt to breathe new life into its most important product will appear to have fallen flat, a sign that even Apple couldn’t bring the potentially lucrative foldable form factor to the masses. For clues on what’s going on with the iPhone, analysts look to a simple but imperfect metric: wait times for delivery when customers try to buy a device. When the new iPhone Pro was available to pre-order, analysts at both Bank of America and UBS observed muted demand compared with last year’s models. “Globally, on average, ship time for the iPhone 18 Pro is currently at 14 days (vs. 18 days for iPhone 17 Pro) while iPhone 18 Pro Max stands at 18 days (vs. 25 days last year),” the Bank of America noted at the time. Sales of the Duo will be a fraction of the more than 250 million iPhones that Apple is expected to ship this year, but those sales will cement any perception of whether Apple’s top product still has room to grow.



UBS saw a smaller difference but the same trend: muted demand for the iPhone 18 Pro. “While we acknowledge the possibility that muted wait times for the Pro and Pro Max could suggest consumers are delaying their purchase decisions for the Duo,” its analysts wrote, “we believe that the $US1999 ($2862) starting price could limit incremental unit upside.” (In other words: Don’t count on it being Duo demand holding the Pro back.) In the couple of weeks since, UBS has noted an uptick in demand for the Pro and Pro Max – that is, a lengthening of delivery times. It is an imperfect metric. Apple might have just had more inventory ready to go this year compared with 2025. And this is the first year that Apple has split the launch of its premium and basic tiers into different seasons – the less expensive non-Pro iPhones come out next year – so inventory management might be a little more straightforward. Loading But it also might be the case that some consumers have been turned off by the $US100 price increases across the board for Apple’s flagship products, mainly caused by the ballooning cost of memory. The company and the carriers it works with have been trying to soften the blow by increasing trade-in value of old devices and introducing new payment options, most notably Apple’s new leasing program. It still may not be enough. A poor iPhone cycle is bad for Apple’s stock unless something significant elsewhere in its business – such as its services segment – is able to offset the news. This year’s offset, if iPhone Pro sales require one, could be a frenzy at Apple’s glistening stores across the world, as users clamour for the iPhone Duo when it’s released. Apple would need IDC’s estimate of 10 million iPhone Duos sold in the first 12 months to be on the money. To reach that, Apple will need to overcome reported manufacturing challenges that could impact initial supply. Then again, a headline-grabbing shortage of a hot new product has its upside. Sales of the Duo will be a fraction of the more than 250 million iPhones that Apple is expected to ship this year, but those sales will cement any perception of whether Apple’s top product still has room to grow.



Related Article Exclusive

Telecommunications Your next phone could take four years to pay off As it happened, I spent more than an hour at Apple’s downtown Brooklyn store recently, waiting on a repair to my iPhone 15 Pro which, like its owner, is ageing but still sufficiently capable. As I sat, to my right was a table of glowing iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models, attracting only limited interest. Other than different colours and incremental improvements to the camera and battery, there’s nothing much to see. Yet, I heard at least three people inquire about the iPhone Duo. “Are you getting a lot of that?” I asked the staff member when she came to help me. “Oh yeah,” she laughed. “All day.” Whether those kinds of customers are ready to spend, or are just curious, will set the mood for Apple this year. World.title: India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaIndia India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest Saurabh Sharma , Sarita Chaganti Singh and Sakshi Dayal Updated October 11, 2026 — 9:48am ,first published 12:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

New Delhi: Police detained more than 2000 protesters and the founder of the “cockroach” youth movement in Delhi on Saturday (New Delhi time) as security forces locked down parts of the capital to thwart a rally demanding the resignation of India’s election chief. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended in the central business district and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as authorities moved to stop a demonstration organised by the Cockroach movement. The protest was aimed at chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Police officers detain a protester. Getty Images The movement had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, but the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began.



A home ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters more than 2000 people were detained in Delhi. Local media said about 400 protesters were held in India’s financial hub, Mumbai. Related Article Protests India’s ‘cockroach’ protesters claim surprise victory as government accepts their demands There was no immediate comment from police on the detentions. The United Nations human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests. “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled,” UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said in a statement.



He also urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed. The Indian mission to the UN in Geneva, however, called the UN’s concerns “misplaced” and said they constitute “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”. Indian police women stop opposition party members shouting anti-government slogans, as they tried to march on roads during the protest. Getty Images It stressed that the right to peaceful assembly was guaranteed by India’s Constitution. “As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order,” the statement added. Movement leaders held



Police detained Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and senior leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka when their flight from Mumbai landed in Delhi, the group said in a statement. Television footage showed Dipke challenging officers who approached him on board the aircraft. Police officers detain a protester. Getty Images “I have come to be arrested, arrest me ... I am not afraid of you guys,” he said. “No, this is not an arrest,” one officer replied. “Please co-operate.”



The movement condemned what it called the “authoritarian detention” of its leaders, demanded their release and vowed to continue protesting. “We will continue our protest tomorrow, day after ... until Gyanesh Kumar resigns. We will be on the streets,” CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde told reporters. CJP also said authorities refused to provide updates on the leaders’ whereabouts or health, even after news arrived of the death of Dipke’s grandmother. Police said Dipke was informed of her death and was offered help to return home for the funeral. Some opposition lawmakers and former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi, and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala were also detained, TV channels showed. Representatives of two digital news outlets said police briefly detained four of their reporters while they were covering the demonstrations. A Reuters journalist was also detained briefly before being released.



Across the capital of about 20 million people, security forces set up checkpoints on major roads and entry points, boarded buses searching for protesters and inspected vehicles. Barricades and concrete blocks disrupted traffic while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers guarded key routes. New challenge to Modi The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter rolls ahead of recent state polls. Protestors shout slogans against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Bloomberg Protests intensified after the Indian Express reported last week that two election commissioners had questioned Kumar’s voter-list revisions that removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists.



Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing. The BJP says its electoral success reflects Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation. The near-daily protests come just months after demonstrations over exam paper leaks forced his education minister to quit. The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027. Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main opposition Congress party, said Modi’s opponents would not back down.



A senior BJP member, Ravi Shankar Prasad, said the party was not opposed to demonstrations but the street protests had been “weaponised” by rivals due to election defeats. Deletions affected state polls, opposition alleges Opposition parties say the deletions affected the outcome of recent state elections won by the BJP and have cast a shadow over voting in the world’s largest democracy. Election Commission data show about 130 million voter entries were removed during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated, 30 million who could not be traced and 28 million who had died. The commission says the removals relate to entries identified during the draft revision process and that any eligible voter incorrectly deleted can re-enrol.

World.content:
SportAthleticsMelbourne Marathon This athletics great says the Melbourne Marathon track was the ‘best ever’ Michael Gleeson October 11, 2026 — 12:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.
