Eliud Kipchoge might be the greatest marathon runner of all time, a two-time world record holder and dual Olympic gold medallist, but he’s also 42 and hadn’t won a marathon in three years. When he came for this year’s Melbourne Marathon, it felt like he was here to run, not race, a sort of grand farewell world tour, an exhibition run around the world. Seven marathons on seven continents. Oceania? That’ll be Melbourne. Tick. Eliud Kipchoge, winner of the men’s Melbourne Marathon. Luis Enrique Ascui On Sunday, the best we have seen won his first marathon since Berlin in 2023. The field in Melbourne might not have been the strength of Berlin, but his time was a sharp 2:09.08, a Melbourne Marathon race record. (As distinct from a course record, as the course changes a bit.) “I want to celebrate with the people of Melbourne. I want to celebrate with the people of the world. You know, to show people that sport is about actually crossing the finishing line and coming together,” Kipchoge said once he got his head clear of a mob of cameras that closed in on the diminutive Kenyan at the line.



His hardest push might not have been the killer last 10 kilometres so much as getting from the finish line clear of a camera pack to reach the thousands of fans in the stands of the MCG. “After three years, I’ve never won, but this is my first win. I believe that my body is still [good], still able to compete with the next generation. I am the oldest athlete still competing, but I am happy to run with the Gen Zs – those who are under 30, yes,” he said. A young fan meets Kipchoge after the race. Luis Enrique Ascui “My best message to Melbourne is that please, let us all be one. Let us come out in line. Let us run every day. You know, let us run for health. Let us run for education. Let us run for environment. Thank you, everybody. Thank you very much.” Jimmy Webster, the former pro cyclist, was on Kipchoge’s shoulder for 20 kilometres with a lead pack, but by the 30-kilometre mark, Kipchoge had opened up a 30-second gap. At 32 kilometres, Webster blew up and faded back, but Kipchoge was not completely right either.



At that point, he was on track to run 2.05 or 2.06, but had a side or abdominal problem that seemed to hamper him and ease him back for a couple of kilometres. The question was whether, at his age, he would flag. But with age comes experience; instead, Kipchoge knew to pull his stride for a couple of kilometres, reset and he went again. He cruised into the MCG to thousands of fans in the northern stands, fireworks and Jess Hull and Cam Myers holding the ribbon at the line. Tom De Canto came in second, 1.26 behind Kipchoge. Kipchoge celebrates after the race. Luis Enrique Ascui “Actually, the crowd is wonderful. I have never seen a crowd like this,” Kipchoge said. “Melbourne is really, really a sporting city. I know it’s more than a sporting city because as the people take their culture is wonderful. It’s above everything as far as sport is concerned. “With the tennis [the race started outside the tennis centre], finishing at cricket where Olympics was actually there in 1956, ran on the Formula 1 track, so it was four sporting events in one competition.



“So I’m happy. I will come back to Melbourne, you know, to watch tennis, to watch Formula 1 next year, to see, you know, people of Melbourne playing cricket. This is the best track ever.” New Zealand’s Camille French won the women’s marathon in 2:28.25, 23 seconds ahead of Australian Olympian Sinead Diver. Key points DANCE: The Stuttgart Ballet bring The Sleeping Beauty to Regent Theatre

MUSIC: Isata Kanneh-Mason peforms at the Melbourne Recital Centre

MUSIC: Pekka Kuusisto performs with the ACO at Legends and Luminaries

DANCE

The Sleeping Beauty ★★★★

Regent Theatre, until October 18 The Stuttgart Ballet is in town, offering a rare chance to see a major European company dance one of its signature storybook ballets – with all the old-world charm and seriousness you could want. It’s also a chance to see a handful of genuine international ballet stars. First among them is Elisa Badenes, who danced Aurora on opening night, a dancer with exceptional composure and the silkiest of turns. The Stuttgart Ballet is in town. Kate Longley Her Prince Désiré was Henrik Erikson: neat as a folded napkin in everything he does. His partnering with Badenes was compelling throughout, culminating in an exquisite grand pas de deux during the marriage festivities. The highlight was a diagonal of supported turns and plunging fish dives where, for one blissful moment, the two dancers appeared so connected, so entirely at one, that it was unclear who was supporting who. The wicked fairy Carabosse was danced by Jason Reilly, a veteran dramatic dynamo. He has a distinctive presence: quick, harassed, mocking, but earnest even when parodying the classical steps of the others.



Carabosse has an elevated significance in Marcia Haydée’s version of the ballet. Haydée has transformed the contest between Carabosse and the Lilac Fairy into a sort of epic contest between good and evil. It can seem a little absurd – too much drama for the fey conceit – but this is a production that is very much of its time. Created in 1987, it’s essentially a Cold War fairy tale, showing a world dominated by two great powers. Mizuki Amemiya of The Stuttgart Ballet. Kate Longley Abigail Willson-Heisel brought unflappable presence to the Lilac Fairy, while among the other dancers, Brazilian-born Adhonay Soares drew the eye with the height and energy of his leaps as the bare-chested Ali Baba. It’s a long way to travel just to perform The Sleeping Beauty, even if it is a defining production. Once upon a time, they might have brought a second ballet to show another side of their repertoire. But visits by international companies of this stature – any stature, really – are few and far between these days.

Reviewed by Andrew Fuhrmann



MUSIC

Isata Kanneh-Mason ★★★★

Melbourne Recital Centre, October 9 Navigating a journey from darkness to light, pianist Isata Kanneh-Mason’s Australian debut recital offered plenty of familiar music. Bookended by two of Beethoven’s most popular sonatas, the “Moonlight” and the “Waldstein”, it also included Ravel’s astoundingly imaginative but fiendishly difficult Gaspard de la nuit. Two works by Bulgarian-English composer Dobrinka Tabakova provided a contrasting contemporary aesthetic. Isata Kanneh-Mason performs at Melbourne Recital Centre on October 9, 2026 Laura Manariti In Beethoven’s famous moonlit opening, Kanneh-Mason’s striking ability for extremely restrained dynamics and tone colour might have suggested a burgeoning sense of drama, yet this remained unrealised. The blazing finale displayed her prodigious technique, even if greater detail could have been revealed with lighter pedalling. In Ravel’s brightly hued triptych, the water sprite Ondine splashed around in a luxurious aqueous soundscape while Kanneh-Mason’s trademark restraint lent the scene of the scaffold appropriate eeriness. She also convincingly captured Scarbo’s caprice, mischief and malevolence.



After a symbolic change from dark evening gown to shorter pale blue dress, Kanneh-Mason turned to two works by Tabakova, containing the nucleus of the program. Nocturne, an attractive minimalist miniature summoned up night. Using harmonics and repeated notes, Halo effectively evoked a lunar halo which becomes increasingly bright. Editor's pick Melbourne live reviews Jealousy, friendship and love take centre-stage in this story Clearly close to her heart, Kanneh-Mason played the “Waldstein” with great devotion, ensuring that the finale’s beginning did point to the dawn (an alternative nickname for the work). The blazing sunshine of the closing pages, however, were clouded over by some heavy pedalling. Impressive as Kanneh-Mason’s playing is, trading some technical brilliance for a wider tonal palette and greater emotional abandon would have taken the performance to a higher level. An over-the-top arrangement of the 1960s hit I Say a Little Prayer for You provided a buoyant encore for the enthusiastic audience.

Reviewed by Tony Way



MUSIC

Pekka Kuusisto: Legends and Luminaries ★★★★

Australian Chamber Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, October 10 Ebullience is at the heart of Pekka Kuusisto’s artistic DNA. Joy, passion, commitment and a sense of fun are among the enviable qualities the Finnish violinist and composer brought to his latest collaboration with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Pekka Kuusisto (left) performs with the Australian Chamber Orchestra. Nic Walker As guest leader, Kuusisto helmed the orchestra through a program of contrasting styles, all with their own aural appeal. In Kuusisto’s thoughtful arrangement of excerpts from Mozart’s The Magic Flute, a little messiness was the price paid for an overture that ran at bullet train speed. Once the high-octane excitement subsided, beautifully shaped lyrical moments emerged before leading into the Queen of the Night’s aria. Written for Kuusisto and premiered with the ACO Collective in 2019, American composer Nico Muhly’s Shrink: Concerto for Violin and Strings is a tour de force that is a perfect fit for the dedicatee’s mercurial personality.



Across the work’s 22 minutes, Muhly weaves an intricate, compelling tapestry of textures, while the soloist jumps through every technical hoop imaginable. Kuusisto clearly thrives on such challenges, bringing unflagging zeal and a wealth of colour and emotion to the cleverly constructed score that exploits narrowing intervals alluded to in the title. Editor's pick Melbourne Fringe Festival Not just red noses and creepy characters: Why it’s time to give clowning another chance Receiving its first Australian performances on this tour, Pulitzer Prize-winning composer Ellen Reid’s “paean to the Californian landscape”, West Coast Sky Eternal elicited an empathetic performance. Its shifting textural perspectives are intriguing at first before an extended pizzicato passage tends to unbalance its structure. Clearly revelling in Kuusisto’s leadership, an arrangement of Mendelssohn’s String Quintet No. 2 in B-flat, Op. 87 received classic ACO treatment. Ebullience certainly radiated through the outer movements, while an elegant second-movement scherzando preceded an exquisite, heart-tugging slow movement. A superbly judged encore came with Reger’s arrangement of one of Bach’s most intimately rhapsodic works for organ, the chorale prelude O Mensch, bewein’.

Reviewed by Tony Way The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

The Bathurst 1000 is underway with Aaron Seton holding on to the lead after his co-driver Zach Bates secured pole position for the team – the first time a rookie has done so since 2001.

World.title: Ben Roberts-Smith joins 600 veterans as Albanese marks Australia’s 25 years in Afghanistan
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAustralian War Memorial Ben Roberts-Smith joins 600 veterans as Albanese marks Australia’s 25 years in Afghanistan Rob Harris October 11, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anthony Albanese has paid tribute to Australian troops who endured a battlefield where every footstep could conceal an explosive and threats could come from within their own ranks, as about 600 veterans gathered to mark 25 years since the beginning of Australia’s longest war. Among those attending Sunday’s national commemoration at the Australian War Memorial in Canberra was Victoria Cross recipient Ben Roberts-Smith, who faces five charges of war crime murder over the alleged executions of Afghan detainees. He strongly denies the allegations. Ben Roberts-Smith arrives for a National Commemorative Service recognising the 25th anniversary of Australian service in Afghanistan. Alex Ellinghausen The prime minister honoured those who served in Afghanistan, the 47 Australian personnel who died as a result of their service and the families who continue to live with their loss. “It was an environment in which vigilance had to be as relentless as the dust that we saw depicted in the video that began today’s solemn ceremony,” the prime minister said.



“Where every footstep could feel heavy in a landscape sown with explosives, where any crowd might hold a suicide bomber, and where the threats came from without, and sometimes devastatingly from within.” Front row: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Minister for Veterans’ Affairs and Minister for Defence Personnel Matt Keogh, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and Opposition Spokesman for Veterans’ Affairs Michael McCormack, at the Australian War Memorial on Sunday. Alex Ellinghausen He paid tribute to Afghan soldiers and interpreters who risked their lives to assist Australian forces, many of whom attended the ceremony. “What shone brightly amid all of this was the courage of so many Afghans, the soldiers, the interpreters, all who stood against their oppressors and put their own safety on the line to help,” he said. Albanese also recognised those who returned wounded in body or mind, and the families who endured the pride and pain of military service.



“We honour all who went and all who fell,” he said. Former Prime Minister Tony Abbott and Opposition Spokesman for Industry and Sovereign Capability Andrew Hastie ahead of the service. Alex Ellinghausen The gathering marked a quarter of a century since Australian forces deployed to Afghanistan following the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks in the United States. The conflict became Australia’s longest military engagement, spanning operations against al-Qaeda and the Taliban, counter-insurgency campaigns and efforts to train Afghan security forces. About 26,000 to 30,000 Australians served under Operations Slipper and Highroad, with 263 wounded. The Taliban’s return to power in August 2021, following the withdrawal of international forces, left many veterans questioning the outcome of the two-decade campaign.



Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, former Prime Minister John Howard, former Prime Minister Scott Morrison and Opposition spokesman for Veterans’ Affairs Michael McCormack. Alex Ellinghausen Kahlil Fegan, who served on multiple operational deployments and led multinational teams in Afghanistan, including Mentoring Task Force 4, reflected on the fall of Kabul and the questions it raised for those who served. “Was it worth it? What did we achieve, and how will we be remembered?” he said. Fegan said wars were often judged by their endings, but the meaning of military service could not be measured solely by political outcomes. “It is measured in such things as duty, courage, sacrifice, and by standing by your mates when it matters,” he said.



Roberts-Smith, a former Special Air Service Regiment corporal, sat in the front row alongside his partner, Sarah Matulin. He was granted permission by a judge last month to travel from Brisbane to Canberra for the service, subject to strict bail conditions. His prosecution has become a focus of debate over alleged unlawful killings by Australian special forces and the investigation of veterans accused of war crimes. No trial date has been set. Ben Roberts-Smith (2nd from left) during the National Commemorative Service. Alex Ellinghausen Fellow Victoria Cross recipient Dan Keighran also attended, alongside former prime ministers John Howard, Tony Abbott and Scott Morrison. Liberal MP Andrew Hastie, a former SAS captain who served in Afghanistan and gave evidence in Roberts-Smith’s defamation trial, sat behind the former prime ministers with his children.



Chief or Defence Force, Admiral Mark Hammond laid a wreath alongside chief of airforce, Air Marshal Stephen Chappell and Lieutenant General Susan Coyle, the chief of army. Janny Poate, whose son Robert was killed at 23, in a “green on blue” attack, also read a tribute. Hugh and Janny Poate at their home in Canberra with a photograph of their son Private Robert Poate. Janny Poate paid tribute at the service. Alex Ellinghausen “We remember a human story that includes the families who waited, worried, endured separation, and who suffered loss? Most of all, we remember this: their strength and resilience.” Albanese said the service of Australian personnel demonstrated what was worth fighting for, regardless of the eventual outcome of the conflict. “What Australians serving in Afghanistan embody is something that we must never lose,” he said.

World.title: Apple’s big question: will customers rush to buy its $3500 foldable phone?
World.content:
TechnologyPhones Opinion Apple’s big question: will customers rush to buy its $3500 foldable phone?

Dave Lee October 11, 2026 — 11:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A big question Apple analysts are asking is: how many consumers are waiting for the iPhone Duo? The answer is hugely important to Apple’s stock this year and beyond. The new iPhone Pro range has been out for nearly three weeks, and from the get-go analysts noted somewhat flat consumer interest compared with last year’s Pro models. Apple’s new chief John Ternus is desperate for a breakout hit to begin his tenure. Bloomberg One theory is that a significant number of would-be buyers are waiting for Apple’s new foldable model, which doesn’t come out until October 23. If that’s true, then it’s good news for Apple, its investors and the company’s new chief executive officer, John Ternus – who would love a breakout hit to begin his tenure. At a starting price of $3499 in Australia, the Duo would boost the iPhone’s average selling price – a key metric watched by Wall Street. Add the signal that Duo’s success would suggest Apple still has the innovative “juice,” as they say, and the stock could build on what’s already been a banner 12 months – up 22 per cent since the start of the year.



Related Article Opinion

Phones I’d pay $3500 for an iPhone. So should you David Swan Technology editor But if it’s not the case, and consumers are just holding off on an upgrade altogether, Apple’s bold attempt to breathe new life into its most important product will appear to have fallen flat, a sign that even Apple couldn’t bring the potentially lucrative foldable form factor to the masses. For clues on what’s going on with the iPhone, analysts look to a simple but imperfect metric: wait times for delivery when customers try to buy a device. When the new iPhone Pro was available to pre-order, analysts at both Bank of America and UBS observed muted demand compared with last year’s models. “Globally, on average, ship time for the iPhone 18 Pro is currently at 14 days (vs. 18 days for iPhone 17 Pro) while iPhone 18 Pro Max stands at 18 days (vs. 25 days last year),” the Bank of America noted at the time. Sales of the Duo will be a fraction of the more than 250 million iPhones that Apple is expected to ship this year, but those sales will cement any perception of whether Apple’s top product still has room to grow.



UBS saw a smaller difference but the same trend: muted demand for the iPhone 18 Pro. “While we acknowledge the possibility that muted wait times for the Pro and Pro Max could suggest consumers are delaying their purchase decisions for the Duo,” its analysts wrote, “we believe that the $US1999 ($2862) starting price could limit incremental unit upside.” (In other words: Don’t count on it being Duo demand holding the Pro back.) In the couple of weeks since, UBS has noted an uptick in demand for the Pro and Pro Max – that is, a lengthening of delivery times. It is an imperfect metric. Apple might have just had more inventory ready to go this year compared with 2025. And this is the first year that Apple has split the launch of its premium and basic tiers into different seasons – the less expensive non-Pro iPhones come out next year – so inventory management might be a little more straightforward. Loading But it also might be the case that some consumers have been turned off by the $US100 price increases across the board for Apple’s flagship products, mainly caused by the ballooning cost of memory. The company and the carriers it works with have been trying to soften the blow by increasing trade-in value of old devices and introducing new payment options, most notably Apple’s new leasing program. It still may not be enough. A poor iPhone cycle is bad for Apple’s stock unless something significant elsewhere in its business – such as its services segment – is able to offset the news. This year’s offset, if iPhone Pro sales require one, could be a frenzy at Apple’s glistening stores across the world, as users clamour for the iPhone Duo when it’s released. Apple would need IDC’s estimate of 10 million iPhone Duos sold in the first 12 months to be on the money. To reach that, Apple will need to overcome reported manufacturing challenges that could impact initial supply. Then again, a headline-grabbing shortage of a hot new product has its upside. Sales of the Duo will be a fraction of the more than 250 million iPhones that Apple is expected to ship this year, but those sales will cement any perception of whether Apple’s top product still has room to grow.



Related Article Exclusive

Telecommunications Your next phone could take four years to pay off As it happened, I spent more than an hour at Apple’s downtown Brooklyn store recently, waiting on a repair to my iPhone 15 Pro which, like its owner, is ageing but still sufficiently capable. As I sat, to my right was a table of glowing iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models, attracting only limited interest. Other than different colours and incremental improvements to the camera and battery, there’s nothing much to see. Yet, I heard at least three people inquire about the iPhone Duo. “Are you getting a lot of that?” I asked the staff member when she came to help me. “Oh yeah,” she laughed. “All day.” Whether those kinds of customers are ready to spend, or are just curious, will set the mood for Apple this year. World.title: India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaIndia India detains thousands, locks down Delhi to foil election chief protest Saurabh Sharma , Sarita Chaganti Singh and Sakshi Dayal Updated October 11, 2026 — 9:48am ,first published 12:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

New Delhi: Police detained more than 2000 protesters and the founder of the “cockroach” youth movement in Delhi on Saturday (New Delhi time) as security forces locked down parts of the capital to thwart a rally demanding the resignation of India’s election chief. Thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed across the city, mobile internet services were suspended in the central business district and dozens of metro stations and markets were shut as authorities moved to stop a demonstration organised by the Cockroach movement. The protest was aimed at chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a revision of voter lists that critics say disproportionately benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). Police officers detain a protester. Getty Images The movement had planned to gather thousands of people at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, but the area was sealed off by security forces before the demonstration began.



A home ministry official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told Reuters more than 2000 people were detained in Delhi. Local media said about 400 protesters were held in India’s financial hub, Mumbai. Related Article Protests India’s ‘cockroach’ protesters claim surprise victory as government accepts their demands There was no immediate comment from police on the detentions. The United Nations human rights office expressed concerns over mass detentions before and during the protests. “We call on the authorities to ensure that the right to peaceful assembly is fully respected and fulfilled,” UN human rights spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said in a statement.



He also urged authorities to engage in “meaningful dialogue” to address the “broadly held” concerns expressed. The Indian mission to the UN in Geneva, however, called the UN’s concerns “misplaced” and said they constitute “an unwarranted interference in the internal affairs of India”. Indian police women stop opposition party members shouting anti-government slogans, as they tried to march on roads during the protest. Getty Images It stressed that the right to peaceful assembly was guaranteed by India’s Constitution. “As in every democracy, Indian citizens exercise this right subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order,” the statement added. Movement leaders held



Police detained Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and senior leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka when their flight from Mumbai landed in Delhi, the group said in a statement. Television footage showed Dipke challenging officers who approached him on board the aircraft. Police officers detain a protester. Getty Images “I have come to be arrested, arrest me ... I am not afraid of you guys,” he said. “No, this is not an arrest,” one officer replied. “Please co-operate.”



The movement condemned what it called the “authoritarian detention” of its leaders, demanded their release and vowed to continue protesting. “We will continue our protest tomorrow, day after ... until Gyanesh Kumar resigns. We will be on the streets,” CJP leader Ajinkya Shinde told reporters. CJP also said authorities refused to provide updates on the leaders’ whereabouts or health, even after news arrived of the death of Dipke’s grandmother. Police said Dipke was informed of her death and was offered help to return home for the funeral. Some opposition lawmakers and former chief ministers Mamata Banerjee of West Bengal, Arvind Kejriwal of Delhi, and Pinarayi Vijayan of Kerala were also detained, TV channels showed. Representatives of two digital news outlets said police briefly detained four of their reporters while they were covering the demonstrations. A Reuters journalist was also detained briefly before being released.



Across the capital of about 20 million people, security forces set up checkpoints on major roads and entry points, boarded buses searching for protesters and inspected vehicles. Barricades and concrete blocks disrupted traffic while anti-riot vehicles equipped with tear-gas launchers guarded key routes. New challenge to Modi The demonstrations represent one of the most serious tests yet for Modi, stemming from allegations that election authorities improperly revised voter rolls ahead of recent state polls. Protestors shout slogans against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Bloomberg Protests intensified after the Indian Express reported last week that two election commissioners had questioned Kumar’s voter-list revisions that removed roughly 130 million names from voter lists.



Kumar has not commented but the Election Commission and the BJP have denied allegations of wrongdoing. The BJP says its electoral success reflects Modi’s popularity and India’s economic growth, and accuses opposition parties of spreading misinformation. The near-daily protests come just months after demonstrations over exam paper leaks forced his education minister to quit. The unrest also comes ahead of a series of important state elections beginning in early 2027. Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main opposition Congress party, said Modi’s opponents would not back down.



A senior BJP member, Ravi Shankar Prasad, said the party was not opposed to demonstrations but the street protests had been “weaponised” by rivals due to election defeats. Deletions affected state polls, opposition alleges Opposition parties say the deletions affected the outcome of recent state elections won by the BJP and have cast a shadow over voting in the world’s largest democracy. Election Commission data show about 130 million voter entries were removed during the verification exercise, including 63 million people who had relocated, 30 million who could not be traced and 28 million who had died. The commission says the removals relate to entries identified during the draft revision process and that any eligible voter incorrectly deleted can re-enrol.

World.title: ACT sets out plan to raise retirement age, cut debt, spending and disability benefits
World.content:
The ACT Party's fiscal plan promises to cut debt and spending, raise the superannuation age by three months every year, and cut disability benefits by $653 million.

The superannuation changes would also put contributions to the NZ Super Fund on hold, and would include "compassionate access" for those who had spent "a substantial portion of their career in physically demanding jobs".

Similar to the plan unveiled at the last election, the document sets out a goal of returning to 2017 per-capita spending, adjusted for inflation and population growth.

This would be achieved partly by abolishing "demographic" ministries, bringing disability benefits "under control", cutting foreign aid and back-office spending, and preventing migrants claiming benefits for five years after entering the country.

Operating allowances - spending - would be reduced by $400m a year, while non-welfare spending would be reduced over three years to 2017 levels - adjusted for inflation and wage growth, with increases in health, education, defence, police and children's services remaining untouched.

Two policies in the plan remained mysterious: one costing $100 million a year, and the other being some kind of tax relief costing $264m in its first year rising to $303m in 2031.

Leader David Seymour announced the plan at The Ever Room photography studio on Auckland's Karangahape Road, saying it was fully costed and showed ACT was "taking the hard road of truth-telling this election".

"Taxpayers know the Government has too much debt. When you're paying over a million dollars an hour in interest on government debt, it's not time to make a virtue of saving money slowly," he said.

New spending in the plan includes the party's proposed $2b cancer centre. The idea for the centre was put forward by candidate Paul Henry. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"Labour and their allies seem to believe greater spending is needed ... ACT rejects that thinking for two reasons. The New Zealand Government already spends as much as, or more than, most of our Pacific Rim neighbours and competitors. More fundamentally, nobody who has seen how government works would think it can make better decisions than families and businesses."

The promise to scrap KiwiSaver tax is tempered by scrapping the scheme's subsidies, and revenue from the Emissions Trading Scheme would be paid out rather than reinvested in cutting emissions.

The document laid out the plans to curb disability benefits by $12m in the first year, rising to $124m, $231m and $286m in subsequent years.

The party would achieve this by requiring "independent medical certification against clear criteria" to access them, with "phased reassessment of existing recipients".

"People with genuine, enduring conditions will retain appropriate long-term support. Consistent assessment helps distinguish those unable to work from those who can work with support, protecting the safety net and reducing avoidable dependency.

"Our costing is based on bringing the number of mental health claimants back to its pre-pandemic level, relative to the working-age population, over four years."

New spending in the plan includes the party's already-announced policies like electronic money management for beneficiaries, a $2b cancer centre, an overstayers investigation unit, $2m for cameras to detect "anti-social noise", $150m capital contingency for a new secondary school in Epsom, and $500 investment funds for Year 11 students.

World.title: The fury behind Sarah-Kate Lynch's new crime novel
World.content:
"I'd had what I thought was pretty good success. I really felt wow, now I know why old people are grumpy, because I felt like I in a way never had more to give and never more to offer, and nobody wanted it.



"It was proper heart break. I had to go to a therapist and say why is this happening to me? And she rather helpfully said what an idiot I was expecting the world to be a fair place, so I should get over that to begin wit. Not helpful - but not bad advice."



Lynch was forced to unpick her own expectation that she would have more agency over when she would stop working.



"Also I didn't know what to do with myself - I've been a writer since I was 18, so I just didn't know what to do. My fingers are used to typing and my brain is used to thinking that way."



At the same time, friends in their early 60s were going through similar experiences in other professions, she says.



"It's not really the letting go that counts, it's the moving on from there. I'd been let go from jobs before, but I was younger and so I just went out and got another job. But it's a horrible shock to be let go from something and then find out that well, there's no place for you out there in the world anymore.



"I felt sidelined from my own life, and part of my anger was that 'well, somebody should have asked me if that was okay, because I would have said no'."



That feeling of heartbreak changed to rage: "I thought 'well, you know what, I can write a book' and I don't care if nobody wants it, but I can do it."



The resolve was oddly freeing, she says. It was the first time she set out to write a book without a publisher, and all of the expectations and direction that go along with that.



"And with the rage actually came a point of view, so it ended up being helpful."



The novel's lead character Detective Sergeant Claudia Russo is not a people pleaser. She's spiky and difficult, and Lynch says she brings to mind the well-known saying that: ‘It's not actually very hard to be considered a difficult woman, that's why there's so many of us’.



"She is a detective, so she doesn't have my exact experience - but that feeling of life not being fair and wanting to do something about it definitely comes straight from me.



"I guess that being sidelined made me feel like I didn't have a voice. So that was what I was trying to get back, and trying to give it to Claudia by saying 'well, this isn't right, and I want to do something about it’."



Russo is searching for an 18-year-old girl missing in Melbourne, the daughter of a former prominent All Black who has been living a double life.



But the initial scenario was inspired by a real life road rage incident that Lynch experienced in Melbourne.



In 2021, living in Melbourne - a city wired tightly amid Covid-19 lockdowns, Lynch's husband had just picked her up after a stay of several days in hospital.



"I was in a very strange frame of mind… I felt very fragile... and a guy in a high vis vest driving like a flatdeck ute-type thing with road cones in the back pulled out without looking, and so we almost collided and we both got stuck on the median strip on the road."



The driver gave them the fingers and mouthed a curse at them, Lynch says, and as her husband checked the car for damage, she went over.



"I got out of the car in a very calm for some reason frame of mind, and I went over to his window and I said 'of all the things in the world you could have done then, why did you have to do that, with the fingers?’ Which was bizarre in itself."



In that moment, she says she read in his face that he "didn't want to be that guy", he was embarrassed and felt cornered by the situation.



"And I saw all this in his eyes, and I said to him 'well maybe next time you can do something different, like be kind'. And then I went and got back in the car and off we drove."



It left her mulling the what ifs, what those words and that moment could lead to for both parties. "What if what I said to him actually had an impact on him, and made him improve his life? And what if the person that he collided with, what if it had an impact on their life, but in the opposite direction?"



That question, and thoughts about rage, toxicity, and women’s agency, were the fuel for her story, Lynch says.

World.title: Football Ferns trying to leave Panama after strong quake causes cancellation of matches
World.content:
The Football Ferns are safe and well and looking to get out of Panama as soon as possible after both their matches in the central American nation were cancelled in the wake of a powerful earthquake that struck there on Saturday (NZT).

The quake measured a magnitude 7.7. Some buildings were damaged but there have been no reports of any casualties.

The first game was to be played in Panama City at Estadio Rommel Fernández Gutiérrez this morning (Sunday NZT).

It was cancelled before kickoff, but New Zealand Football has since announced that the second match, which had been scheduled for Wednesday (NZT), has also been called off.

Football Ferns coach Michael Mayne said players and staff were in a team meeting when the earthquake struck.

"First and foremost we want to acknowledge the people most impacted by the earthquake and hope they are safe and well," he said in a video message.

"We are safe and well, we are working right now on how to get our people out of Panama and where they can be safe again and get back to work as we continue to build towards Brazil.

Football Ferns head coach Michael Mayne. Photosport

The Women's Football World Cup is in Brazil next year and the two internationals against Panama were part of the Ferns' lead-up to the cup.

"(In) the last 24 hours we have had to navigate very carefully and make important decisions for the players and staff of both teams."

Panama's football federation and NZF management back in New Zealand had been very supportive leading up to the decision to cancel both games.

"I want to acknowledge the players and staff for the way they have navigated the last 24 hours, their patience and professionalism in a very tricky situation," Mayne said.

"I am super proud as a coach of this team with how they stayed connected, supported each other but also made sure that we could made some robust decisions as a team to look after our people," he said.

World.title: Four All Blacks ruled out of Sydney trip; fan favourite Du'Plessis Kirifi included
World.content:
All Blacks Leroy Carter, Asafo Aumua, Anton Segner and Ethan Blackadder have all been ruled out of the second Bledisloe Cup test against Australia due to injury.

Wing Carter suffered a high ankle sprain when scoring a late try in his team's 50-19 victory at Eden Park on Saturday night and is likely to be a long-term absentee, with his participation in next month's Nations Championship tests in the United Kingdom in doubt.

He left Eden Park on crutches and nursing a badly swollen left ankle after a "hip drop" tackle by Wallabies loose forward Rob Valetini.

The tackle technique was last week outlawed by World Rugby but the ban does not take effect until 1 November.

Carter has been replaced in the squad for next Saturday's match at Accor Stadium by midfielder Anton Lienert-Brown.

Hooker Aumua failed a second head injury assessment and must serve a minimum 12-day concussion stand-down, with loose forward Anton Segner similarly sidelined after also joining Saturday night's test off the reserves bench.

Loose forward Anton Segner, right, holds the Bledisloe Cup with wing Josh Moorby after the All Blacks retained it with their victory at Eden Park. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

Aumua has been replaced by George Bell, with Segner replaced by Du'Plessis Kirifi - the Wellington and Hurricanes loose forward joining the All Blacks squad for the first time this year.

Ethan Blackadder, not named in the match-day squad for Saturday night's test, injured a calf in the warm-up but the issue is not thought to be serious.

He has been replaced for the trip to Sydney by lock Jamie Hannah.

The news is better for lock Scott Barrett, who passed a second head injury assessment after leaving the field in the second half and who has travelled with the squad.

Fans of 29-year-old Kirifi, the inspirational Hurricanes co-captain who made his test debut last year, will be pleased at their man's inclusion after he was seen as one of the unluckier players to miss selection for the recent tour of South Africa.

All Blacks attack coach Mike Blair told reporters at Auckland airport on Sunday morning of the loose forward: "It's great that we get this opportunity to look at him. He's not been in with the group yet. But for us to get to know him a little bit more - his personality, his leadership, the impact he can have on the group is exciting for him and exciting for us as well."

Blair said the value of the "Greatest Rivalry" tour had already been seen in the depth the All Blacks have built this year.

World.title: New Zealand scientists hope to develop more effective vaccines for older people
World.content:
The leader of a project to build a world-first, detailed picture of how immune cells change with age is hoping to develop a more effective vaccine for older people.

The project is a collaboration between New Zealand's Malaghan Institute and Scotland's University of Dundee.

The institute's chief scientist, Michelle Linterman, who is leading the project, told RNZ that vaccination is one of the most powerful tools for preventing disease, but age-related changes in how immune cells make and manage their proteins mean vaccines work less well as people get older, leaving them more vulnerable.

"So what happens in all of the cells of your body is that, to function, they produce protein, but those proteins need to be regulated.

"It's kind of like a housekeeper keeping your house in order that, you know, if something gets broken, it gets disposed of, and what we know is that as we get older, the housekeeper becomes less effective and things get a little bit messier with respect to your proteins, and we think that this is one of the reasons that the immune cells don't function as well in ageing."

Linterman said New Zealand's population is ageing, and developing more effective vaccines for older people is a promising way to help reduce avoidable illness and allow people to live longer, healthier lives.

"Better vaccines for older adults would mean fewer hospitalisations, but it would also mean a better quality of life for older adults, and that's something that we all want, you know, for our whānau, for ourselves, as we all age."

Linterman said the project involved taking immune cells from older people, which is difficult because the immune cells the project wanted to study were rare in the small blood samples that it had.

"These typically come from the blood after vaccination, so they're available in very, very small numbers.

"What we're going to do is do an unbiased survey of the proteins in those cells, and that's where the collaboration with the University of Dundee is really important, because they've developed some new technology that allows you to actually do that in small numbers of cells, whereas previously that was a real barrier to our research, and what that will tell us is the levels of different proteins in the immune cells, and then we'll be able to link those to functional changes in how the cells respond to vaccines."

As part of the project, researchers will also work with Hamilton's Rauawaawa Kaumātua Charitable Trust to engage with kaumātua, as Linterman said that vaccines only make a difference when communities trust the research behind them.

World.title: Labour says its school lunches would be made on-site, cover all 244,400 students already involved
World.content:
Labour has confirmed more details of its plan to reinstate the former school lunch programme from Term 1 2028, if elected.

The party has released a cost of living action plan, tying a bow on the cost of living policy blitz it's been conducting in recent weeks.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6406615626112

While mostly a re-cap of already-announced policies like the three free GP visits, public transport fare caps, and student debt cut, there are two new policies on the list.

The document said the lunches would continue to cover 244,400 students in the 1014 schools already included. Lunches would be $5 a meal, and $6.50 for students in years 9 to 13.

The lunches would be made in school kitchens, by iwi and hapū partners or by local caterers.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins. RNZ / Sam Rillstone

Labour's fiscal plan, released last week, said it would continue to fund the existing programme at $146.2 million for the 2027/28 fiscal year, $295.4m for 2028/29, and then $149.2m in 2029/30.

The cost of living policy plan also included a commitment to restore rural school bus routes.

Labour said if it could not restore a cancelled route, then it would work with rural communities and local councils to find an alternative.

The Green Party also has promised to reinstate the former school lunch programme.

Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson said the Greens' election policy would restore the Ka Ora Ka Ako programme so lunches were provided through schools or local providers, and would expand it to approximately 400 more schools.

Davidson said this would ensure 150,000 more children would get a lunch every day.

The current Government has also funded the Healthy School Lunches programme for another year, committing $212m towards an extension.

World.title: Suns stamp AFLW top-four credentials as Crows rebound
World.content:
Gold Coast have rubber-stamped their AFLW top-four credentials with a historic 22-point victory over Melbourne.

The Suns posted their sixth straight win on Saturday night, faring better in sweltering heat at Mackay's Great Barrier Reef Arena to down the Demons 9.7 (61) to 5.9 (39).

Gold Coast had not beaten Melbourne in their four previous clashes since the Suns entered the women's competition in 2020.

"It's been a long few years for us and we've been slowly building every year," Suns co-captain Lucy Single told Fox Footy after the landmark triumph.

"So to kind of get that win under our belt has been so awesome and I think that's really boosted our confidence."

The Suns find themselves sitting pretty with three rounds left before finals, drawing level with Melbourne at 7-2.

Melbourne took a three-point lead into quarter-time, but Gold Coast kicked away in the second term and did not look back.

Midfielder Charlie Rowbottom had a game-high 33 possessions and six clearances as Ava Usher, Mikayla Nurse and Havana Harris (two goals apiece) all fired up forward.

Despite the mercury hovering in the mid-20s, Usher said the Suns were not fazed by the conditions.

"We knew it was going to be a really tough arm-wrestle and in the end we just got over the line in really hot conditions," the first-year Sun said.

"We're pretty used to it."

Adelaide had too much firepower for Richmond in the earlier game, winning 9.8 (62) to 4.6 (30) at Melbourne's Princes Park.

The 32-point victory put the Crows back in the finals hunt at 4-5, although they remain just outside the eight with three games of round nine to play.

Prolific ball-winner Ebony Marinoff collected 40 disposals, 13 tackles and a goal.

St Kilda send Dal Santo out a winner It's been an AFLW season to forget for St Kilda, but Saturday's win over Collingwood has given departing Saints coach Nick Dal Santo a perfect send-off.

The 40-possession game was one shy of her career-best mark.

The Crows captain said it had been a tough week following a 14-point Showdown loss to Port Adelaide.

"I'd be lying [to say] we didn't know what was on the line tonight," Marinoff said.

"But really proud of the girls' efforts just to really start well … because we hadn't over the last fortnight."

Earlier in the day, Geelong took top spot — at least for now — with a 63-point win over GWS at Kardinia Park, with Jacqueline Parry and Aishling Moloney each kicking four goals.

The Cats will fall back to second, however, if North Melbourne beats Fremantle on Sunday.

The other early game saw St Kilda win their first game for the season, with a two-point win over Collingwood at Moorabbin.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Matt Renshaw's 190 turns Durban Test, providing Aussie batting blueprint
World.content:
Like many great plans, it was deceptively simple. Stillness. Balance. Patience. Concentration. No frills, no fast moves and no undue risks, just decisive action when needed.

Not for the first time at Test level, a burly Queenslander, a three-pound cleft of willow and a healthy dose of self-confidence was the difference between Australian success and failure.

That Matt Renshaw resurrected an Australian first innings which teetered near oblivion at 6-124 was the first point of order.

Of consequences further-reaching, the left-hander resurrected his entire Test career overnight in Durban, sweeping, clipping and crashing his way to 190 from 397 deliveries across 465 minutes of life-affirming Test batting.

Numerous records fell or threatened to. Renshaw's epic was the highest score by an Australian in Durban, the fourth highest overall by an Aussie against South Africa, and the best by a number-five of any nation at Kingsmead.

It was also a new Test personal best for Renshaw, usurping the 184 he made nine years ago as a boyish tyro against Pakistan in Sydney, back when the world was at his feet.

Renshaw is 30 now — a husband, a father of two children and an entirely different cricketer. He knows his own mind and understands his place in the scheme of things.

For a nation which has been crying out for big, important runs by someone not named Smith or Head, his Daddy hundred here was one for the ages.

Practically speaking, Renshaw helped Australia to a first-innings total of 390, which was at least 150 more than had seemed optimistic when he first took guard.

On a deeper level, it restored belief in the value of grinding out an innings of depth and character. It was the real deal — the proper Test match batting the Australian cricketing public has been craving.

No mistake should be made about the high degree of difficulty, either. When Renshaw began shepherding the tail a day earlier, Australia was at the mercy of a vigorous and versatile South African pace attack jagging the ball all over the place.

Waiting in the wings were the Proteas' twin spin options of Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer, with 1700+ first-class wickets between them.

Australia has struggled against left-arm spin in recent times. Last time they played a Test in Durban, Maharaj took nine wickets. And Australia's selection for this match — four left handers in the top six — was said to favour right-arm off-spinner Harmer even more.

Matt Renshaw blunted South Africa's spin attack with judicious use of the sweep and reverse sweep in Durban. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

So much for that, in the end. Renshaw swept, reverse-swept and paddled Maharaj into irrelevance and by the time Harmer finally removed the top-scorer for spin's first wicket of the game, the horse had well and truly bolted.

As it turned out, the sterner challenge was curbing the influence of the quicks, who'd posed constant difficulties for the rest of Australia's batters.

A microcosm came when Renshaw was on 130, yet still not able to relax. He was struck a scary blow to the grille of his helmet from an absolute snorter by Anrich Nortje, who bowled with genuine pace and accuracy in short, sharp spells.

Handling the wily and indefatigable Wiaan Mulder was no cinch either. Early on day two, the all-rounder scythed through Pat Cummins and Mitchell Starc and threatened to blow the game open.

Wiaan Mulder (centre) took two wickets on day two and proved hard to play for Australia's batters. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Gerhard Duraan)

That he didn't was not exclusively a matter of Renshaw's dominance but of the rearguard partnerships which have so often saved Australia's bacon in recent times.

Renshaw shared stands of 86 across 32 overs with Pat Cummins and a monumental and possibly series-shaping 134 from 47 overs with Nathan Lyon.

Australia will not be looking too far ahead, but there was a blueprint here, not just of personnel but of general batting philosophy: know your game, make them bowl to you, stick around and wear them down.

Australia's total was the most obvious metric of success, but its innings duration of 137.2 overs will surely please Andrew McDonald and his analysts just as much.

In Australia's 35 Test innings in the two years before this match, they'd batted past the 100-over mark only six times, compared with 13 times in the 42 innings of the two-year period preceding.

That downward trend has, of course, coincided with a proliferation of the result pitches which characterise the World Test Championship era.

Concurrently, it is agreed by most involved in the Australian domestic scene, it has been difficult for Test batting candidates to put their best feet forward, or get in the habit of playing long innings, when the primary bloc of red-ball cricket occurs in spring, when Sheffield Shield pitches sometimes resemble Monty Don's perennial beds.

Without peering too far into the future or wishing disruption on a player who's just delivered something so special, one awkward talking point that will be aired soon enough is if and when Renshaw might move up to his normal position of opener.

The theory going into this game was that in batting down the order, he could blunt the influence of the spinners, which he assuredly did. But he would surely be just as assured against the new ball as he was here against the second new ball.

And yet, who'd be an opener these days? Late on day two, Ryan Rickelton provided a study in contrasts for the Proteas.

Having spent the better part of two days chasing leather in the field, and perhaps daydreaming that he was in Renshaw's shoes, he lasted only three deliveries before chasing Josh Hazlewood outside his off-stump and sending an edge to the cordon.

The more telling image of day two arrived an hour earlier, on the stroke of tea, when an exhausted Renshaw removed his helmet and trudged off for refreshments.

Appearing on the balcony of the player's area, Australian skipper Cummins peered down on the centurion with something like a look of love on his face.

Ray Illingworth once said a captain needs the patience of a saint, the diplomacy of an ambassador, the compassion of a social worker and the skin of a rhino. Colleagues who can bat for eight hours help, too.

World.title: Quick hits: AFL star in the sheds as Aussies go better than Bradman
World.content:
Matt Renshaw and Nathan Lyon outdo Sir Donald Bradman while Gold Coast Suns AFL star Noah Anderson watches on from the stands.

Here are the quick hits from day two of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.

1. Renshaw's drought-breaking century

DURBAN, SOUTH AFRICA - OCTOBER 10: Matthew Renshaw of Australia during day 2 of the 1st Dafabet Test match between South Africa and Australia at Hollywoodbets Kingsmead Stadium on October 10, 2026 in Durban, South Africa. (Photo by Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images) (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

It had been over nine years and nine months since Matt Renshaw's last and only Test century.

Opening the batting on January 3, 2017, a then 20-year-old Renshaw peeled off 184 against Pakistan in Sydney, a match in which he lined up alongside the likes of two-Test white-ball specialist Hilton Cartwright and New South Wales great Steve O'Keefe.

A few false dawns, a short-format reinvention and a red-ball renaissance later, and the Queenslander brought up his drought-breaking ton with an immaculately timed clip through mid-wicket for four.

Having lost overnight partner Pat Cummins and number nine Mitch Starc in quick succession after starting the day on 46, Renshaw was almost chanceless in reaching three figures.

It was a classic Test dig by Matt Renshaw. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

It was a richly deserved milestone for a player, who, at 30, still has plenty of good years ahead of him.

And Renshaw just kept going.

And going.

He received much more than able support from Nathan Lyon as he passed 150, before kicking on with number 11 Josh Hazlewood to set a new Test best of 190, falling just short of a maiden double ton as he nicked off after tea.

2. Better than Bradman

The first innings appeared not long for this world when the best betters in the tail, Cummins and Starc, departed.

But Lyon picked up the mantle to knuckle under with Renshaw, albeit in slightly less expressive fashion. At least so it seemed.

After helping Renshaw to triple figures, there was no loss of application from the Aussie batters out in the middle and when Lyon clipped Anrich Nortje off his hip for four in the 108th over, they passed some pretty big names.

In the 124-year history of Tests against South Africa, no Australian ninth-wicket partnership had ever surpassed 78 runs until day two in Durban.

And the two pairings who had reached that mark included some all-time greats: Ian Meckiff and Ken McKay in Johannesburg in 1958, and Sir Donald Bradman with Bill O'Reilly in Adelaide Oval way back in 1932.

Renshaw and Lyon heaped the pain on South Africa. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

And the records kept tumbling as the runs kept coming, with the pair ticking past two Steve Waugh specials, the first a 130-run stand with Geoff Lawson in 1989, and the second a 133-run effort in tandem with Jason Gillespie in 2001.

By the time Lyon was eventually dismissed for a 92-ball 27 and the stand was over on 134, there was only one greater ninth-wicket partnership in the history of Australian cricket — and that had come in the 19th century.

3. Australia's best recovery in over a century

Given the shakiness of Australia's top order over the past decade or so, there have been plenty of opportunities for inspired rearguard actions.

And we certainly have been treated to some remarkable recoveries — think Steve Smith's partnerships with Peter Siddle and Nathan Lyon that took Australia from 8-122 to 284 at Edgbaston in 2019, or Lyon and Cummins combining for a 55-run stand to guide Australia home during the 2023 Ashes.

But not for over 100 years have we seen an Australian comeback as dramatic as the one we were treated to on day two.

Per ABC Sport statistician Ric Finlay, Australia's recovery from 6-124 to 390 was the country's best rebuild since 1925, when an unbeaten double century to number seven Jack Ryder took Australia from 6-119 to 489.

4. Another selection shock for the Aussies?!

With the Australian rearguard action showing no signs of abating, the broadcast camera panned to the tourists' dugout, where it found an unexpected but familiar face for Aussie sports fan.

Dressed in full training kit and looking slightly surprised to be there himself, there he was, Gold Coast Suns AFL star Noah Anderson.

Loading Instagram content

Anderson has travelled with the Australians to South Africa as part of a leadership fact-finding mission, according to Fox commentator Mark Howard.

As the cameras focused in on Anderson, a Sherrin suddenly appeared in the hands of Marnus Labuschagne, sitting alongside the Suns star.

Marnus Labuschagne (second from left) got out the Sherrin to make Noah Anderson (left) feel at home. (Supplied: Fox Cricket)

5. Lyon walks off despite review

Nathan Lyon enjoyed a gutsy, record-breaking dig alongside Matt Renshaw, but when it was over it was pretty obvious.

Marco Jansen's return to the attack brought with it a short-pitched barrage that seemed to rattle the Aussies out of their methodical tactics of Renshaw seeing off the first four balls before giving Lyon a look.

After being twisted up by a bouncer, Renshaw scurried off strike and left Lyon with three balls to negotiate, but it only took Jansen one as he surprised the number 10 with a full one that smashed into his pads.

Nathan Lyon knew he was out but reviewed anyway. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan/Gallo Images)

Jansen, the rest of South Africa's fielders and umpire Chris Gaffaney all knew it was out, and so did Lyon, despite deciding to review.

He made an immediate "T" sign before just as quickly walking off the field before the replays were finished.

By the time his dismissal was confirmed he was already halfway up the stairs.

World.title: South Melbourne stuns Melbourne Victory to claim Australia Cup
World.content:
A-League aspirants South Melbourne have become the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup after beating Melbourne Victory on penalties in an emotion-charged blockbuster final.

In one of the greatest nights in Australian domestic soccer history, former NSL powerhouses South first took Victory to extra time then fought back from 1-0 down to level it at 1-1 at the death before winning 4-3 on penalties in front of a pumping sellout crowd of 29,911 fans at AAMI Park.

South Melbourne, who have long craved an A-League licence, only strengthened their bid for that with a win that capped off an extraordinary evening.

Denis Genreau scored an athletic, improvised half-volley in the 95th minute to put Victory in front, before Max Mikkola forced home an equaliser in the 117th minute to send the game to penalties and the crowd into ecstasy.

In the penalty shootout, South goalkeeper Javier Lopez was the hero and won the Mark Viduka Medal as man of the match.

Lopez initially saved former South captain Harrison Sawyer's penalty but was ruled to have come off his line, but then saved the re-take too.

South scored all their penalties before Victory skipper Jason Davidson, son of South great Alan Davidson, hit his must-score spot-kick over the bar.

In becoming the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup, Sinisa Cohadzic's South succeed where Heidelberg last year and Sydney United 58 in 2022 could not.

With the win, South also technically claim a berth in next season's Asian Champions League 2 competition.

The defeat also extends Victory's silverware drought, with the club's most recent trophy the 2021 Australia Cup.

South certainly played up to the occasion, taking the game to Giovanni Savarese's Victory and making their mark on their biggest night in years in an incredible atmosphere.

A huge contingent of their fans packed the south end of AAMI Park, holding banners of club legends including Ange Postecoglou, Ferenc Puskas and John Margaritis.

The only lowlight of the night was a section of the crowd at the South end booing the Welcome to Country before the match.

On the field, South Melbourne attacking pair Juach and Yuki Uchida gave the Victory defence headaches all night.

Lopez made several great saves while Victory counterpart Jack Duncan was called into action on multiple occasions in regular time.

Victory should have taken the lead in the 78th minute when Guillermo May squared the ball to Santos but the Brazilian's poor shot allowed Lopez to make an extraordinary save with his knees.

Denis Genreau's hooked volley hit the crossbar and bounced in, but Victory could not hold onto the lead. (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

But there was nothing Lopez could do in extra-time to stop himself being lobbed by Genreau's strange half-volley, which bounced over the line before he could grab it.

Juach spurned a couple of great chances to equalise and the game appeared lost for South.

Then, with the clock winding down, South substitute Jordan Swibel burst down the right and sent in a ball that caused chaos and ended with Mikkola toe-poking home.

AAMI Park erupted and when the game was sent to penalties minutes later, only one club ever felt on top.

AAP

World.title: Piastri caught up in last-lap crash with teammate in Singapore GP sprint
World.content:
World champion Lando Norris has apologised to his McLaren team after a final-lap collision with stablemate Oscar Piastri wrecked their ​pursuit of a podium finish at a chaotic Singapore Grand Prix sprint race.

The McLaren duo were chasing Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, who was struggling with his tyres in the dying stages of ​the 20-lap sprint, ‌when disaster struck on the final lap.

Norris, running fifth behind Piastri in fourth, attempted to overtake his teammate but clipped the Australian's rear tyre with his front wheel, ‌sending both cars spinning and handing Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli fourth ⁠place.

"Sorry about that. Obviously, I didn't want that to happen, ‌but I thought I was ​fully alongside. I just ‌ran out of space at the apex, but I was there," Norris said over the team radio.

While Norris limped home to eighth place to claim the final point available, Piastri was forced to retire as he ​became ‌one of nine cars that did not finish — a record number of retirements for a Formula 1 sprint race.

"I'd rather just go back ⁠and review it," Norris told Sky Sports.

"I ‌apologised to them that one ‌of the cars is out but, like I said, the rest of it we'll ‌go review."

Elsewhere Norris suggested he was entitled "to go for a big gap" because everyone should be fighting for places in a competitive race.

"What's the title of the race?" he asked an interviewer who implied his move on the inside was "unnecessary".

"What's after 'sprint'?"

When the interviewer replied "race", he laughed and sarcastically said: "Wow, good job".

Piastri said he had not seen the incident properly to comment but downplayed its significance as they were not ‌in high ​points scoring positions.

"From ⁠where I sit, it's for fourth and fifth for a sprint race, so I'm not that bothered either way," Piastri said.

"Just obviously it's a lot of work now for the team to get both cars ⁠fixed [ahead of qualifying for Sunday's race]. Just a shame for the team."

Both McLaren drivers were summoned to ‌the stewards ‌after the collision.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the sprint and ​the Dutchman leapfrogged Norris to climb to fifth in the world championship standings.

Verstappen also took pole for the main race in Singapore ahead of Leclerc, with Norris fifth and Piastri seventh.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Bathurst 1000 weather, start time, how to watch and starting grid
World.content:
The Great Race is finally here.

The Bathurst 1000, the jewel in the Supercars crown, will be raced at the world-famous Mount Panorama circuit today.

Fifty-two drivers across 26 cars will tackle the mountain in the 1,000km endurance race.

From the weather to the start time, here is what you need to know ahead of today's Bathurst 1000.

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of the Great Race from 10am AEDT.

Sunny weather forecast for Bathurst 1000

It is perfect news for drivers and teams, and more importantly, the fans.

The weather forecast for the Bathurst 1000 is sunny, with a high temperature around 27 degrees Celsius.

There is virtually no chance of rain, according to the Bureau of Meteorology.

So, we will not be having the wet weather chaos that befell the Great Race last year.

Good for the heart rate. Not so great for the tension and theatre.

Bathurst 1000 race start time

Here is when the lights will go out in your state or territory.

11:30am AEDT: NSW, Victoria, ACT, Tasmania

11am ACDT: South Australia

10:30am AEST: Queensland

8:30am AWST: Western Australia

World.title: The unconventional coach out to extend the Jillaroos reign
World.content:
Jessica Skinner is standing beside the silverware she hopes to lift at the Women's Rugby League World Cup final in Brisbane next month.

But when asked what raising the trophy would mean, her answer isn't about winning.

"I feel like I'm lifting my people, Australians, my community in Trangie (regional NSW), my family," she tells ABC Sport.

Skinner is a proud Barkindji and Māori woman, who is preparing for her first World Cup as head coach of the Jillaroos, Australia's national women's rugby league team.

The World Cup is the pinnacle of the women's game, and Australia has enjoyed over a decade of dominance, winning the last three tournaments.

Skinner admits the pressure is there to secure a fourth at the 2026 tournament, which will be co-hosted across Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea.

"To know that you're stepping into big shoes, and there's an expectation that we win a World Cup, or that we win all the time, especially in the green and gold, it's nerve racking," she says.

"But [I'm] really excited as well."

Skinner says she knows she's stepping into big shoes, with a fourth title on the line. (ABC Sport: Dan Irvine)

Skinner rarely talks about herself, even when discussing one of the biggest moments of her career. For her, this tournament is just as much about others.

It shows in her unique coaching style, where she strives to always put the person before the player.

"I want to be known as a coach, who, when people leave my environments, they feel valued, seen and cared for," Skinner says.

It's this philosophy that has helped her rise to the top.

From the bush to the World Cup

Skinner hails from Trangie, a town of about 1,000 people in the central west of New South Wales.

She lives there with her son, 16, and daughter, 13, surrounded by what she calls her village.

"I love that I get to represent the bush," she says.

"I love the female game, the Indigenous, the Māori.

"I carry that responsibility and I'm proud to do so. What you can't see, you can't be."

For a long time, Skinner didn't think her coaching style was 'elite', because she believes in putting the person before the player. (Supplied: NRL Photos)

Skinner was a school teacher before anything else, and fell into coaching women's football at the grassroots when there was nobody else to do it.

The initial plan wasn't to go professional.

"It started out with wanting to be involved in my community, and [have] a sense of belonging," Skinner says.

"To [now] having a seat at the table I suppose in the women's game, and with the Jillaroos, it's massive."

But it hasn't been quick, with Skinner working away in the shadows for a while.

Her elite coaching career began in 2019 as assistant coach of the Prime Minister's XIII.

It led to other coaching roles with the Newcastle Knights NRLW side, the NRL Indigenous Women's Academy, the Women's Indigenous All Stars and First Nations Gems.

Jess Skinner led the Indigenous Women's All Stars to victory over the Maori Women's All Stars in 2024. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

Skinner was assistant coach to Brad Donald at the 2021 World Cup, which was played in 2022, because of COVID-19.

"[He's] a great mentor and someone who's really passionate about bringing women through," Skinner says.

The natural progression to head coach came after Donald resigned last year.

"It feels like a massive jump, but it's been 16 years in the making," she says.

"I've done my craft; I've done my trade and my apprenticeship and [I'm] ready to take it on."

Skinner first stepped into the role for last year's historic Test against England in Las Vegas, where the Jillaroos won 90 — 4.

Eight months later, she led the team to the 2025 Pacific Cup Crown.

Jess Skinner was appointed as interim Jillaroos coach for the 2025 Las Vegas Test Match against England. (Supplied: NRL Photos)

A challenging road to the top

The call-up to be head coach arrived during a period of grief. Skinner's mother had just passed away.

"I lost her three days before I got a call from the CEO, Andrew Abdo," she says.

"So, it's been quite a hard time."

There were multiple times when Skinner could have changed paths, but she had the courage to persevere.

"It hasn't been the easiest ride," she says.

Skinner says she's been up against it in a male dominated space. (Supplied: NRL Photos)

She says one of the biggest challenges has been the lack of women coaching at the elite level.

"You have to have resilience, grit and thick skin through this journey," she says.

There's also the sacrifice of time away from her children.

"I'm on my own with my two children, so I'm relying on my village to help me, and my parents have been a part of that," she says.

Then there's the fact her nearest NRLW team is almost 500 kilometres away.

"If I want to go outside of the Jillaroos program, go to NRLW, that means a relocation, and as an Aboriginal woman on country, that means a lot to me [to stay]," Skinner says.

Skinner takes great pride in connecting with her culture, and paving the way for other Indigenous women to play, or work in rugby league. (Supplied: Chloe Davies)

"It's all helped me be a better version [of myself] and to grow, [but] it has been a lot."

A lot, that has been worth it.

"I feel like I've got the best of both worlds, my community obligations, being a mum and being able to lead this team," Skinner says.

She is moved when speaking about her parents and what it means personally when she pulls on the Jillaroos jersey.

It's a stirring topic for someone so humble.

"You don't ever think about you in the jersey, it's always about others," Skinner says.

A Proud Barkindji woman, Jess Skinner has a deep connection to community and country. (Supplied: THRIV3)

"[But] for me, and I feel a bit emotional about it, it's representing my parents. My mum as an Aboriginal woman in this country and my dad as a Māori man coming to this country. And then my sisters and brothers.

"It's my community, the students, every team that I've coached, every male or female that's invested in me to continue to be the best version of myself.

"I think when I get into this campaign and hopefully if it is us [holding] the trophy up, I'm holding them with me."

Women coaches bring unique skills

Skinner believes the intuition she brings to the table is her superpower.

"I've got this human radar to recognise when our women are not themselves and I can action it to get the support they need.

"That genuine care that I've carried from my grassroots journey to now in the World Cup, I think that's something that's missing in coaching, particularly in the elite space."

Skinner is a prominent member of the community in Trangie, being involved in growing the game from the grassroots up. (Supplied: THRIV3)

Skinner will be the only female head coach at the upcoming World Cup, and is one of three women coaching rugby league internationally.

Roosters assistant coach Melissa Spero is leading Nigeria and former Jillaroo Meg Ward currently coaches Tonga.

Out of this year's 12 NRLW teams, Gold Coast Titans coach Karyn Murphy was the sole female head coach.

Skinner says the main things that have helped her get to where she is today are her village in Trangie, and her network of mentors.

She lists a number of male mentors, who have helped her along the way.

Loading Instagram content

"We talk about women elevating women, but we actually have a lot of great men that are elevating woman and investing in us," Skinner says.

There's also her solid network of female coaches.

"It's a small little crew and we help keep each other on track and motivated to keep pushing through," she says.

Beyond earning another trophy, Skinner says a successful World Cup campaign would result in more full-time female staff within elite rugby league, particularly NRLW.

"We've got female coaches, performance staff, physios, doctors coming through our programme and I'd loved to be able to see post World Cup, more female head coaches, head of performance, full-time within the game," she says.

"I take a large amount of pride when I'm coming through that I'm bringing others with me."

Putting the person before the player

Skinner wants every one of her players to feel valued. (Supplied: NRL Photos)

Jessica Skinner's identity as a coach can be distilled into one idea — that the person comes before the player.

"If people leave my environments and they're not feeling that sense of belonging, that hurts me more than a loss," she says.

"For a long time, I felt like [my style of coaching] wasn't elite because I had those values."

Skinner is not only out to build great rugby league players, but great women.

"Bringing your whole self to the team is why you're selected and is our superpower," she says.

And when asked what the most important part of coaching is for her, Skinner brings it back to being about others.

"I [also] hope that I show that women, mothers, Indigenous, Māori [and] coloured people can be at the elite level.

"I hope I get the opportunity to succeed this year, and stay in the role long term to keep proving that it can be done."

Tech.title: Satya Nadella says we should assume all AI models are ‘compromised’
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In a lengthy post on X, Microsoft’s CEO laid out his views on the dangers posed by highly advanced AI models and how to confront those risks. Nadella says we can no longer accept a world where AI is treated as a “set of nested black boxes” whose advice and actions we simply accept or reject. He calls for building a more transparent system where models can be contained, observed, and leaves behind “tamper-proof human readable evidence.”

Many of his recommendations align with what we’ve heard from others in the industry: timely incident disclosure, independent audits, verifiable data, and containment. It’s on that last point that he appears to go slightly farther than some others in the field, saying:

We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start. Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorized person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task. More advanced models will require more advanced containment technologies that we need to standardize on.

Unfortunately, Nadella also refers to AI as “super intelligence” throughout the post.

Tech.title: DistroKid has been quietly taking down songs in response to UMG lawsuit
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Artists are taking to social media to complain that DistroKid has unceremoniously removed their work without notice. Now DistroKid has confirmed to The Verge that the takedowns are a direct response to claims made by UMG. The label filed a lawsuit in September claiming that DistroKid has created an “AI-slop pipeline.” Artists are saying that their non-AI works are being caught up in the purge, however.

Musician and self-described “Video Game boy” McGwire reported that six of his songs had been removed from streaming. As has been the case with others, McGwire says that there was no communication from DistroKid before or after the removals, and that he had to contact the company for an explanation.
